questions.question: A CIO has drafted the IS audit charter and plans to sign it off as final authority. What should the head of internal audit's PRIMARY concern be?

options.A: External legal counsel has not yet reviewed the charter
options.B: Approval rests with the CIO rather than the audit committee
options.C: The charter does not yet define the audit reporting line
options.D: The charter does not list next year's audit subjects

questions.key_concept: The audit charter grants the audit function its authority, so it must be approved by the audit committee or board, not by auditee management.
questions.pre_read: Notice who is drafting and signing off the charter. Ask which gap would undermine the audit function's authority and independence at the root.
questions.correct_explanation: The charter is the source of the audit function's authority, so it must be approved by the audit committee or board, a level above the management being audited. A charter owned by the CIO makes audit subordinate to the auditee, however good the text is. A missing reporting line is a real gap, but it can be added; it is fixed properly only once the right body approves the charter.

wrong_explanations.A: Legal review may improve wording, but it confers no authority. Independence depends on who approves the charter, not on counsel's sign-off.
wrong_explanations.C: The reporting line matters, but it is a content gap that the audit committee would set when it approves the charter.
wrong_explanations.D: Specific audit subjects belong in the risk-based audit plan. The charter sets purpose, authority and responsibility, not a list of engagements.

tips: Eliminate: A adds legal review, which grants no authority, and D confuses the charter with the annual audit plan.
Final two: B beats C because a missing clause can be added, but approval by the auditee undermines independence at its source.
Exam cue: for charter questions, ask who approves it; the answer that restores audit committee ownership usually wins.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1001 (Audit Charter); ITAF section 1001

questions.question: An IS auditor led the engineering of a company's IAM system before moving to audit six months ago and is now assigned to audit it. What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.A: Proceed, since six months have passed since the transfer
options.B: Proceed, with an independent peer review of the audit conclusions
options.C: Reassign the engagement to an auditor with no involvement
options.D: Proceed, with the project team validating the findings

questions.key_concept: Auditing a system you designed or built is a self-review threat; removing the threat by reassignment beats mitigating it.
questions.pre_read: Notice the auditor's former role on the same system. Decide whether the threat should be mitigated or removed.
questions.correct_explanation: Leading the build of the IAM system and then auditing it is a classic self-review threat: the auditor would be judging their own design decisions. Reassigning the engagement to someone with no involvement removes the threat entirely. A peer review of conclusions is a reasonable safeguard, but the fieldwork, sampling and judgements would still come from the conflicted auditor, so the threat remains.

wrong_explanations.A: Six months does not cure self-review. The auditor would still be assessing design decisions they made personally.
wrong_explanations.B: Peer review mitigates the threat but leaves the conflicted auditor doing the fieldwork and judgements; removing the threat is stronger.
wrong_explanations.D: Letting the auditee validate findings adds a second independence problem rather than solving the first.

tips: Eliminate: A assumes time cures self-review, and D hands the auditee control over the findings.
Final two: C beats B because reassignment removes the self-review threat, while peer review only mitigates it after the work is done.
Exam cue: when a reasonable alternative auditor exists, avoiding the independence threat beats disclosing or reviewing around it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor's Professional Independence); ITAF Performance Standards on Independence; ISACA Code of Professional Ethics

questions.question: An audit function has always covered systems on a fixed three-year rotation. What is the BEST basis for the IS audit lead to select next year's audit subjects?

options.A: Continue the rotation so each system gets even coverage
options.B: Systems with the most findings in last year's audits
options.C: Systems that can be audited within the smallest budget
options.D: Systems ranked highest by a refreshed risk assessment

questions.key_concept: Risk-based audit planning selects subjects by current residual risk, refreshed each cycle, rather than by rotation, history or convenience.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word BEST and the fixed rotation. Ask which basis reflects how risk has changed since the last cycle.
questions.correct_explanation: IS audit standards call for risk-based planning: audit resources go where current residual risk is highest, and the risk assessment is refreshed each cycle to capture new systems, regulations and incidents. Prior-year findings are a useful input to that assessment, but on their own they look backward and ignore emerging risks in areas that were never audited or have changed since.

wrong_explanations.A: Rotation gives even coverage but ignores how risk has shifted; a high-risk system could wait three years.
wrong_explanations.B: Prior findings are one risk indicator. Used alone they look backward and miss new or changed high-risk systems.
wrong_explanations.C: Cost is a resourcing constraint, not a selection basis. Cheap audits of low-risk systems give the committee little assurance.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps a rotation that ignores changing risk, and C selects by cost rather than risk.
Final two: D beats B because prior findings are only one input; a refreshed risk assessment also captures new and changed risks.
Exam cue: for audit planning questions, the answer that ties selection to a current risk assessment is usually BEST.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Engagement Planning); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 9.4 (Internal Audit Plan)

questions.question: An IS auditor is testing whether an application enforces password complexity rules. Which of the following provides the MOST reliable evidence that the control is operating effectively in production?

options.A: A signed statement from the IT manager confirming the setting
options.B: Auditor inspection of the system's password parameter settings
options.C: A vendor document stating the product supports complexity rules
options.D: Auditor's own attempt to set a noncompliant password

questions.key_concept: Evidence the auditor obtains directly by observation or reperformance is more reliable than representations, documents or configuration inspection.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem asks whether the control is operating, not merely configured. Rank options by who generated the evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence the auditor obtains directly by observing or reperforming a control is the most reliable, because it does not depend on anyone else's claim. Attempting a noncompliant password and watching the system reject it proves the rule operates in production now. Inspecting parameters is strong evidence of design, but settings can be overridden by exceptions or other policies.

wrong_explanations.A: A management representation is the weakest evidence type. It is a useful starting point, never proof that a control operates.
wrong_explanations.B: Inspecting settings shows the control is configured, not that it works; exceptions or overrides could still let weak passwords through.
wrong_explanations.C: A vendor document describes product capability in general, not how this installation is configured or whether the rule is enabled.

tips: Eliminate: A is a management representation and C describes product capability, not this system's configuration.
Final two: D beats B because reperformance proves the control operates, while inspecting settings only proves it is configured.
Exam cue: for MOST reliable evidence, prefer what the auditor directly observes or reperforms over anything someone hands over.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Evidence

questions.question: An IS auditor wants to confirm that a workflow enforces second-person approval on production schedule changes. Which testing approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Substantive testing of schedule values against production output
options.B: Compliance testing of sampled changes for approval evidence
options.C: Interviews with planners about following the approval workflow
options.D: Inspection of the workflow's approval configuration settings

questions.key_concept: Compliance (control) testing shows whether a control operated over a period; substantive testing checks the accuracy of the data itself.
questions.pre_read: Notice the objective is about a control being enforced, not about data accuracy. Then ask which evidence shows it operated over time.
questions.correct_explanation: The objective is whether a control, second-person approval, is operating, so compliance testing fits. Sampling actual changes and checking each for evidence of approval shows the control operated across the period. Inspecting the configuration is useful evidence of design, but settings show only how the workflow is set up today, not whether changes were approved throughout the period.

wrong_explanations.A: Substantive testing checks whether the schedule data is correct. It does not show whether the approval control operated.
wrong_explanations.C: Inquiry alone is weak evidence. Planners describing the workflow does not prove each change was actually approved.
wrong_explanations.D: Configuration inspection shows design at one point in time, not that approvals happened on changes across the period.

tips: Eliminate: A tests data accuracy rather than the control, and C relies on inquiry, which never stands alone.
Final two: B beats D because sampling actual changes proves the control operated over time; settings show only its design today.
Exam cue: when the objective is whether a control works, choose compliance testing of a sample over design inspection.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Testing

questions.question: An IS auditor finds cardholder data stored unencrypted in a development database for over a year. To whom is it MOST appropriate to address the formal audit report?

options.A: The development manager who owns the affected database
options.B: The card brands and the company's acquiring bank
options.C: The audit committee, with copies to accountable executives
options.D: The CISO, as owner of the security program

questions.key_concept: Formal audit reports go to the governance body the audit function reports to, with copies to management accountable for remediation.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word formal. Ask which audience the audit function reports to, rather than who will fix the issue.
questions.correct_explanation: Formal audit reports are addressed to the audit committee or equivalent governance body, which oversees the audit function and holds management to account. Executives responsible for the affected systems receive copies so they can commit to remediation. The CISO is an important stakeholder and will likely act on the finding, but is part of management being reported on, not the reporting line.

wrong_explanations.A: The development manager is too low to own remediation of a year-long cardholder data exposure, and is part of the auditee.
wrong_explanations.B: External notification decisions belong to management and legal counsel. The auditor reports internally through the governance line.
wrong_explanations.D: The CISO is a key operational stakeholder, but formal reports go to the governance body overseeing audit, not one manager.

tips: Eliminate: A reports too low within the auditee, and B makes the auditor notify outsiders, which is management's decision.
Final two: C beats D because the formal report goes to the audit committee; the CISO is management, not the reporting line.
Exam cue: formal audit report addressee questions point to the audit committee or board, with accountable management copied.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 15.1 (Final Engagement Communication)

questions.question: Billing disputes average $35 across thousands each month, but the reconciliation compensating for dispute-module weaknesses ran in only 4 of the last 12 months. How should the IS auditor MOST appropriately scope the module?

options.A: Exclude it, because average dispute values are immaterial
options.B: Rely on the reconciliation for assurance over the module
options.C: Test high-value disputes above a set dollar threshold
options.D: Test the module fully, as its compensating control fails

questions.key_concept: Materiality considers aggregate volume and control reliance, not average values; a failing compensating control raises residual risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice three facts: small average values, high monthly volume and a compensating control that rarely runs. Decide which drives the scope.
questions.correct_explanation: Low average values do not make a module immaterial when volume is high and the control that compensates for its weaknesses is not operating. With the reconciliation running in only a third of months, residual risk is elevated across all disputes, not just large ones. Limiting testing to high-value disputes would miss systematic errors spread over many small items, which can aggregate to a material amount.

wrong_explanations.A: Materiality looks at aggregate volume and control reliance, not average values. Thousands of disputes monthly can add up to a material amount.
wrong_explanations.B: The reconciliation has been skipped in most months, so it cannot provide the assurance the module depends on.
wrong_explanations.C: High-value testing assumes risk sits in large items. With the compensating control failing, systematic errors across small disputes go unexamined.

tips: Eliminate: A judges materiality by average value, and B relies on a control that rarely operates.
Final two: D beats C because a failed compensating control exposes every dispute; a value threshold misses systematic small-item errors.
Exam cue: when a compensating control is not operating, residual risk rises; expand scope rather than narrowing it by value.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1204 (Materiality); ITAF Performance Standards on Materiality and Risk

questions.question: An IS auditor tests a compensating control requiring an independent peer review of every privileged session. Which finding represents the GREATEST risk?

options.A: Some sessions were reviewed by the session holder
options.B: Many reviews contain only generic, boilerplate approval text
options.C: A small percentage of review tickets remain open
options.D: The review closure target was set below 100 percent

questions.key_concept: When a compensating control relies on independent review, a self-review breaks segregation of duties and creates false assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word independent in the stem. Ask which finding removes the element that makes the control work at all.
questions.correct_explanation: The control's value depends on segregation of duties: someone other than the session holder reviews the activity. A self-review removes that element entirely, so the control provides no assurance while still appearing complete in metrics. Boilerplate notes weaken review quality, but an independent person still looked at the session.

wrong_explanations.B: Boilerplate notes degrade review quality and evidence, but an independent reviewer was still involved, so segregation of duties is preserved.
wrong_explanations.C: Open tickets are visible exceptions that management can track and chase. The risk is small and already detectable.
wrong_explanations.D: A target below 100 percent is a design choice open to management view. It does not create hidden false assurance.

tips: Eliminate: C is a small, visible exception, and D is an openly known target-setting choice.
Final two: A beats B because self-review removes segregation of duties entirely, while boilerplate review is weak but still independent.
Exam cue: when a control relies on a second person, a breach of that independence outranks poor quality of the review.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1203 (Performance and Supervision); COBIT MEA02; NIST SP 800-53 AC-6 (Least Privilege) + AU-6 (Audit Review)

questions.question: The audit committee wants high confidence that a manual eligibility-review control over financial-aid disbursements operates effectively. Which sampling approach is MOST appropriate for the IS auditor?

options.A: Statistical attribute sampling sized for the required confidence
options.B: Stratified sampling weighted toward the highest-dollar grants
options.C: Judgmental sampling of items the auditor considers risky
options.D: A fixed sample of 25 items regardless of population

questions.key_concept: Testing a control for a stated confidence level calls for statistical attribute sampling, which measures deviation rates and supports projection.
questions.pre_read: Notice two facts: the test is of a control, and the committee wants a stated confidence. Match the sampling method to both.
questions.correct_explanation: The objective is a control test with a required confidence level. Statistical attribute sampling measures the rate of control deviations and lets the auditor size the sample to support a defensible conclusion at that confidence. Stratifying by dollar value is a strong technique for substantive testing of amounts, but this question asks how often the eligibility review fails, which is a rate, not a value.

wrong_explanations.B: Dollar stratification suits substantive testing of balances. A control test measures how often the control fails, regardless of amount.
wrong_explanations.C: Judgmental samples can target risk but cannot be projected statistically, so they cannot deliver a stated confidence level.
wrong_explanations.D: A fixed size chosen without reference to confidence or tolerable rate cannot support the high assurance the committee asked for.

tips: Eliminate: C cannot be projected statistically, and D is not sized to any confidence level or tolerable rate.
Final two: A beats B because a control test measures a deviation rate; dollar weighting suits substantive tests of amounts.
Exam cue: control test plus required confidence points to attribute sampling; testing amounts points to variable or stratified sampling.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Sampling; AICPA AU-C 530 (Audit Sampling)

questions.question: During fieldwork, an IS auditor finds repeated high-value payments processed through an emergency override, all initiated and approved by the same two employees. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Interview both employees to obtain their explanations
options.B: Expand testing to all override transactions for the year
options.C: Disable the emergency override until the matter is resolved
options.D: Document the facts and escalate per fraud procedures

questions.key_concept: On finding fraud indicators, the IS auditor first documents facts and escalates through the fraud-response procedure, not investigating alone.
questions.pre_read: Notice the red flags suggest collusion and the stem says FIRST. Ask who is authorized to investigate before more testing happens.
questions.correct_explanation: Indicators of possible fraud should be documented factually and escalated through the established fraud-response channel, typically the chief audit executive, so investigation is properly authorized and evidence is preserved. The IS auditor's role is to detect and report, not to investigate independently. Expanding the sample is a sound later step, but acting before escalation risks working without authority or alerting suspects.

wrong_explanations.A: Approaching the suspects alerts them, risks evidence destruction and draws the auditor into an investigation they are not authorized to run.
wrong_explanations.B: Expanding the sample may be appropriate, but only after escalation, so scope and investigative approach are properly authorized.
wrong_explanations.C: Disabling a system function is a management decision. An auditor who changes operations loses independence.

tips: Eliminate: A tips off the suspects, and C has the auditor changing operations, which is management's decision.
Final two: D beats B because escalation must come first; more testing is valid only once the right authority directs it.
Exam cue: suspected fraud plus FIRST almost always means document and escalate, never confront or investigate alone.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1207 (Irregularities and Illegal Acts); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 3.1 (Competency); ISA 240 (The Auditor's Responsibilities Relating to Fraud)

questions.question: Before fieldwork on a new payments platform, the CAE asks an IS auditor to prepare an audit program. What is the PRIMARY purpose of the audit program?

options.A: Notify management in advance of the areas to be tested
options.B: Define planned procedures so work is consistent and supervisable
options.C: Set the engagement's budget and deadline for cost control
options.D: State the engagement objectives and scope agreed with stakeholders

questions.key_concept: An audit program sets out the procedures to be performed, guiding consistent fieldwork, supervision and a record of work done.
questions.pre_read: Notice the program is prepared just before fieldwork. Ask what fieldwork staff and supervisors need from it.
questions.correct_explanation: The audit program translates the engagement's objectives into step-by-step procedures. It guides staff through fieldwork, lets the supervisor review the plan and check that the work followed it, and leaves a record of what was done. Objectives and scope are set earlier in engagement planning; the program depends on them but its purpose is to define how they will be tested.

wrong_explanations.A: Advance notice to management may happen through an engagement letter, but it is not the purpose of the program.
wrong_explanations.C: Budgets and deadlines are set in engagement planning and resourcing. The program describes procedures, not cost controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Objectives and scope come from the engagement plan. The program sets out the procedures that will address them.

tips: Eliminate: A is a courtesy notice to the auditee, and C is a resourcing matter, not the program's purpose.
Final two: B beats D because objectives and scope are set first; the program defines the procedures that test them.
Exam cue: plan sets the why and what; program sets the how. Match the document to the question it answers.

questions.question: An IS auditor reviews a fraud-scoring engine that rates card payments and blocks suspicious ones before they complete. How is this control BEST classified?

options.A: Preventive control
options.B: Detective control
options.C: Corrective control
options.D: Compensating control

questions.key_concept: Controls are classified by when they act: preventive before the event, detective after it occurs, corrective to repair its effects.
questions.pre_read: Notice when the engine acts relative to the loss. Classify by the effect on the transaction, not by the technique used.
questions.correct_explanation: Classification depends on when a control acts. The engine blocks suspicious payments before they complete, so the fraudulent loss never occurs, which makes it preventive. It does identify suspicious activity, which tempts a detective label, but detective controls report events that have already happened, leaving the loss to be corrected later. Stopping the transaction is what decides the classification.

wrong_explanations.B: Detective controls identify events after they have occurred. This engine stops the transaction before any loss happens.
wrong_explanations.C: Corrective controls repair effects after an event, such as refunds or restores. Nothing has occurred yet to correct.
wrong_explanations.D: Compensating controls substitute for a missing or weak primary control. Nothing suggests this engine stands in for another control.

tips: Eliminate: C repairs harm after the event, and D substitutes for a missing control, which the stem does not describe.
Final two: A beats B because the engine blocks the payment before loss; detective controls only report events already completed.
Exam cue: classify by timing and effect; if the control stops the event from completing, it is preventive.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 (Control Categories); NIST Cybersecurity Framework (NIST CSF) v2.0 (February 2024); ITAF Performance Standards on Control Evaluation

questions.question: A CIO calls a 24/7 anomaly-detection tool a 'continuous auditing' capability; its alerts go to IT operations for response. What is the IS auditor's MOST appropriate observation?

options.A: The label fits, as detection runs automatically around the clock
options.B: The tool needs audit committee approval before it continues
options.C: It is continuous monitoring, since operations owns the response
options.D: It becomes continuous auditing once auditors can read alerts

questions.key_concept: Continuous monitoring is management's operational control; continuous auditing is performed by the audit function for independent assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice who receives and acts on the alerts. Classify the capability by owner and purpose, not by technology.
questions.correct_explanation: The difference between continuous auditing and continuous monitoring is ownership and purpose, not technology. A tool whose alerts are handled by IT operations is a management control, which is continuous monitoring. Giving auditors read access does not change that; continuous auditing is designed and run by the audit function to provide independent assurance, although auditors may assess and rely on management's monitoring.

wrong_explanations.A: Running automatically around the clock describes the technique, not the owner. Both monitoring and auditing can run continuously.
wrong_explanations.B: Operational tools are management's decision. The audit committee oversees audit, not approval of management's monitoring tools.
wrong_explanations.D: Read access lets auditors use the output, but operations still owns the tool and response, so it remains monitoring.

tips: Eliminate: A labels by technology, and B misplaces approval of operational tools with the audit committee.
Final two: C beats D because ownership defines the capability; read access does not turn management's monitoring into audit work.
Exam cue: who owns and acts on it decides the label; management runs monitoring, the audit function runs auditing.

questions.question: A supervisor is reviewing an IS auditor's work papers for an access-control review before sign-off. What is the MOST important quality for the supervisor to verify?

options.A: They follow the department's standard formatting template
options.B: They cite each applicable ISACA standard by number
options.C: They show every audit program step marked as completed
options.D: They hold sufficient evidence to support each conclusion

questions.key_concept: Work papers must contain sufficient, appropriate evidence for a reviewer to trace every conclusion back to its support.
questions.pre_read: Notice the supervisor is reviewing before sign-off. Ask what would make the audit opinion indefensible if it were missing.
questions.correct_explanation: Work papers exist so an independent reviewer can trace each conclusion back to sufficient, appropriate evidence. Without that, the opinion cannot be defended to the committee or a regulator. Completed program steps show the planned work was performed, which a supervisor does check, but a step can be ticked off while the evidence gathered still fails to support the conclusion drawn from it.

wrong_explanations.A: Consistent formatting helps readability but says nothing about whether the conclusions are supported.
wrong_explanations.B: Citing standards by number is not required and does not show the work met them.
wrong_explanations.C: Completed steps show work was done, not that the evidence obtained actually supports each conclusion.

tips: Eliminate: A is presentation, and B is citation housekeeping; neither shows the conclusions are supported.
Final two: D beats C because a ticked step proves activity, while sufficient evidence proves the conclusion.
Exam cue: for work paper review, the winning answer links each conclusion to sufficient, appropriate evidence.

questions.question: Management reports that all findings from a prior IS audit have been remediated. What is the PRIMARY purpose of the auditor's follow-up?

options.A: Re-perform the original audit program in full
options.B: Verify the agreed corrective actions were implemented
options.C: Help management design any remaining corrective actions
options.D: Issue a revised audit opinion on the audited area

questions.key_concept: Audit follow-up independently verifies that agreed corrective actions were implemented; it is narrower than a new audit or opinion.
questions.pre_read: Notice that management has only reported remediation. Ask what the auditor must independently confirm, and how wide the scope should be.
questions.correct_explanation: Follow-up is a verification procedure bounded by the original findings. The auditor independently confirms that each agreed corrective action has actually been implemented, rather than relying on management's self-report. It is deliberately narrower than a new audit; repeating the full program or forming a fresh opinion belongs to a separate engagement planned through the risk-based audit plan.

wrong_explanations.A: Re-performing the whole program is a new audit. Follow-up targets only the agreed remediation for the reported findings.
wrong_explanations.C: Designing corrective actions is management's responsibility. An auditor who designs fixes impairs objectivity when later assessing them.
wrong_explanations.D: A revised opinion needs a full new engagement. Follow-up reports on remediation status, not a fresh opinion.

tips: Eliminate: C has the auditor designing fixes, which is management's job, and D requires a full new engagement.
Final two: B beats A because follow-up is scoped to the agreed actions; re-running the whole program is a new audit, not follow-up.
Exam cue: when management says it is fixed, the auditor's job is to verify independently, not to trust or redo everything.

questions.question: A regional CFO repeatedly pressures the IS audit team to drop a critical finding before the report reaches the audit committee. What is the auditor's BEST action?

options.A: Escalate the pressure to the audit committee chair
options.B: Remove the finding to preserve the working relationship
options.C: Soften the finding's wording to avoid alarming readers
options.D: Record the CFO's objection in the management response

questions.key_concept: Management pressure to suppress findings threatens audit independence and is escalated to the audit committee, which protects that independence.
questions.pre_read: Notice the CFO wants the finding gone, not corrected. Ask who has authority to protect the audit function from that pressure.
questions.correct_explanation: Management has no authority to remove audit findings, and pressure to suppress one is itself an independence threat. The audit committee chair is the right escalation point because the committee oversees the audit function and protects its independence. Recording the CFO's objection is normal when management disputes facts, but here it leaves the suppression attempt unaddressed and unknown to the body that must know.

wrong_explanations.B: Dropping a critical finding under pressure abandons independence and leaves the audit committee unaware of a significant risk.
wrong_explanations.C: Softening a critical finding to avoid alarm distorts its significance; the committee needs an accurate picture of risk.
wrong_explanations.D: Management responses capture factual disagreement, but they do not address an attempt to suppress the finding.

tips: Eliminate: B suppresses the finding, and C dilutes it; both give in to the pressure.
Final two: A beats D because a suppression attempt is an independence threat that must reach the committee; noting disagreement leaves it hidden.
Exam cue: when management pressures audit over findings, escalate to the body that oversees audit, usually the audit committee.

questions.question: A firm's trading algorithms feed positions directly into its regulatory financial filings. What is the GREATEST consideration for the CAE when choosing an integrated audit over separate IT and financial audits?

options.A: Lower cost and disruption from running a single engagement
options.B: Dependence of financial reporting on the IT controls
options.C: The audit committee's preference from prior years
options.D: Each team's familiarity with the other's methods

questions.key_concept: An integrated audit is chosen mainly because IT controls and financial reporting are interdependent; separate audits can leave gaps at the boundary.
questions.pre_read: Notice that IT outputs flow straight into financial filings. Ask what risk separate audits would leave unaddressed.
questions.correct_explanation: When IT controls directly produce financial reporting outputs, separate audits risk a gap at the boundary: the IT audit tests the algorithm, the financial audit tests the filings, and neither tests how one feeds the other. That interdependency is what justifies an integrated approach. Lower cost and disruption are real benefits of a combined engagement, but they are by-products, not the basis for the decision.

wrong_explanations.A: Efficiency is a welcome benefit, but choosing an approach for cost rather than risk coverage puts convenience ahead of assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Past preference does not reflect the current platform's risk profile, which should drive the engagement design.
wrong_explanations.D: Team familiarity is a delivery challenge that training and planning can solve; it does not decide whether integration is needed.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on habit, and D is a team-readiness issue rather than a scoping driver.
Final two: B beats A because control interdependency drives coverage; lower cost is a by-product, not the reason.
Exam cue: integrated audit questions turn on interdependency; when IT outputs feed financial reporting, test them together.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Engagement Planning); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 9.5 (Coordination and Reliance); ITAF Performance Standards on Integrated Audits

questions.question: An IS audit team uses a vendor AI tool to flag suspicious access events, but the vendor cannot explain how its model classifies them. What is the GREATEST risk in relying on it?

options.A: Flagged events are a small share of total access events
options.B: Investigating false positives consumes audit staff time
options.C: Auditors cannot explain or defend conclusions drawn from it
options.D: Auditors may defer to the tool over their own judgement

questions.key_concept: Evidence from an automated tool is only as reliable as the auditor's understanding of how it works; unexplainable output cannot support conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Notice the vendor cannot explain the model. Ask what that does to the quality of evidence the auditor can rely on.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit evidence must be sufficient and reliable, and the auditor must be able to explain how each conclusion was reached. If the tool's logic cannot be explained, the auditor cannot assess its reliability or defend conclusions built on it. Over-reliance on the tool is a real behavioural risk, but it is a symptom; the core problem is that the evidence itself cannot be validated.

wrong_explanations.A: A small flagged share is expected of an anomaly tool and does not by itself indicate a problem.
wrong_explanations.B: Some false positives are normal. Wasted effort is an efficiency cost, not a threat to the validity of conclusions.
wrong_explanations.D: Over-reliance is a concern, but even careful auditors cannot validate evidence from a model whose logic is opaque.

tips: Eliminate: A describes normal anomaly-tool behaviour, and B is an efficiency cost rather than an evidence problem.
Final two: C beats D because opaque logic undermines the evidence itself; over-reliance is a behaviour that follows from it.
Exam cue: with any audit tool, the auditor must understand and be able to defend how its output was produced.

questions.question: An IS auditor tests 25 of 6,800 privileged-access transactions and finds 2 failures (8%) against a 1% tolerable rate. What is the auditor's MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: Pass the control, since just two items failed
options.B: Conclude the control is not operating effectively
options.C: Expand the sample to refine the deviation-rate estimate before concluding
options.D: Ask the audit committee to raise the tolerable rate

questions.key_concept: When the sample deviation rate clearly exceeds the tolerable rate, the auditor cannot rely on the control and evaluates the deviations' cause.
questions.pre_read: Compare the sample rate with the tolerable rate. Ask whether more testing could realistically change the conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: An 8% sample deviation rate against a 1% tolerable rate means the auditor cannot rely on the control, whatever allowance is made for sampling risk. The auditor concludes it is not operating effectively, evaluates the cause and nature of the deviations, and adjusts substantive work. Extending suits results near the threshold; even a far larger sample would almost certainly leave the upper deviation limit above 1%.

wrong_explanations.A: Two failures in 25 is an 8% rate, eight times the tolerable rate. Absolute counts are not the test.
wrong_explanations.C: Extension helps when results are borderline. With 8% against 1%, more items would only delay an inevitable conclusion.
wrong_explanations.D: Tolerable rates are set before testing from risk. Changing them to fit results undermines the whole test.

tips: Eliminate: A judges by raw count, not rate, and D moves the threshold to fit the result.
Final two: B beats C because extending a sample helps only near the threshold; 8% against 1% is already conclusive.
Exam cue: if the sample rate already exceeds the tolerable rate by a wide margin, conclude rather than keep sampling.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Sampling; AICPA AU-C 530 (Audit Sampling)

questions.question: An IS auditor reduced independent testing because business-unit control self-assessments rate controls as effective, yet security incidents keep occurring. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: Self-assessment is replacing, not supplementing, audit testing
options.B: Self-assessors lack sufficient technical expertise in IS controls
options.C: The incidents indicate widespread fraud across the business units
options.D: Self-assessment programs are inherently unsuitable for assessing IS controls

questions.key_concept: Control self-assessment complements but never replaces independent audit assurance, especially when self-reports conflict with actual outcomes.
questions.pre_read: Notice two facts: the auditor reduced testing, and results contradict incidents. Look for the root cause, not a symptom.
questions.correct_explanation: Control self-assessment complements independent audit work; it cannot replace it. Here self-reported results contradict actual incidents, yet the audit function has stepped back, so no one is providing reliable assurance. That structural over-reliance is the root concern. Weak assessor expertise is a real contributing cause, but even expert self-assessors would not justify replacing independent testing.

wrong_explanations.B: Limited expertise contributes to unreliable results, but it is a cause, not the core problem of reduced independent assurance.
wrong_explanations.C: Incidents may stem from errors, misconfiguration or training gaps. Nothing in the stem establishes fraud.
wrong_explanations.D: Control self-assessment remains a useful complementary tool. Abandoning it overcorrects; the fix is restoring independent testing alongside it.

tips: Eliminate: C jumps to fraud without evidence, and D overcorrects by discarding a useful tool.
Final two: A beats B because over-reliance on self-assessment is the root cause; assessor skill is only one contributing factor.
Exam cue: control self-assessment supplements independent assurance and never replaces it; look for the option naming that over-reliance.

questions.question: A new IS audit team member asks how ITAF relates to ISACA's audit Standards and Guidelines. Which explanation from the senior auditor is BEST?

options.A: ITAF contains the Standards, Guidelines, and Tools and Techniques
options.B: ITAF is guidance explaining how to apply the separate ISACA Standards
options.C: ITAF is a checklist auditors complete before fieldwork begins
options.D: ITAF is technical guidance for operating audit software tools

questions.key_concept: ITAF is ISACA's umbrella framework containing mandatory Standards, supporting Guidelines and informational Tools and Techniques.
questions.pre_read: Notice the question is about the relationship between the parts. Decide whether ITAF sits beside the Standards or around them.
questions.correct_explanation: ITAF is ISACA's umbrella professional-practices framework for IT audit and assurance. It contains the mandatory Standards, the Guidelines that support applying them, and Tools and Techniques that give practical examples. Describing ITAF as guidance on applying separate Standards confuses the whole with one of its parts: that is the role of the Guidelines, and the Standards sit inside ITAF rather than outside it.

wrong_explanations.B: Explaining how to apply Standards is the Guidelines' role. ITAF is the framework that contains both, not a separate guidance layer.
wrong_explanations.C: ITAF is a professional-practices framework covering the whole engagement, not a pre-fieldwork checklist.
wrong_explanations.D: ITAF addresses audit practice broadly; it is not a manual for operating audit software.

tips: Eliminate: C shrinks ITAF to a checklist, and D confuses it with software operating guidance.
Final two: A beats B because the Standards sit inside ITAF; guidance on applying them describes the Guidelines layer.
Exam cue: in ITAF, Standards are mandatory, Guidelines support them, and Tools and Techniques illustrate them, all in one framework.

questions.subtopic: Effect of Laws and Regulations on Audit Planning
questions.question: A cross-border data-transfer law takes effect in six months and will affect a logistics company's daily shipping data flows. What is the IS auditor's BEST action for the upcoming audit plan?

options.A: Wait until the law is in force, then test compliance
options.B: Interpret the law independently and add tailored tests
options.C: Confirm its impact with legal and compliance, then adjust scope
options.D: Recommend that external counsel own the compliance response

questions.key_concept: The IS auditor must understand regulatory impact for planning, but relies on legal and compliance for interpretation rather than reading the law alone.
questions.pre_read: Notice the law is not yet in force. Ask who should interpret it and when the audit plan should respond.
questions.correct_explanation: The auditor must consider laws and regulations that affect the audit subject when planning, and six months gives time to build them into scope. Legal interpretation, however, belongs to legal and compliance. Interpreting the law alone risks testing against a misreading and puts the auditor in a role they are not qualified for, so coordinating first and then adjusting scope is better.

wrong_explanations.A: Waiting forfeits the chance to assess readiness and leaves the plan reacting to non-compliance after the fact.
wrong_explanations.B: The auditor needs to understand the law, but solo interpretation risks a misreading; legal and compliance own interpretation.
wrong_explanations.D: Compliance remains management's responsibility. The auditor's task here is to adjust the audit plan, not to assign ownership.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores a known upcoming risk, and D shifts the question away from the audit plan.
Final two: C beats B because legal and compliance own interpretation; the auditor translates their view into audit scope.
Exam cue: for new regulations, the auditor coordinates with legal and compliance, then reflects the impact in the risk-based plan.

questions.question: The COO asks an IS auditor whether strong internal controls over content distribution will guarantee no operational incidents. What is the auditor's MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Yes, well-designed controls prevent every operational incident
options.B: No, they give reasonable assurance, not absolute prevention
options.C: No, internal controls cover financial reporting, not operations
options.D: No, because management override can defeat the controls

questions.key_concept: Internal controls provide reasonable, not absolute, assurance over operations, reporting and compliance objectives because of inherent limitations.
questions.pre_read: Notice the COO asks about a guarantee. Look for the answer that states the general principle, not one example.
questions.correct_explanation: Internal controls provide reasonable assurance that objectives in operations, reporting and compliance will be met; they reduce risk to an acceptable level but cannot eliminate it. Management override is a real inherent limitation and part of the reason, but it is only one of several, alongside human error, collusion and cost-benefit trade-offs. The principle of reasonable assurance answers the COO completely.

wrong_explanations.A: No set of controls eliminates risk entirely; inherent limitations such as human error and collusion always remain.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal control frameworks cover operations and compliance objectives as well as financial reporting.
wrong_explanations.D: Override is one inherent limitation, but the full answer is the broader principle of reasonable assurance.

tips: Eliminate: A promises absolute prevention, and C wrongly limits internal control to financial reporting.
Final two: B beats D because reasonable assurance is the governing principle; management override is just one limitation behind it.
Exam cue: when a question asks if controls guarantee an outcome, look for reasonable assurance rather than one specific limitation.

questions.question: Before fieldwork on a pipeline-monitoring system, the CAE asks an IS auditor to define engagement objectives. What is the PRIMARY purpose of well-defined audit objectives?

options.A: Document the auditor's credentials and independence for the committee
options.B: Estimate the budget and staff hours for management's approval
options.C: State what the audit must determine, anchoring procedures and conclusions
options.D: List the specific test steps fieldwork will perform on each control

questions.key_concept: Audit objectives state what the engagement must determine; scope, procedures, evidence and conclusions all trace back to them.
questions.pre_read: Notice objectives come before fieldwork. Ask what everything later in the engagement needs to trace back to.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit objectives state what the engagement must determine, such as whether access to the system enforces segregation of duties. Every procedure should trace back to an objective and every conclusion should answer one. Listing specific test steps is the job of the audit program, which is built from the objectives; without clear objectives first, the steps have nothing to anchor them.

wrong_explanations.A: Credentials and independence are addressed elsewhere in quality and engagement records, not by the objectives.
wrong_explanations.B: Budget and staffing follow from objectives and scope but are a resourcing output, not the objectives' purpose.
wrong_explanations.D: Detailed test steps belong in the audit program, which is derived from the objectives rather than replacing them.

tips: Eliminate: A concerns auditor credentials, and B is a resourcing estimate that follows from planning.
Final two: C beats D because objectives define what must be concluded; test steps belong to the audit program built from them.
Exam cue: objectives state what the audit must determine; the program states how. Pick the answer at the right level.

questions.question: An IS auditor will interview IT staff and front-desk users to understand how a new property-management system's controls operate. Which interviewing approach is MOST effective?

options.A: Read questions from a fixed script to avoid bias
options.B: Confirm conclusions already drawn from the documentation review
options.C: Use a standard yes-or-no checklist for consistency
options.D: Review documentation first, then ask open-ended questions

questions.key_concept: Effective audit interviews combine preparation with open-ended questions and active listening to reveal how controls really operate.
questions.pre_read: Notice the goal is to understand how controls operate in practice. Ask which approach surfaces detail interviewees would not volunteer.
questions.correct_explanation: Preparing by reviewing documentation and prior findings lets the auditor ask informed questions. Open-ended questions and active listening then let staff describe the process in their own words, exposing workarounds and inconsistencies. A yes-or-no checklist offers consistency across many interviewees, but closed questions invite the expected answer and miss how controls actually operate, which is exactly what the auditor needs to learn.

wrong_explanations.A: A rigid script prevents follow-up on surprising answers, so important nuance and inconsistencies go unexplored.
wrong_explanations.B: Seeking confirmation of early conclusions introduces confirmation bias and defeats the purpose of interviewing.
wrong_explanations.C: Closed questions are consistent but invite expected answers and miss how staff actually perform the controls.

tips: Eliminate: A blocks follow-up questions, and B builds confirmation bias into the interviews.
Final two: D beats C because open, prepared questioning reveals how controls really work; closed checklists invite scripted answers.
Exam cue: for interviews, prefer preparation plus open-ended questions and active listening over rigid formats.

questions.question: An IS auditor is testing the integrity of a gaming platform that processes 3 million microtransactions daily. Which reason BEST justifies using CAATs for this engagement?

options.A: The volume makes manual testing of transactions impractical
options.B: Tools can replace the auditor's professional judgement
options.C: Standards require CAATs on every engagement
options.D: Automated tools reduce the engagement's cost and hours

questions.key_concept: CAATs add most value when objectives involve large volumes, full-population testing or pattern detection that manual testing cannot achieve.
questions.pre_read: Notice the transaction volume. Ask what the audit objective requires that manual methods cannot deliver.
questions.correct_explanation: CAATs are justified when the audit objective needs analysis that manual testing cannot achieve, such as full-population tests or pattern detection across very large volumes. Three million transactions a day is squarely that case. Lower cost and effort often follow, but efficiency is a by-product; the decision is driven by what the objective requires, and CAATs can sometimes cost more than manual sampling.

wrong_explanations.B: CAATs support professional judgement; the auditor still designs the tests, interprets results and draws conclusions.
wrong_explanations.C: No standard mandates CAATs on every engagement. Their use depends on the objective and the data available.
wrong_explanations.D: Efficiency is a welcome side effect, but CAATs are chosen because the objective requires them, not to save money.

tips: Eliminate: B hands judgement to a tool, and C invents a universal requirement that standards do not impose.
Final two: A beats D because the objective's need for volume analysis justifies CAATs; savings are a by-product.
Exam cue: high volumes or full-population and pattern testing point to CAATs; judgement always stays with the auditor.

questions.question: An IS auditor must rate risk for three systems: one with five years of incident data and two newer ones with little or none. Which risk-assessment approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Quantitative ratings for each, extrapolating where data is sparse
options.B: Quantitative for the data-rich system, qualitative for the others
options.C: Qualitative ratings for every system to keep results consistent
options.D: Defer rating the newer systems until data accumulates

questions.key_concept: The risk-assessment technique should match data availability: quantitative where reliable history exists, qualitative where it is sparse.
questions.pre_read: Notice how much data each system has. Ask whether one technique fits all three without losing accuracy.
questions.correct_explanation: Quantitative methods need reliable historical data, which only the first system has; there, they give defensible, precise ratings. For the newer systems, extrapolating numbers from little data creates false precision, so qualitative ratings are more honest. Rating everything qualitatively keeps results uniform, but it throws away five years of good data and makes the most mature system's rating less precise than it could be.

wrong_explanations.A: Extrapolating numbers from sparse or absent data gives an appearance of precision the evidence cannot support.
wrong_explanations.C: Uniformity is convenient, but discarding reliable historical data reduces the accuracy of the data-rich system's rating.
wrong_explanations.D: New systems often carry the most uncertainty; leaving them unrated leaves gaps in the plan.

tips: Eliminate: A manufactures precision from missing data, and D leaves the newest systems unassessed.
Final two: B beats C because matching technique to data keeps precision where it exists; uniformity sacrifices it.
Exam cue: quantitative needs reliable data; when data quality varies, a hybrid approach is usually the most appropriate.

questions.question: IT staff surveys show 60% fear retaliation for raising security concerns, and most incidents are discovered by outsiders, though policies are comprehensive. What is the IS auditor's GREATEST concern about the control environment?

options.A: A culture that discourages staff from speaking up
options.B: Monitoring tools that fail to detect incidents internally
options.C: Policies too detailed for IT staff to follow in practice
options.D: The cost of maintaining such comprehensive policy documents

questions.key_concept: The control environment underpins all other controls; a culture where staff fear reporting undermines controls however well documented.
questions.pre_read: Notice the link between retaliation fear and outsiders finding incidents. Look for the root cause, not a symptom.
questions.correct_explanation: The control environment is the foundation of every other control. When most staff fear retaliation, incidents go unreported, which explains why outsiders discover them first. Weak monitoring tools could also explain late detection, but the survey points to people who see problems and stay silent; better tools would not fix a culture where findings are suppressed, and comprehensive policies cannot compensate.

wrong_explanations.B: Tool gaps may exist, but the survey shows staff who see problems stay silent; better tools would not change that.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing indicates the policies are unusable. Their comprehensiveness is a strength, though it cannot offset a weak culture.
wrong_explanations.D: Documentation cost is an efficiency matter and does not explain why incidents go unreported.

tips: Eliminate: C invents a usability problem the stem does not show, and D is a cost issue unrelated to the risk.
Final two: A beats B because fear of reporting is the root cause of external discovery; tools address only a symptom.
Exam cue: in control environment questions, culture and tone outweigh documentation; strong policies cannot fix fear of speaking up.

questions.question: A credit-scoring model is retrained monthly, engineering ships weekly, and the audit committee wants earlier assurance. Which approach is MOST appropriate for the IS audit team?

options.A: Defer the audit until the model stops changing monthly
options.B: Outsource the engagement to an external audit firm
options.C: An agile audit delivering assurance in short sprints
options.D: A traditional audit cycle with an interim progress update

questions.key_concept: Agile auditing suits fast-changing subjects, agile organizations and stakeholders who want frequent, incremental assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice three facts: monthly change, weekly releases and a request for earlier assurance. Match the audit cadence to them.
questions.correct_explanation: All three facts favour agile auditing: the subject changes monthly, engineering works in short cycles, and the committee wants earlier assurance. Short sprints with incremental reporting keep conclusions current. A traditional cycle with an interim update offers some earlier visibility, but the main conclusions would still arrive months later, after several retrains, describing a model that no longer exists.

wrong_explanations.A: A continuously retrained model may never stabilize, and deferring leaves the committee without the assurance it requested.
wrong_explanations.B: Outsourcing changes who audits, not the cadence; a traditional cycle run by any firm would still deliver stale conclusions.
wrong_explanations.D: An interim update helps, but the main conclusions still lag several retrains behind the model in production.

tips: Eliminate: A waits for stability that may never come, and B changes the auditor without changing the cadence.
Final two: C beats D because sprints keep pace with monthly change; an interim update still leaves conclusions stale.
Exam cue: fast-changing subject plus requests for earlier assurance point to agile auditing over a traditional cycle.

questions.question: An audit function's QA program relies on annual self-assessments by team leads, and its last external review was 12 years ago. What is the GREATEST weakness for the IS audit lead to report?

options.A: Reviews cover documentation but not fieldwork techniques
options.B: The program has not been redesigned in over a decade
options.C: Self-assessments raise few findings each year
options.D: No independent review has validated the QA program

questions.key_concept: A QA program needs periodic independent external assessment; self-assessment alone gives the audit committee unverified, potentially false assurance.
questions.pre_read: Notice who performs the reviews and when outsiders last looked. Ask which gap lets every other weakness go unnoticed.
questions.correct_explanation: A quality assurance program needs both internal assessment and periodic independent external review, commonly at least every five years. With only self-assessment by the people being assessed and no outside review for 12 years, the committee's assurance rests on self-attestation. Narrow review scope is a real gap, but without independent challenge no one objective is positioned to detect it or any other weakness.

wrong_explanations.A: Narrow scope matters, but an independent reviewer would identify it; the lack of independence is the deeper, enabling weakness.
wrong_explanations.B: Age alone is not a weakness. A long-running program can remain effective if it is independently validated.
wrong_explanations.C: Few findings may reflect good performance or weak self-review; it is a symptom to investigate, not the weakness itself.

tips: Eliminate: B treats age as a defect, and C reads a low finding count as a weakness in itself.
Final two: D beats A because missing independent review lets every gap, including scope, go undetected.
Exam cue: for QA programs, independence of review outranks scope or format; self-assessment alone gives false assurance.

questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit QA program weaknesses — self-assessment without independent review = false assurance'. Public source: IIA International Standards 1300 and 1312. questions.question: A client's CFO offers an IS audit manager's firm a future advisory contract if a damaging finding is removed. If the manager removes it, which ISACA Code principle is MOST directly violated?

options.A: Maintain competency and keep knowledge current in relevant fields
options.B: Support the professional education of stakeholders and the public
options.C: Perform duties with objectivity, due diligence and professional care
options.D: Disclose all significant facts when reporting work results

questions.key_concept: Removing a finding for an inducement breaches the ISACA Code's duty to disclose all significant facts that would otherwise distort reported results.
questions.pre_read: Notice what the CFO wants removed. Ask which principle covers what must appear in reported results.
questions.correct_explanation: Removing a damaging finding to win future business withholds a significant fact. The Code's requirement to inform appropriate parties of all significant facts, so results are not distorted, addresses this directly. Objectivity is also compromised by the inducement, but that principle governs how work is performed; removing the finding specifically corrupts what is reported.

wrong_explanations.A: Competency concerns skills and knowledge. Nothing suggests the manager lacks ability; the problem is misconduct.
wrong_explanations.B: Supporting stakeholder education is a separate obligation and has no bearing on an inducement to suppress a finding.
wrong_explanations.C: Objectivity is impaired by the inducement, but the act requested, suppressing a finding, falls most directly under the duty to disclose significant facts.

tips: Eliminate: A is about skills, and B concerns stakeholder education; neither addresses an inducement.
Final two: D beats C because removing the finding hides a significant fact; objectivity covers bias in performing the work.
Exam cue: suppressing or distorting findings points to the duty to disclose significant facts; bias in fieldwork points to objectivity.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (disclosure of significant facts; objectivity); ITAF General Standards

questions.subtopic: Using the Work of Other Experts
questions.question: An IS auditor without cryptographic expertise engages an external cryptographer to assess an encryption design. What should the auditor do FIRST before relying on the cryptographer's conclusions?

options.A: Obtain a signed confidentiality agreement from the cryptographer
options.B: Evaluate the cryptographer's competence and objectivity
options.C: Reperform a sample of the cryptographer's tests
options.D: Have the cryptographer report directly to the audit committee

questions.key_concept: Before relying on an expert, the IS auditor assesses competence, objectivity and relevance of the work, and keeps responsibility for conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Notice the auditor lacks the expertise. Ask what makes someone else's work safe to rely on.
questions.correct_explanation: Before relying on an expert's work, the IS auditor must assess the expert's competence, objectivity and the relevance of the work, because the auditor keeps responsibility for the conclusion. Reperforming tests can add assurance, but an auditor without cryptographic skill cannot reperform them meaningfully, and reperformance does not show the expert was qualified or independent.

wrong_explanations.A: A confidentiality agreement protects the client's information. It is a contractual matter and says nothing about whether the expert's conclusions can be relied on.
wrong_explanations.C: Reperformance needs the very expertise the auditor lacks, and it does not establish whether the expert was qualified or free of conflicts.
wrong_explanations.D: The IS auditor remains responsible for the audit conclusion, so the expert's work must flow through the auditor, not around them.

tips: Eliminate: A is a contractual protection, and D bypasses the auditor, who stays responsible for the conclusion.
Final two: B beats C because reliance rests first on the expert's qualifications and independence, which reperforming tests cannot replace.
Exam cue: before using another expert's work, assess their competence and objectivity first.

questions.question: Management decides not to patch a legacy ERP flaw because the outage would cost far more than the expected loss, and the CIO signs the decision. Which risk response BEST describes this?

options.A: Risk avoidance
options.B: Risk mitigation
options.C: Risk acceptance
options.D: Risk transfer

questions.key_concept: Risk acceptance is a formal, documented decision by an authorized owner to tolerate a known risk, usually when treatment costs exceed benefits.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the risk still exists after the decision. If the activity continues unchanged, it was not avoided.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk acceptance is a documented, approved decision to tolerate a known risk because treating it costs more than the benefit. The CIO sign-off and the cost comparison mark it as formal acceptance. Avoidance would mean stopping the activity that creates the risk, such as retiring the ERP component, yet the system keeps running with the flaw.

wrong_explanations.A: Avoidance removes the risk by ending the activity that causes it. The ERP keeps running, so the exposure remains.
wrong_explanations.B: Mitigation means adding or strengthening controls to reduce the risk. Management chose not to act.
wrong_explanations.D: Transfer shifts the impact to a third party, such as an insurer or vendor. Nothing is shifted outside the organization here.

tips: Eliminate: B needs new or stronger controls, and D needs a third party to bear the impact; neither appears here.
Final two: C beats A because the vulnerable system stays in use; avoidance would end the activity, not tolerate it.
Exam cue: a signed decision to live with a known risk after weighing cost is acceptance.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 31000:2018 (Risk Management); COBIT 2019 (APO12 Managed Risk); ITAF Performance Standards on Risk Treatment
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'risk acceptance — formal management decision not to act with sign-off'. Public source: ISO/IEC 31000 + COBIT 2019. All scenario specifics (auto manufacturer, legacy ERP vulnerability, 4-day outage, $40M cost) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A change policy states the objective 'all production changes are peer approved.' An IS auditor finds a rule requiring one designated approval before code merge. How should the auditor BEST classify this rule?

options.A: A detective control identifying unapproved changes after merge
options.B: A control objective stated in technical terms
options.C: A governance policy requiring board approval
options.D: A control measure implementing the stated objective

questions.key_concept: A control objective states the desired outcome; a control measure is the specific mechanism implemented to achieve it.
questions.pre_read: Separate the goal written in the policy from the mechanism the auditor observed in the workflow.
questions.correct_explanation: A control objective states the outcome the organization wants; a control measure is the specific mechanism put in place to achieve it. The merge-approval rule is how this team delivers the peer-approval objective, and another team could meet the same objective differently. Treating the rule as an objective confuses the means with the goal.

wrong_explanations.A: The rule stops unapproved code before it merges, so it is preventive. A detective control would find unapproved changes after they occur.
wrong_explanations.B: The objective is the desired outcome stated in the policy. The merge rule is one way to achieve it, so it is the measure.
wrong_explanations.C: Nothing in the rule involves the board. It is an operational mechanism inside the development workflow.

tips: Eliminate: A misreads a pre-merge gate as detective, and C invents a board role the rule does not have.
Final two: D beats B because the objective is the goal in the policy, while the merge rule is one way to meet it.
Exam cue: an objective says what must be achieved; a measure says how it is achieved here.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019 (Control Objectives and Practices); COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework (2013); ITAF Performance Standards on Control Evaluation
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'control objective vs control measure — goal vs implementation'. Public source: COBIT 2019 + COSO Internal Control – Integrated Framework. All scenario specifics (edtech company, pull request approval workflow) invented for this question. questions.question: The audit committee asks an IS auditor for a report that executives, committee members and operational managers can each use. Which report structure is BEST?

options.A: Executive summary first, then detailed findings and responses
options.B: Separate reports with tailored content for each audience
options.C: A findings spreadsheet without narrative or summary
options.D: One continuous narrative without section breaks

questions.key_concept: A layered report, with an executive summary followed by detail, serves several audiences while keeping one consistent set of conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Picture each reader in turn. Which structure lets all three get value without conflicting versions?
questions.correct_explanation: A layered report lets each reader find the depth they need: leaders read the executive summary, while operational managers use the detailed findings, ratings, recommendations and management responses. Everyone works from one consistent set of conclusions. Separate tailored reports also reach each audience, but they risk inconsistent messages and duplicate effort, and they fragment the record the committee oversees.

wrong_explanations.B: Tailored versions can drift apart in wording and emphasis, so readers may act on different conclusions. One layered report avoids that.
wrong_explanations.C: A spreadsheet gives operational detail but no context, conclusions or summary, so executives and the committee cannot quickly judge significance.
wrong_explanations.D: A continuous narrative forces every reader through all the detail and hides the key messages leaders need.

tips: Eliminate: C lacks the summary leaders need, and D buries key messages in one unbroken narrative.
Final two: A beats B because one layered report gives every audience the same conclusions at different depths.
Exam cue: for several audiences, choose one report with a summary up front and detail behind it.

questions.subtopic: Types of IS Audit Reports / Opinion Types
questions.question: An IS auditor finds two significant control weaknesses, but other major control areas operate effectively and there was no scope limitation. Which opinion is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Unmodified opinion, as most controls operate effectively
options.B: Qualified opinion, except for the noted weaknesses
options.C: Adverse opinion, given the significant weaknesses found
options.D: Disclaimer of opinion, owing to insufficient evidence

questions.key_concept: Opinion type turns on significance and pervasiveness: qualified for contained significant issues, adverse for pervasive ones, disclaimer for scope limits.
questions.pre_read: Ask two questions: are the issues significant, and are they pervasive? Then check for any scope limitation.
questions.correct_explanation: A qualified opinion fits when specific issues are significant but not pervasive: controls are effective except for the named weaknesses. Here the problems are confined to two areas while other major areas work. An adverse opinion is reserved for weaknesses so pervasive that controls are ineffective overall, which would overstate two contained findings and mislead readers.

wrong_explanations.A: An unmodified opinion signals no significant issues. Two significant weaknesses must be reflected in the opinion, not left out of it.
wrong_explanations.C: Adverse opinions apply when weaknesses are pervasive across the area. Effective controls elsewhere show these weaknesses are contained.
wrong_explanations.D: A disclaimer is used when the auditor cannot obtain enough evidence, such as under a scope limitation. None occurred here.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores two significant weaknesses, and D requires a scope limitation the stem rules out.
Final two: B beats C because the weaknesses are significant but contained, not pervasive across the control environment.
Exam cue: significant but contained points to qualified; pervasive points to adverse; missing evidence points to disclaimer.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Reports; ISA 705 (Modifications to the Opinion)

questions.question: An IS auditor is ranking four risks for next year's risk-based audit plan. Which risk should the auditor rank FIRST?

options.A: A risk with medium likelihood, medium impact and easily quantified loss
options.B: A risk with low likelihood, high impact and a tested failover
options.C: A risk with high likelihood, high impact and regulatory exposure
options.D: A risk with low likelihood but very high reputational impact

questions.key_concept: Risk-based audit planning ranks risks on combined likelihood and impact, adjusted for existing mitigation, not on a single dimension.
questions.pre_read: Score each option on both likelihood and impact before reacting to dramatic wording.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based prioritization weighs likelihood and impact together. The risk with high likelihood and high impact, compounded by regulatory exposure, scores highest on the combined rating. The reputational risk has an even larger impact, but its low likelihood pulls its combined rating well below, so ranking on worst-case impact alone would misdirect limited audit resources.

wrong_explanations.A: Medium on both dimensions gives a moderate score. Being easy to quantify does not make a risk more important.
wrong_explanations.B: Low likelihood and an existing, tested failover reduce this risk's residual level well below the top candidate.
wrong_explanations.D: Very high impact alone does not make a risk the top priority; its low likelihood lowers the combined rating.

tips: Eliminate: A is moderate on both dimensions, and B is unlikely and already mitigated by a tested failover.
Final two: C beats D because C is high on both likelihood and impact, while D is extreme on impact alone.
Exam cue: rank risks on likelihood and impact together, not on the single scariest dimension.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ITAF Performance Standards on Risk Assessment; ISO/IEC 31000:2018 (Risk Management)

questions.question: A US defense contractor subject to DFARS also runs EU plants under NIS2, and management wants one unified control set. What should the IS auditor MOST appropriately recommend?

options.A: ISO/IEC 27001 alone, as the international standard
options.B: CIS Controls alone, as the lightest option
options.C: COBIT 2019 alone, as a governance framework
options.D: NIST SP 800-171 mapped to ISO/IEC 27001

questions.key_concept: When regimes overlap, map the framework a regulation mandates to other recognized standards to build one control set.
questions.pre_read: Check which regulation names a specific framework. That requirement cannot be traded away for convenience.
questions.correct_explanation: DFARS contractually requires defense contractors to implement NIST SP 800-171, so it cannot be dropped. NIS2 sets outcomes rather than naming a framework, and ISO/IEC 27001 is widely recognized by EU regulators. Mapping the two into one control set meets both regimes with a single reporting structure. ISO/IEC 27001 alone is broad and international, but it leaves the DFARS requirement unmet.

wrong_explanations.A: ISO/IEC 27001 suits the EU operations, but DFARS specifically requires NIST SP 800-171, so this choice leaves a contractual obligation unmet.
wrong_explanations.B: CIS Controls are a useful baseline but do not satisfy the DFARS requirement for NIST SP 800-171 or EU regulatory expectations.
wrong_explanations.C: COBIT 2019 governs and manages enterprise IT; it is not the prescriptive security control set DFARS requires.

tips: Eliminate: B is a lightweight baseline that meets neither regime, and C is a governance framework, not a prescriptive control set.
Final two: D beats A because DFARS mandates NIST SP 800-171, so any single control set must map to it.
Exam cue: when a regulation names a framework, start there and map other regimes onto it.
questions.framework_ref: NIST SP 800-171; ISO/IEC 27001:2022 (Information Security Management Systems); DFARS 252.204-7012; EU NIS2 Directive
