questions.subtopic: Communicating Audit Results. Follow-up Communication Cadence
questions.question: An IS auditor issued a report with one critical, three high and four moderate findings, with remediation dates spread over 18 months. Which follow-up approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Leave tracking to management with no audit follow-up
options.B: Follow up every finding quarterly on one uniform schedule
options.C: Vary follow-up frequency according to each finding's severity
options.D: Review every finding once before next year's audit

questions.key_concept: Audit follow-up is risk-based: the frequency and depth of verification scale with each finding's severity.
questions.pre_read: Notice the findings range from critical to moderate. Ask whether they deserve equal follow-up attention.
questions.correct_explanation: Follow-up should be proportional to risk: the critical finding warrants early verification, often within weeks, with status reported to the audit committee, while high and moderate findings get progressively lighter checks. A uniform quarterly schedule is orderly and better than waiting a year, but it under-monitors the critical issue and spends effort on moderate ones.

wrong_explanations.A: Management owns remediation, but auditors must still verify it; skipping follow-up leaves the committee without assurance.
wrong_explanations.B: A uniform cadence treats the critical finding like a moderate one, leaving the critical risk under-monitored and wasting effort on low-risk items.
wrong_explanations.D: A single review a year later leaves the critical finding unverified for too long and gives the committee no interim assurance.

tips: Eliminate: D waits a year on a critical risk, and A drops the auditor's follow-up duty.
Final two: C beats B because follow-up effort should track risk; a uniform schedule under-watches the critical finding.
Exam cue: when findings differ in severity, choose the answer that scales effort to risk.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1402 (Follow-up Activities); ITAF Performance Standards on Follow-up
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'follow-up communication cadence - tiered by severity, with critical findings receiving near-term verification'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1402. questions.subtopic: Communicating Audit Results. Tone Calibration for Sensitive Findings
questions.question: An IS auditor's report includes a finding that a senior partner repeatedly accessed deal data beyond assigned scope. Which approach to wording this finding is BEST?

options.A: Soften the wording in view of the partner's seniority
options.B: State the facts and evidence in the usual neutral tone
options.C: Omit it and raise the matter privately with the partner
options.D: Use strong wording to stress the seriousness of the conduct

questions.key_concept: Audit findings are reported factually and objectively, with the same rigor regardless of the seniority of those involved.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option keeps the report objective, then check whether it errs toward either softening or dramatizing.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit reports must be objective and evidence-based regardless of who the finding concerns. The partner's conduct is described with the same factual precision as any other finding, neither diluted nor dramatized. Strong wording may seem to protect the organization, but emotive language undermines objectivity and invites challenge; the facts and their impact convey seriousness on their own.

wrong_explanations.A: Adjusting language for seniority compromises objectivity and independence. The same standard applies to every finding.
wrong_explanations.C: Suppressing a reportable finding to handle it privately compromises the report's completeness and the auditor's independence.
wrong_explanations.D: Emotive emphasis undermines the report's objectivity and gives the subject grounds to dispute tone rather than facts.

tips: Eliminate: A bends to seniority, and C suppresses a reportable finding.
Final two: B beats D because objectivity cuts both ways: no softening and no dramatizing, just facts and impact.
Exam cue: on sensitive findings, choose factual, evidence-based reporting applied equally to everyone.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ITAF Performance Standards on Communication of Results; ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (Objectivity)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'tone calibration for sensitive findings - factual rigor preserved regardless of subject seniority'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1401 + Code of Professional Ethics. All scenario specifics (private-equity firm, deal-data-room platform, partner-level employee out-of-scope access) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_050 severity-rating dynamics. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor must determine whether an AI model that classifies contract clauses is auditable. Which characteristic is MOST important?

options.A: The model achieves the highest accuracy available for the task
options.B: The model is trained on the largest available dataset
options.C: The model uses the same algorithm as industry leaders
options.D: Decisions are reproducible and can be explained for any input

questions.key_concept: An auditable AI model is reproducible, giving the same output for the same input and version, and explainable at a risk-appropriate depth.
questions.pre_read: Separate performance from verifiability. The stem asks whether the auditor can check the model, not how good it is.
questions.correct_explanation: To audit a model, the auditor must be able to rerun an input on a given version, get the same output, and trace why a decision was reached. Reproducibility and explainability make verification possible. High accuracy is valuable and tempting, but an accurate black box cannot be verified; the auditor would have to trust performance claims rather than test them.

wrong_explanations.A: Accuracy is a performance attribute. Without reproducibility and explainability, the auditor cannot verify how any decision was reached.
wrong_explanations.B: Dataset size says nothing about traceability, and undocumented sources make the model harder, not easier, to audit.
wrong_explanations.C: Copying a leader's algorithm says nothing about whether this model's decisions can be reproduced or explained.

tips: Eliminate: B focuses on data volume and C on imitation; neither makes decisions traceable.
Final two: D beats A because auditability means verifying decisions; an accurate but opaque model must be taken on trust.
Exam cue: auditable means the auditor can re-perform and trace, so look for reproducibility and explainability.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA "Auditing Artificial Intelligence" (IT Audit and Assurance Program); NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0); ITAF guidance on AI in IS Audit
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI/ML algorithmic auditability - reproducibility plus explainability as the two pillars'. Public source: ISACA Auditing AI program + NIST AI RMF. All scenario specifics (legal-tech SaaS, contract-clause-classification model) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor at a mining company is evaluating general IT controls. Which control is MOST representative of a general control?

options.A: Access provisioning and revocation procedures applied across all systems
options.B: Dual signatures required on large capital equipment purchases
options.C: Batch totals reconciled between the dispatch and billing systems
options.D: Input validation rejecting invalid weights in the grading application

questions.key_concept: General IT controls operate across the IT environment, such as access and change management; application controls govern specific processing.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each control protects the environment as a whole or checks particular transactions.
questions.correct_explanation: General IT controls operate across the IT environment, covering access management, change management and operations, and they support reliance on every application. Access provisioning and revocation applied to all systems fits that definition. Batch reconciliation between two systems looks broad because it spans an interface, but it checks the completeness of specific processing, which makes it an application control.

wrong_explanations.B: Dual signatures on purchases are a manual business process control, not an IT control.
wrong_explanations.C: Reconciling batch totals verifies completeness and accuracy of a specific data flow. That is an application control, even though two systems are involved.
wrong_explanations.D: Input validation inside one application is a classic application control over data entering that system.

tips: Eliminate: D is input validation within one application, and B is a manual business approval.
Final two: A beats C because general controls govern the whole environment; reconciling a data flow checks specific processing.
Exam cue: general controls cover access, change, operations and infrastructure; anything tied to specific transactions is an application control.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Performance Standards on Application Audits; COBIT 2019 DSS05 (Managed Security Services); COBIT 2019 DSS06 (Managed Business Process Controls); ISACA CISA Review Manual on General vs Application Controls
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'general IT controls vs application controls - environment-wide scope vs application-specific scope'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + ITAF. All scenario specifics (copper-mining, ore-grading, truck-dispatch, capital-equipment purchases) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Control Objectives. IS Control Objectives Sub-area
questions.question: An IS auditor is documenting control objectives for an engineering-design system subject to export-control regulations. Which characteristic of the objectives is MOST important?

options.A: A single broad statement covers the whole system
options.B: Each lists every control ever proposed for the system
options.C: Each is testable and traced to a risk or requirement
options.D: Each maps to a control already implemented in the system

questions.key_concept: Well-stated control objectives are specific, testable and traceable to a business risk or regulatory requirement.
questions.pre_read: Ask what should drive a control objective: the risks and rules, or the controls already in place?
questions.correct_explanation: Control objectives state what must be achieved to address a risk or requirement, here export-control obligations. They should be specific, testable and traceable to that risk, so controls can be designed and evaluated against them. Mapping each objective to an existing control seems practical, but objectives derived from current controls hide gaps where no control yet exists.

wrong_explanations.A: One broad statement cannot be tested and gives no basis for designing or evaluating specific controls.
wrong_explanations.B: Listing every proposed control confuses objectives with controls and includes items never implemented.
wrong_explanations.D: Starting from existing controls reverses the logic. Objectives must come from risks and requirements, or uncovered risks never appear.

tips: Eliminate: A is too broad to test, and B confuses objectives with a list of controls.
Final two: C beats D because objectives come from risk and regulation; deriving them from existing controls hides gaps.
Exam cue: control objectives flow from risk to objective to control, never backward from the controls already in place.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; COBIT 2019 (Management Objectives); ITAF Performance Standards on Application Audits

Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: CAATs as Continuous Online Audit Approach
questions.question: An IS auditor is designing continuous online auditing over a brokerage's high-volume order-routing system. Which design feature is MOST important?

options.A: Embedded audit modules that block suspicious orders in real time
options.B: Near-real-time anomaly alerts without degrading production performance
options.C: Manual queries run by auditors after each day's close
options.D: Analysis performed once during the annual audit cycle

questions.key_concept: Continuous online auditing applies automated techniques to live data, alerting auditors promptly without degrading production performance.
questions.pre_read: Ask which option gives timely detection while respecting the auditor's role and the system's performance.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuous online auditing works on live or near-live data and flags anomalies to auditors quickly, while being designed so the production system is not slowed. Embedded modules that block orders also act in real time, which makes them tempting, but stopping transactions is a preventive operational control owned by management, and inline blocking adds latency to a critical system.

wrong_explanations.A: Blocking transactions is management's operational control. An auditor doing it loses independence, and inline blocking can slow a high-volume trading system.
wrong_explanations.C: Manual queries after close are periodic, labor-intensive testing, not a continuous automated technique.
wrong_explanations.D: Annual analysis is traditional periodic auditing, the opposite of continuous online auditing.

tips: Eliminate: C is manual periodic work and D is annual; neither is continuous.
Final two: B beats A because auditors detect and report; blocking orders is management's control and slows production.
Exam cue: continuous auditing means timely automated detection for auditors, never auditors running operational controls.

questions.subtopic: Fraud. Evidence Handling and Chain of Custody
questions.question: An IS auditor finds evidence suggesting bid rigging by a manager and expects the matter may lead to litigation. What is MOST important when handling the evidence?

options.A: Passing the documents to the manager's supervisor for review
options.B: Filing originals in the standard audit work-paper archive
options.C: Keeping the evidence informally in the auditor's personal files
options.D: Maintaining a documented chain of custody for each original

questions.key_concept: Evidence likely to be used in litigation needs documented chain of custody to preserve its integrity and admissibility.
questions.pre_read: Note the expected litigation. Ask what a court would need to trust that evidence was not altered.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence that may be used in litigation must show an unbroken record of who collected it, when, where it was stored and who handled it, or its admissibility can be challenged. The work-paper archive is a secure, familiar home, which makes it tempting, but routine filing does not record handling history and may give access to many staff.

wrong_explanations.A: Sharing evidence with the suspect's line management risks tipping off the subject and compromising the investigation.
wrong_explanations.B: The archive keeps documents safe but does not log each handling step, so the integrity of originals could be disputed in court.
wrong_explanations.C: Informal personal storage breaks any custody record and invites claims of tampering or loss.

tips: Eliminate: C breaks custody entirely, and A risks alerting the suspect.
Final two: D beats B because secure storage is not enough; litigation demands a documented record of every handling step.
Exam cue: whenever evidence may reach court, choose chain of custody over convenience.

questions.question: Data scientists propose that an IS auditor rely on a high-stakes model's self-reported accuracy metrics. Which approach is BEST for the auditor to detect drift?

options.A: Accept the metrics because the model passed external validation
options.B: Compare model outputs with an independent challenger model's outputs
options.C: Recalculate the weekly accuracy metrics from production logs
options.D: Defer model testing until a failure occurs in production

questions.key_concept: For high-stakes AI models, an independent challenger model exposes drift and systematic errors that self-reported metrics cannot reveal.
questions.pre_read: Notice the evidence is self-reported. Ask which option gives the auditor an independent basis for comparison.
questions.correct_explanation: A challenger model built independently and run on the same inputs reveals systematic deviations, bias and drift that the production model cannot see in itself. Recalculating the weekly metrics confirms the arithmetic is right, but it still measures the model against its own yardstick, so correlated or systematic errors stay hidden.

wrong_explanations.A: Past validation does not prove current performance. Drift appears after deployment, so self-reported metrics need independent challenge.
wrong_explanations.C: Recomputing the same metrics verifies their accuracy, not their adequacy. A model's own measures cannot reveal errors it is systematically blind to.
wrong_explanations.D: Waiting for a failure makes the audit reactive. For a high-stakes model, the goal is detecting drift before harm occurs.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on old validation, and D waits for harm instead of detecting drift early.
Final two: B beats C because an independent reference exposes systematic errors; recalculating the model's own metrics only confirms the arithmetic.
Exam cue: when evidence comes from the system being audited, look for the option that adds an independent point of comparison.

questions.question: An IS auditor must test a dual-approval control, estimate dollar errors in freight charges, and confirm zero-tolerance hazmat approvals. Which sampling approach is BEST?

options.A: One stratified random sample designed to meet every objective at once
options.B: A judgmental sample of the largest routing changes by dollar value
options.C: Separate attribute, variable and full-population tests per objective
options.D: Management representations for controls and ad hoc analysis for dollars

questions.key_concept: Each audit objective drives its own sampling design; zero-tolerance populations require 100 percent testing rather than sampling.
questions.pre_read: List the three objectives separately. Ask what kind of answer each one needs: a rate, a dollar amount or certainty.
questions.correct_explanation: Sampling design follows the audit objective. A yes-or-no control test calls for attribute sampling, a dollar estimate calls for variable or monetary-unit sampling, and a zero-tolerance population must be tested in full because no sample can prove zero errors. A single stratified sample looks efficient, but no stratification can serve three different objectives and evidence needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Stratification improves precision within one design, but one sample cannot answer an attribute question, a dollar estimate and a zero-tolerance test together.
wrong_explanations.B: A judgmental sample of large items cannot be projected statistically and may skip small hazmat changes entirely.
wrong_explanations.D: Management representations are weak evidence and cannot replace testing; ad hoc analysis gives no defensible dollar estimate.

tips: Eliminate: B cannot be projected and may miss hazmat items, and D replaces testing with weak representations.
Final two: C beats A because each objective needs its own design; one stratified sample cannot serve three evidence needs.
Exam cue: match the method to the objective: attribute for controls, variable or MUS for dollars, full testing for zero tolerance.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling; AICPA AU-C 530 (Audit Sampling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'multi-objective sampling design - separate designs for separate objectives, with 100% testing for zero-tolerance sub-populations'. Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling. All scenario specifics (freight rail, car-routing, dual approval, dollar estimation, hazmat-cars sub-population) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor's spouse works in an unrelated department, and the auditor consulted on unrelated firewalls three years ago; the audit committee knows only the first fact. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Proceed without further disclosure because both facts are unrelated
options.B: Restate the spouse's role to the committee and omit the consulting
options.C: Request reassignment to avoid any appearance of impaired independence
options.D: Disclose the consulting work and document safeguards for both threats

questions.key_concept: Independence threats are assessed by severity: disclose and apply safeguards for low threats; withdraw only when safeguards cannot reduce the threat.
questions.pre_read: Notice both facts are unrelated to the audited system and one is undisclosed. Weigh severity before choosing a drastic response.
questions.correct_explanation: Independence is judged with a threat-and-safeguard approach: identify each threat, assess its severity, disclose it to those charged with governance and apply safeguards. Both threats here are low because the roles and work are unrelated and the consulting has lapsed, so disclosure plus documented safeguards is proportionate. Reassignment is reserved for threats that safeguards cannot reduce to an acceptable level.

wrong_explanations.A: Withholding a relevant prior relationship denies governance the information it needs to judge independence, even when the threat itself is low.
wrong_explanations.B: Repeating a fact the committee already knows while leaving out the undisclosed consulting fails the transparency the framework requires.
wrong_explanations.C: Reassignment overcorrects. Low threats that disclosure and safeguards can reduce do not require the auditor to step away.

tips: Eliminate: A and B both leave the consulting work undisclosed, so governance cannot assess the threat.
Final two: D beats C because low threats are managed with disclosure and safeguards; removal is for threats safeguards cannot reduce.
Exam cue: for independence, match the response to the threat's severity; disclosure plus safeguards for low threats, reassignment for severe ones.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor's Professional Independence); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1002 (Organizational Independence); ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (Objectivity); ITAF General Standards on Independence
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'independence threat-and-safeguard - low-severity threats addressable by disclosure plus safeguards, distinct from total-recusal response to severe threats'. Public source: ISACA Code of Professional Ethics + Standard 1002. All scenario specifics (regional public utility, customer-billing audit, spouse role, three-year-old consulting) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_002 self-review angle. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS audit director is scoping an audit of a production-control system whose IT, operational and financial-reporting components depend on one another. Which scope is BEST?

options.A: An integrated audit covering the three components together
options.B: Three separate specialist audits performed one after another
options.C: An IS audit limited to the application and its interfaces
options.D: An operational audit supported by ad hoc IT procedures

questions.key_concept: Integrated audits suit subjects whose IT, operational and financial components are interdependent; narrower or separate scopes miss risks at the seams.
questions.pre_read: Notice the components depend on one another. Ask which scope sees how a failure in one affects the others.
questions.correct_explanation: When IT, operational and financial-reporting components are interdependent, a failure in one cascades into the others, so an integrated audit evaluates the risks together, including the handoffs between them. Separate specialist audits cover every component, but each team stops at its own boundary, so risks at the seams between components are missed and fieldwork is duplicated.

wrong_explanations.B: Sequential specialist audits cover each area but stop at boundaries, so cross-component risks fall between teams and effort is duplicated.
wrong_explanations.C: An IT-only scope misses how control failures flow into operations and financial reporting.
wrong_explanations.D: Ad hoc IT procedures give no structured coverage of system controls or of the financial-reporting impact.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores operations and reporting, and D gives IT and financial controls only ad hoc attention.
Final two: A beats B because interdependent components need one coordinated view; separate audits miss risks at the seams.
Exam cue: when the stem says components depend on one another, look for the integrated approach.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Techniques; ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Engagement Planning); IIA Practice Guide on Integrated Auditing
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'integrated audit scope decision - integrated when components are interdependent, narrower scope creates seam-risk blind spots'. Public source: ITAF + ISACA Standard 1201 + IIA Practice Guide. All scenario specifics (semiconductor manufacturer, wafer fabrication, three component domains) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_017 application angle. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: During fieldwork, an IS audit director finds an exploitable privileged-access flaw, already reported to management, that may trigger a five-day regulatory notice; the audit committee meets in 45 days. What should the director do FIRST?

options.A: Include the finding in the formal report at the next meeting
options.B: Escalate to the audit committee chair now and involve counsel
options.C: Leave the notification decision to the general counsel alone
options.D: Confirm management's remediation plan and escalate if dates slip

questions.key_concept: Critical findings with regulatory exposure warrant prompt escalation to the audit committee chair outside the normal reporting cycle.
questions.pre_read: Compare the deadlines: a five-day notice window against a 45-day meeting gap. Then ask who must know now.
questions.correct_explanation: A critical, exploitable weakness with a possible short regulatory deadline cannot wait for the regular reporting cycle, so the director escalates to the audit committee chair between meetings and coordinates with counsel on the notice. Confirming management's remediation plan is sensible follow-up, but it leaves governance uninformed while the exposure and the regulatory clock both run.

wrong_explanations.A: The meeting is 45 days away, far beyond a five-day notice window, and the flaw stays exploitable meanwhile.
wrong_explanations.C: Counsel decides legal questions, but the audit function still owes timely reporting of critical findings to the audit committee.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's commitment does not remove today's exposure or the regulatory deadline; governance needs to know now, not after slippage.

tips: Eliminate: A waits 45 days against a five-day window, and C hands the audit function's reporting duty to counsel.
Final two: B beats D because critical findings with regulatory exposure go to governance promptly; management's promise does not replace escalation.
Exam cue: critical severity plus a deadline shorter than the reporting cycle means escalate between meetings to the committee chair.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ITAF Performance Standards on Communication of Results; IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 8.1 (Board Interaction)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit-committee escalation timing - critical severity + regulatory exposure warrant between-meetings escalation to chair, with parallel work-streams'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1401 + IIA 2060. All scenario specifics (cooperative bank, core-banking privileged-access vulnerability, regulator 5-business-day notification window, 45-day meeting cadence) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_016 application angle. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): stem says management already knows, so escalating to the committee chair is the single best answer.

questions.question: An IS auditor receives a specialist firm's report with undocumented methods, contradictory conclusions and a skipped agreed task; the firm presses for sign-off. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Accept the report because the firm was vetted before engagement
options.B: Approve the invoice and record the gaps as lessons learned
options.C: Withhold reliance and require the firm to correct the deficiencies
options.D: Replace the firm immediately with a different specialist

questions.key_concept: The auditor stays responsible for conclusions when using experts and must evaluate the delivered work, not only the expert's competence.
questions.pre_read: Notice the problems are in the deliverable, not the firm's credentials. Ask what the auditor must do before relying on it.
questions.correct_explanation: The auditor remains responsible for the audit conclusion even when using an expert's work, so the delivered work must be evaluated, not just the expert's credentials. Inadequate work cannot be relied on; the auditor communicates the specific deficiencies and requires correction under the engagement terms. Replacing the firm may eventually be needed, but it skips the step of holding the firm to its agreed scope.

wrong_explanations.A: Vetting competence beforehand does not prove the delivered work is adequate. The auditor must still evaluate what was actually produced.
wrong_explanations.B: Approving deficient work for convenience abandons the auditor's responsibility for the conclusion and the evidence supporting it.
wrong_explanations.D: Replacement is premature. The firm has not been told the deficiencies or asked to fix work it was contracted to deliver.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on vetting instead of the work, and B signs off on deficient work for convenience.
Final two: C beats D because the firm must first be held to its agreed scope; replacement comes only if correction fails.
Exam cue: using an expert never transfers responsibility; evaluate the actual deliverable before relying on it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1206 (Using the Work of Other Experts); ITAF Performance Standards on External Experts
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'external expert inadequate work - auditor remains responsible for conclusion, must reject inadequate deliverable and communicate specifics, not sign off on invoice'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1206. All scenario specifics (ag-tech company, satellite-imagery crop-yield model, four specific problems, invoice pressure) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_032 pre-reliance evaluation angle. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS audit team plans to use an ITAF tools-and-techniques audit program, unchanged, for a client's cloud engagement. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: ISACA does not permit its audit programs on client work
options.B: Tools and techniques carry no authority in an IS audit
options.C: Generic steps may miss this engagement's specific risks
options.D: Using a published program impairs the team's independence

questions.key_concept: ITAF tools and techniques provide adaptable examples, such as audit programs, that must be tailored to each engagement's risks.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word unchanged. Ask what a generic program cannot know about this client's environment.
questions.correct_explanation: ITAF tools and techniques are informational examples, such as audit programs, meant to be adapted to each engagement. Running one unchanged risks testing generic steps while missing risks specific to this client's cloud environment. Doubting the program's authority confuses the layers: tools and techniques are not mandatory, which is why they must be tailored, not a reason they cannot be used.

wrong_explanations.A: ISACA publishes audit programs for practitioners to use and adapt; nothing prohibits using them on client engagements.
wrong_explanations.B: Tools and techniques are informational, not mandatory, but they are legitimate support; the concern is applying one without tailoring.
wrong_explanations.D: Using a published program creates no self-interest or self-review threat; independence is unaffected.

tips: Eliminate: A invents a usage ban, and D links a published program to an independence threat that does not exist.
Final two: C beats B because tools and techniques are meant to be adapted; the risk is skipping tailoring, not lack of authority.
Exam cue: standards are followed, guidelines considered, and tools and techniques adapted to the engagement's risks.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF (IT Audit Framework), 4th ed. — Tools and Techniques; ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Engagement Planning)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ITAF Tools and Techniques layer foundational definition - adaptable practical artifacts, distinct from Standards (mandatory) and Guidelines (advisory)'. Public source: publicly published ITAF framework structure. No legacy bank consulted. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. v2: retargeted to avoid duplicating d1_060.

questions.question: An IS audit team wants results on payment transactions within hours of processing, independent of management's own checks. Which approach BEST meets this objective?

options.A: Continuous auditing using automated audit routines
options.B: Continuous monitoring performed by process owners
options.C: Periodic audits with quarterly sampling of transactions
options.D: Forensic review performed after a control failure

questions.key_concept: Continuous auditing is performed by the audit function on an ongoing basis; continuous monitoring is a management activity.
questions.pre_read: Notice two requirements: speed and independence from management. Ask which option satisfies both, not just one.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuous auditing is performed by the audit function, typically with automated routines, so results arrive shortly after transactions occur while staying independent of management. Continuous monitoring delivers similar speed, but it is a management activity performed by process owners, so it cannot provide the independent assurance the audit team needs.

wrong_explanations.B: Continuous monitoring is management's own control activity. It is timely but not independent, which the objective requires.
wrong_explanations.C: Quarterly sampling cannot deliver results within hours of processing; the timing objective fails.
wrong_explanations.D: A forensic review is reactive and starts only after a failure, so it cannot provide ongoing results.

tips: Eliminate: C is too slow for results within hours, and D only starts after a failure.
Final two: A beats B because continuous auditing is performed by auditors; continuous monitoring is management's own activity.
Exam cue: continuous auditing belongs to auditors, continuous monitoring belongs to management; check who performs it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Tools and Techniques on Continuous Auditing
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'continuous auditing foundational definition - audit team + ongoing + results shortly after activity, distinct from continuous monitoring (management) and periodic / reactive auditing'. Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Continuous Auditing. No legacy bank consulted. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A chief audit executive wants a functional reporting line that BEST protects the IS audit function's independence. To whom should the function report?

options.A: The chief executive officer
options.B: The board audit committee
options.C: The chief information officer
options.D: The external audit firm

questions.key_concept: The audit committee is a board-level committee of independent directors overseeing audit, internal control and financial reporting.
questions.pre_read: Ask which body sits outside management entirely. Seniority alone does not create independence.
questions.correct_explanation: The audit committee is a board-level committee of independent directors that oversees the audit function, internal control and financial reporting. A functional reporting line to it keeps audit outside management's control. The chief executive officer is senior and broad, but still management, so the function could face pressure over findings on the executive's own areas.

wrong_explanations.A: The chief executive is senior but remains management. Audit findings can criticize the executive's own areas, so independence is weaker.
wrong_explanations.C: The chief information officer runs much of what IS audit reviews, creating a direct conflict of interest.
wrong_explanations.D: The external auditor is an independent third party, not the governance body that oversees the internal audit function.

tips: Eliminate: C runs the areas IS audit reviews, and D is an outside firm, not a governance body.
Final two: B beats A because the audit committee is independent of management; the chief executive, however senior, is still management.
Exam cue: for independence questions, the highest level is not enough; choose the body independent of management.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 301 (Audit Committee Requirements); ISACA governance guidance on the audit committee; ITAF General Standards on Audit Charter and Reporting Line
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit committee foundational definition - board-level oversight committee of independent directors, distinct from operational / peer-review / regulator structures'. Public source: SOX Section 301 + ISACA governance guidance. No legacy bank consulted. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a control weakness with a small dollar impact in a system that produces regulatory reports. What should MOST determine whether the weakness is material?

options.A: Whether it could influence decisions of the report's users
options.B: Whether its dollar impact exceeds a set percentage threshold
options.C: Whether management agrees the weakness is significant
options.D: Whether a prior audit reported a similar issue

questions.key_concept: Materiality is the threshold at which a finding could influence intended users' decisions; it includes qualitative factors, not only amounts.
questions.pre_read: Notice the small dollar amount and the regulatory context. Ask which test captures both quantitative and qualitative significance.
questions.correct_explanation: Materiality is the point at which a weakness or misstatement could reasonably influence the decisions of the report's intended users. It is a judgment that includes qualitative factors, such as regulatory consequences, not only dollar size. A percentage threshold is a useful starting point, but a small-dollar weakness in regulatory reporting can still be material.

wrong_explanations.B: A quantitative threshold is a starting point, but qualitative factors like regulatory reporting can make small-dollar weaknesses material.
wrong_explanations.C: Management's view is not the test. Materiality is judged by the auditor against the needs of the report's users.
wrong_explanations.D: A prior finding may raise concern, but it does not decide whether this weakness would influence users' decisions.

tips: Eliminate: C lets management set materiality, and D relies on history rather than impact on users.
Final two: A beats B because materiality includes qualitative factors; a regulatory-reporting weakness can matter despite a small dollar amount.
Exam cue: when the stem mentions small dollars but sensitive context, materiality is about influence on users, not size alone.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1204 (Materiality); ITAF Performance Standards on Materiality
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'materiality foundational definition - decision-influence threshold for intended report users, judgment-based, engagement-specific'. Public source: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1204. No legacy bank consulted. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Audit Evidence. Types and Reliability Ranking
questions.question: An IS auditor needs evidence of how a security officer recorded one specific past safety incident. Which source provides the MOST reliable evidence?

options.A: The officer's verbal account given during interview
options.B: The auditor's re-creation of the workflow in a test system
options.C: The officer's signed paper report prepared afterward
options.D: The system's automated, time-stamped audit log entries

questions.key_concept: Contemporaneous machine-generated records are highly reliable for past events; re-performance shows how a process works, not what happened earlier.
questions.pre_read: Notice the objective is one specific past incident. Ask which source captured that event as it happened.
questions.correct_explanation: A machine-generated, contemporaneous log records what actually happened to that specific incident without depending on anyone's recollection or interpretation. The auditor's re-creation is strong evidence of how the workflow behaves, but it is performed in a test system after the fact, so it cannot show how the actual past incident was recorded.

wrong_explanations.A: Oral testimony from an involved party is the least reliable form of evidence and depends on memory and self-interest.
wrong_explanations.B: Re-creation shows how the workflow works now in a test system, not what happened to this past incident in production.
wrong_explanations.C: A signed report is prepared by an interested party and reflects their account, not an independent system record.

tips: Eliminate: A is oral testimony, and C is a document prepared by the person involved.
Final two: D beats B because the objective is a specific past event; a test-system re-creation cannot show what actually happened.
Exam cue: match evidence to the objective; for a past event, contemporaneous system records beat later re-creation.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Evidence
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'evidence-types reliability ranking - independence of source and contemporaneous machine-generation drive reliability'. Public source: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205. All scenario specifics (cruise line, safety-incident reporting, four evidence types about one incident) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Fraud. Interview Techniques in Suspected Fraud
questions.question: An IS auditor is authorized to interview a manager suspected of click-fraud based on system evidence. Which practice is MOST important during the interview?

options.A: Conduct the interview alone to keep the matter confidential
options.B: Open with accusatory questions to pressure the manager into confessing
options.C: Hold the interview openly so coworkers can corroborate answers
options.D: Have a second interviewer present and record responses as given

questions.key_concept: Fraud-suspect interviews need a second interviewer and contemporaneous documentation so the evidence withstands later legal challenge.
questions.pre_read: Think ahead to how the interview might be used later. Ask which practice keeps what was said provable.
questions.correct_explanation: Fraud interviews may produce evidence used in disciplinary or legal action, so a second qualified interviewer acts as a witness and contemporaneous notes preserve exactly what was said. Interviewing alone does protect confidentiality, but it leaves no corroboration of the conversation, exposing the auditor and the evidence to later dispute.

wrong_explanations.A: Confidentiality matters, but a one-on-one interview leaves no witness, so the subject can later dispute what was said.
wrong_explanations.B: Accusatory openings provoke defensiveness and can taint any admission, undermining its later use as evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: A public setting breaches confidentiality, risks defamation and alerts others before the facts are established.

tips: Eliminate: B taints the evidence with pressure, and C breaches confidentiality in front of coworkers.
Final two: D beats A because a witness and contemporaneous notes protect the evidence; privacy alone leaves the conversation unprovable.
Exam cue: in fraud work, choose the option that preserves evidence for later legal use.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1207 (Irregularities and Illegal Acts); ITAF Performance Standards on Fraud Risk; ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual on Investigative Interviewing
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'fraud-suspicion interview technique - structured: second interviewer, contemporaneous documentation, narrative-before-specific, non-leading questions'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1207 + ACFE Fraud Examiners Manual. All scenario specifics (online gaming platform, click-fraud manipulation, senior product manager subject) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Risk Assessment. Quantitative vs Qualitative Trade-offs
questions.question: An IS auditor is assessing risk for a terminal-operations system with two recorded incidents in five years but highly experienced operators. Which risk assessment method is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Quantitative analysis using annualized loss expectancy figures
options.B: Qualitative workshops drawing on experienced operators' judgment
options.C: Prior-year audit committee priorities without a fresh assessment
options.D: No formal assessment, since few incidents indicate low risk

questions.key_concept: Choose risk assessment methods based on available data; sparse incident history makes quantitative estimates unreliable.
questions.pre_read: Notice what data exists: few incidents, deep expertise. Ask which method that evidence can actually support.
questions.correct_explanation: The method should follow the available data. Two incidents in five years cannot support credible frequency or loss estimates, while deep operator expertise supports structured qualitative judgment. Quantitative analysis looks precise and defensible, but numbers built on sparse data create false precision rather than a better assessment.

wrong_explanations.A: Annualized loss figures need enough history to estimate frequency. Two incidents yield false precision, not reliable numbers.
wrong_explanations.C: Last year's priorities ignore current conditions. Risk assessment must be refreshed rather than carried forward unchanged.
wrong_explanations.D: A low incident count may reflect luck or poor detection. It does not justify skipping risk assessment.

tips: Eliminate: C reuses stale priorities, and D wrongly treats few incidents as proof of low risk.
Final two: B beats A because sparse data cannot support credible quantitative estimates; expert judgment is the stronger evidence available.
Exam cue: let the data decide the method; little history plus strong expertise points to qualitative assessment.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ITAF Tools and Techniques on Risk Assessment Techniques; ISO/IEC 31000:2018 (Risk Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'quantitative vs qualitative method selection - method follows data, not abstract preference for precision'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1202 + ISO 31000. All scenario specifics (port authority, terminal-operations system, two incidents in five years, long-tenured operators) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Control Environment. Independent Evaluation vs Management Monitoring
questions.question: A CFO argues that management's monthly control-monitoring reviews make the IS audit function's independent evaluation duplicative. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Explain both are complementary; audit adds objective assurance
options.B: Reduce audit testing where monthly monitoring reports no issues
options.C: Agree to stop independent evaluation of the monitored controls
options.D: Defer to the regulator's inspections as the independent review

questions.key_concept: Management monitoring and independent evaluation are complementary; audit independently tests controls, including the monitoring itself.
questions.pre_read: Notice who performs the monthly reviews. Ask whether self-review can give the same assurance as an independent evaluation.
questions.correct_explanation: Management monitoring and independent evaluation are complementary parts of internal control. Monitoring is built into operations and catches issues quickly, while independent evaluation gives objective assurance that the controls, including the monitoring itself, work. Reducing testing where monitoring is clean sounds efficient, but it lets management's own unverified results set audit scope.

wrong_explanations.B: Clean monitoring results are management's self-assessment. Using them to cut testing relies on the very process audit should evaluate.
wrong_explanations.C: Stopping independent evaluation removes objective assurance and accepts management's self-review as a substitute.
wrong_explanations.D: Regulators inspect for their own purposes and scope; their work does not replace the organization's independent evaluation.

tips: Eliminate: C abandons independent assurance, and D substitutes a regulator's differently scoped work.
Final two: A beats B because monitoring is management's self-review; letting its clean results shrink testing undermines independent assurance.
Exam cue: management monitoring and independent audit evaluation complement each other; neither replaces the other.
questions.framework_ref: COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework (2013); ISACA IT Audit Standards on Internal Controls; ITAF Performance Standards on Control Evaluation
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'control-environment evaluation - management monitoring vs independent evaluation as complementary activities, not substitutes'. Public source: COSO 2013 + ISACA Standards. All scenario specifics (small-molecule biopharma R&D, GMP context, CFO duplication question) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_028 application angle. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An audit director is designing the ongoing monitoring element of the quality assurance and improvement program. Which design is BEST?

options.A: Daily QA sign-off required before any engagement can proceed
options.B: Each auditor's quarterly self-rating of the quality of their own engagements
options.C: Routine supervision and work-paper review built into every engagement
options.D: An annual deep review of a sample of completed engagements

questions.key_concept: Ongoing QA monitoring is embedded in routine supervision of every engagement; periodic assessments add deeper sampled reviews.
questions.pre_read: Notice the word ongoing. Ask which design operates continuously as part of normal work, not on a schedule.
questions.correct_explanation: Ongoing monitoring is part of the day-to-day management of audit work: routine supervision, work-paper review and standard checklists applied to every engagement. An annual deep review of sampled engagements is valuable, but it is a periodic assessment that complements ongoing monitoring rather than replacing it, and it leaves most work unreviewed between reviews.

wrong_explanations.A: Daily sign-off on everything is impractical and stalls the work; monitoring should be proportionate and built into normal supervision.
wrong_explanations.B: Self-ratings lack objectivity and evidence; auditors cannot meaningfully assure the quality of their own work.
wrong_explanations.D: A yearly sampled review is a periodic assessment. It complements ongoing monitoring but does not cover work continuously.

tips: Eliminate: A is impractical micromanagement, and B relies on auditors rating their own work.
Final two: C beats D because ongoing monitoring is built into every engagement; an annual sampled review is a periodic assessment.
Exam cue: ongoing means embedded in daily supervision; periodic means scheduled deeper reviews. Match the word to the design.
questions.framework_ref: IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 12.1 (Internal Quality Assessment); IIA Quality Assessment and Improvement Program (QAIP); ITAF General Standards on Quality
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ongoing QA monitoring design - continuous lightweight across all + periodic deep on sampled basis'. Public source: IIA Standard 1311 + ISACA QAIP guidance. All scenario specifics (consumer fintech, audit director designing QA cadence) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_048 monitoring failure scenario and d1_076 internal program design. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS audit director at a conglomerate operating in 23 countries is establishing the audit universe. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Every individual IT system enumerated and updated daily
options.B: A risk-mapped catalog of auditable entities refreshed periodically
options.C: A static list of divisions set when the function began
options.D: The systems that management has ranked as its highest business risks

questions.key_concept: An audit universe is a complete, risk-mapped catalog of auditable entities at appropriate granularity, refreshed as the organization changes.
questions.pre_read: Ask what the audit universe is for: risk-based planning. Then check completeness, independence and maintenance.
questions.correct_explanation: A well-maintained audit universe catalogs auditable entities such as processes, systems and regulatory obligations at a sensible granularity, maps each to risk, and is refreshed at least annually as the organization changes. Management's high-risk list is a useful input, but it is incomplete and lets the auditee decide what the audit function can see.

wrong_explanations.A: Enumerating every system daily is impractical at this scale and confuses an asset inventory with a risk-based audit universe.
wrong_explanations.C: A static list goes stale as the organization changes, missing new entities, acquisitions and emerging risks.
wrong_explanations.D: Management's ranking is a useful input, but it covers only part of the universe and lets the auditee shape audit scope.

tips: Eliminate: A is an impractical inventory, and C goes stale as the organization changes.
Final two: B beats D because the audit universe must be complete and independently risk-assessed; management's list is only an input.
Exam cue: the audit universe is complete, risk-mapped and refreshed; beware options that let management define audit coverage.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Planning
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit universe definition and maintenance - structured catalog at appropriate granularity, risk-mapped, periodically refreshed'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1202. All scenario specifics (multinational conglomerate, 23 countries, 8 lines of business) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Audit Documentation. Originals vs Summary Retention
questions.question: After completing an airworthiness-records audit, an IS audit director must decide what evidence to retain. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Detailed evidence sent to the auditee's records office for safekeeping
options.B: Every file kept indefinitely on the team's local drives
options.C: The final report and a summary index of evidence examined
options.D: Evidence supporting the conclusions, protected for the required period

questions.key_concept: Retain documentation sufficient to support conclusions, protected for integrity and kept for the required retention period.
questions.pre_read: Ask what a reviewer would need to reach the same conclusion. Then check integrity and retention.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit documentation must let an experienced reviewer understand the work and see how the evidence supports the conclusions. It must be protected against alteration and kept for the period that regulation and policy require. A report with a summary index is tidy, but it shows only what was concluded, not the evidence that supports the conclusions.

wrong_explanations.A: The auditee should not hold the audit's evidence; independence and integrity of the files would be compromised.
wrong_explanations.B: Indefinite local storage ignores retention schedules and integrity controls, and raises data-protection and loss risks.
wrong_explanations.C: A report and index show conclusions but not the supporting evidence a reviewer needs to re-perform the reasoning.

tips: Eliminate: A hands evidence to the auditee, and B ignores retention rules and integrity controls.
Final two: D beats C because documentation must support the conclusions; a summary index shows results, not the evidence behind them.
Exam cue: work papers must let an independent reviewer reach the same conclusion; summaries alone never meet that bar.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1208 (Audit Documentation); ITAF Performance Standards on Documentation; FAA / EASA records-retention rules (analogous regulator context for MRO)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit documentation retention - originals sufficient to support conclusion + regulatory compliance + integrity controls, distinct from summary-only / indefinite-local / auditee-delegated approaches'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1208. All scenario specifics (aircraft MRO, airworthiness-records audit, evidence types collected) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_043 lifecycle scenario. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): options made grammatically parallel.

questions.question: An IS auditor has gathered a large volume of evidence, nearly all from one application's logs. What should the auditor evaluate FIRST before concluding?

options.A: Whether the sample size meets the statistical plan
options.B: Whether staff can confirm the evidence orally
options.C: Whether the evidence is relevant and reliable
options.D: Whether the auditee agrees with preliminary results

questions.key_concept: Evidence must be sufficient and appropriate; volume addresses sufficiency, while relevance and reliability address appropriateness.
questions.pre_read: Notice the evidence is plentiful but single-sourced. Ask whether the gap is quantity or quality.
questions.correct_explanation: Evidence must be both sufficient and appropriate. A large volume addresses sufficiency, but when nearly everything comes from one source, the auditor must first confirm the evidence is relevant to the objective and reliable, for example that the logs are complete and protected. Checking sample size against the plan only re-confirms quantity, which is not the concern.

wrong_explanations.A: Sample size measures sufficiency, which the large volume already addresses. The single-source concern is about quality, not quantity.
wrong_explanations.B: Oral confirmation is weaker evidence than the logs and cannot establish their reliability.
wrong_explanations.D: Auditee agreement does not establish evidence quality; conclusions rest on evidence, not consensus.

tips: Eliminate: B adds weaker oral evidence, and D seeks consensus rather than evidence quality.
Final two: C beats A because volume settles sufficiency; a single source raises a question of appropriateness that size cannot answer.
Exam cue: lots of evidence from one source signals an appropriateness check; more volume never fixes a quality gap.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Evidence
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'evidence sufficiency vs appropriateness - both required, volume alone does not satisfy appropriateness'. Public source: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205. All scenario specifics (luxury fashion e-commerce, returns-fraud controls, single-source high-volume evidence) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_004 reliability scenario and d1_095 evidence-types ranking. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor plans to use analytical procedures as substantive evidence for reported energy output. Which condition is MOST important for them to be effective?

options.A: A precise expectation built from reliable underlying data
options.B: Business unit agreement on the expectation in advance
options.C: Application of the procedure to every transaction
options.D: An expectation based on prior-period reported output

questions.key_concept: Substantive analytical procedures need a precise expectation built on reliable data so that significant differences indicate possible misstatement.
questions.pre_read: Ask what makes a difference between expected and actual meaningful. Precision and data reliability decide it.
questions.correct_explanation: Analytical procedures work as substantive evidence only when the expectation is precise enough that a significant difference signals possible misstatement, and the data behind it is reliable, such as independent weather and equipment-hour data. An expectation based on prior-period output is common, but it may carry forward past errors and is too imprecise to detect current misstatement.

wrong_explanations.B: Seeking the auditee's agreement on the expectation compromises independence and lets the auditee shape the test.
wrong_explanations.C: Analytics test relationships across aggregated data; they do not require transaction-level application to be effective.
wrong_explanations.D: Prior-period figures may contain the same errors and ignore changes in drivers like weather, so the expectation is imprecise.

tips: Eliminate: B lets the auditee shape the test, and C misunderstands how analytics work on aggregated data.
Final two: A beats D because a precise, independent expectation detects misstatement; prior-period output may carry errors forward.
Exam cue: an analytic is only as good as its expectation; look for precision and reliable, independent inputs.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Techniques; AICPA AU-C 520 (Analytical Procedures, analogous)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'analytical procedures effectiveness - precise expectation + reliable underlying data'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1205 + AICPA AU-C 520. All scenario specifics (solar utility, energy-output reporting, weather + equipment-hours + seasonality drivers) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor is reviewing the change management process for a point-of-sale system. Which characteristic is MOST important for a well-designed control?

options.A: Developers deploy low-risk changes at their own discretion
options.B: Changes are released at peak hours for quick support
options.C: Every change is logged as a ticket in one central tool
options.D: Changes are authorized, tested and migrated by separate roles

questions.key_concept: Change management controls require authorization, testing, approval and segregation between developing and migrating changes to production.
questions.pre_read: Ask which characteristic prevents an unauthorized or untested change from reaching production, not merely records it.
questions.correct_explanation: A well-designed change control ensures each change is authorized, tested and approved, and moved to production by someone other than the developer, so no single person can introduce an unapproved change. Central ticket logging supports traceability, but a logged change can still be untested or self-deployed, so logging alone does not prevent unauthorized changes.

wrong_explanations.A: Letting developers bypass the process on their own judgment defeats the control and allows unauthorized changes into production.
wrong_explanations.B: Peak-hour releases increase business disruption; deployment timing does not make a change control well designed.
wrong_explanations.C: Logging provides traceability, but it does not ensure changes are authorized, tested or deployed by someone independent.

tips: Eliminate: A lets developers bypass the control, and B raises disruption without improving control design.
Final two: D beats C because authorization, testing and segregation prevent unauthorized changes; logging only records them.
Exam cue: for change management design, look for authorization, testing and segregated migration, not record-keeping alone.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); COBIT 2019 BAI06 (Managed IT Changes); ITAF Performance Standards on IT General Controls
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'change-management control design - authorization, testing, approval, and four-role separation'. Public source: COBIT 2019 BAI06 + ISACA ITGC standards. All scenario specifics (QSR chain, POS system, change-management testing) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Independence. Self-Interest Threat Severity Differentiation Mid-Engagement
questions.question: Mid-engagement, an IS auditor's brother joins a competitor of the auditee, and the auditor accepts a future job at the auditee. What is the audit director's BEST response?

options.A: Proceed unchanged because neither fact involves the audited system
options.B: Dismiss the auditor for cause without any chance to remediate
options.C: Treat both threats as low and add supervision to the work
options.D: Reassign the auditor and document the threat assessment

questions.key_concept: Assess each independence threat separately; a future role at the auditee is severe enough to require reassignment.
questions.pre_read: Separate the two facts and rate each threat. Then ask which one decides the response.
questions.correct_explanation: Each threat is assessed separately. A relative at a competitor is a remote threat that disclosure and supervision can manage. An accepted future job at the auditee is a severe self-interest threat, because the auditor now benefits from good relations with the audited party, and supervision cannot reduce it enough. Treating both as low misjudges the second threat's severity.

wrong_explanations.A: Independence concerns the auditor's relationship with the auditee, not just the system. An accepted job offer creates a direct self-interest.
wrong_explanations.B: Dismissal is punitive and disproportionate; reassignment removes the threat without treating the situation as misconduct.
wrong_explanations.C: The brother's role is low, but an accepted job at the auditee is severe; supervision cannot neutralize that self-interest.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores a direct self-interest, and B punishes rather than safeguards.
Final two: D beats C because threats are judged separately; an accepted job at the auditee is too severe for supervision alone.
Exam cue: when several threats appear, rate each one; the most severe threat drives the response.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor's Professional Independence); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1002 (Organizational Independence); ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (Independence); ITAF General Standards on Independence
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'mid-engagement independence threats with different severities - relative-at-competitor (low) vs accepted-future-role-at-auditee (high)'. Public source: ISACA Standards 1002/1003 + Code of Professional Ethics. All scenario specifics (tax-preparation platform, brother at competitor, accepted internal-transfer offer) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_002 self-review and d1_087 dual-low-threat scenarios. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Six months after the annual risk assessment, the organization acquires a foreign competitor, and a new regulation requires attestations within nine months. What is the IS audit director's BEST response?

options.A: Update the risk assessment and audit plan for these changes now
options.B: Wait for the next annual refresh to address both changes
options.C: Restart the entire annual risk assessment from the beginning
options.D: Add a compliance review of the new regulation to the plan

questions.key_concept: Risk assessments are updated mid-cycle when significant changes, such as acquisitions or new regulations, alter the risk environment.
questions.pre_read: Notice both changes are significant and time-sensitive. Ask which response addresses all of them proportionately.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk assessment is performed at least annually but must be updated when the risk environment changes significantly. An acquisition expands the audit universe and a regulation with a short deadline creates new risk, so the director updates the assessment and plan now. Adding a compliance review answers the regulation, but it ignores the newly acquired operations entirely.

wrong_explanations.B: Waiting six months leaves a large new entity unassessed and may miss the regulation's nine-month deadline.
wrong_explanations.C: Rebuilding everything is disproportionate; a targeted update for the changes is enough and preserves completed work.
wrong_explanations.D: A compliance review covers the regulation but leaves the acquired operations outside the risk assessment and plan.

tips: Eliminate: B waits past a pressing deadline, and C rebuilds work that a targeted update can handle.
Final two: A beats D because both changes alter the risk picture; a single added review ignores the acquisition.
Exam cue: significant changes to the organization or its obligations trigger a mid-cycle update, not a wait or a full restart.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ITAF Performance Standards on Risk Assessment; ISO/IEC 31000:2018 (Risk Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'mid-cycle risk-assessment update decision - acquisition (universe change) and regulatory window (deadline) as strongest triggers, distinct from peer-incident or personnel-change'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1202. All scenario specifics (commercial logistics, four mid-cycle developments) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_037 prioritization scenario. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Using monetary-unit sampling, an IS auditor finds three misstatements with differing taint percentages. Which projection approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Report the total of the misstatements found as the result
options.B: Multiply the misstatement total by the population-to-sample count ratio
options.C: Apply each taint to its interval and add precision allowances
options.D: Exclude understatements because they offset the overstatements found

questions.key_concept: MUS projects misstatements by applying each taint to its sampling interval, then adds precision allowances for an upper limit.
questions.pre_read: Recall how MUS selects items: by dollar. Ask which projection respects that selection method.
questions.correct_explanation: In monetary-unit sampling, each misstatement is projected by applying its taint percentage to the sampling interval that contained it. The projections are summed, and basic and incremental precision allowances produce an upper misstatement limit. Scaling by the item-count ratio is a familiar projection method, but it ignores the dollar-weighted selection that MUS relies on.

wrong_explanations.A: Found misstatements are only the sample result. Without projection, the population misstatement is badly understated.
wrong_explanations.B: Count-based scaling suits item sampling, not MUS, which selects by dollar and projects through taints and sampling intervals.
wrong_explanations.D: Understatements cannot simply be dropped; each misstatement must be evaluated, and netting can hide real errors.

tips: Eliminate: A never projects the sample, and D discards misstatements that must be evaluated.
Final two: C beats B because MUS projects by taint and sampling interval; count-ratio scaling ignores dollar-weighted selection.
Exam cue: MUS projection means taint times interval, then precision allowances; any count-based ratio is the trap.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling; AICPA AU-C 530 (Audit Sampling); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'MUS misstatement projection - taint x sampling interval plus precision factors, NOT simple sum or ratio'. Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling + AICPA AU-C 530. All scenario specifics (sports arena, season-ticket transactions, 18,400 population, 100 sample, three found misstatements with specific taints) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_064 MUS mechanics question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An X-ray screening model keeps stable test-set accuracy, but radiologist overrides doubled after expansion to a new patient population. What is the IS auditor's BEST conclusion?

options.A: Performance is acceptable because test-set accuracy remains stable
options.B: Production drift is likely, so recommend monitoring and retraining
options.C: Rising overrides point to inconsistent radiologists needing training
options.D: The issue is outside audit competence and belongs to clinical staff

questions.key_concept: Frozen test-set accuracy cannot detect drift; rising production overrides after a population change are key drift indicators.
questions.pre_read: Compare where each metric comes from: old test data or live production. Then ask what changed.
questions.correct_explanation: Accuracy on a frozen test set shows how the model performs on data like its training data; it cannot reveal that production data has shifted. Rising overrides after a population change are classic drift signals, so the auditor should report likely drift and recommend production monitoring and retraining. Blaming radiologists is plausible, but overrides rose after the population changed.

wrong_explanations.A: A frozen test set reflects old data. Stable results there cannot detect shifts in the live population.
wrong_explanations.C: Overrides rose when the patient population changed, which points to the model's inputs shifting, not reviewer inconsistency.
wrong_explanations.D: Assessing whether a model's performance is monitored and controlled is within audit scope; specialists can support, not replace, the auditor.

tips: Eliminate: A trusts a frozen test set, and D wrongly places model risk outside audit scope.
Final two: B beats C because overrides rose with the population change, a drift signal; reviewer inconsistency would not track that shift.
Exam cue: stable lab metrics plus rising real-world disagreement after a data change signals drift.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA "Auditing Artificial Intelligence" (IT Audit and Assurance Program); NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0); ITAF guidance on AI in IS Audit
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'AI/ML drift detection - rising production disagreement + distribution shift + no retraining as textbook drift signals; internal-test-set accuracy cannot detect drift'. Public source: ISACA Auditing AI program + NIST AI RMF. All scenario specifics (teleradiology, chest X-ray pre-screening, 18-month deployment, four specific observations) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_085 challenger-model and d1_080 algorithmic auditability. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): option D rewritten as a plain conclusion parallel to the others.

questions.question: An IS auditor finds a material revenue cut-off weakness confined to one area, other controls are effective, and management refuses remediation. Which opinion is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Unmodified, because management acknowledged the weakness
options.B: Qualified, describing the material cut-off weakness
options.C: Adverse, because management refuses to remediate
options.D: Disclaimer, because future effectiveness is uncertain

questions.key_concept: Qualified opinions address material but contained weaknesses; adverse opinions address pervasive failure; disclaimers address insufficient evidence.
questions.pre_read: Notice the weakness is material but confined to one area. Ask how widespread the failure is.
questions.correct_explanation: A qualified opinion fits a material weakness confined to a defined area when the rest of the control environment operates effectively. The report describes the weakness and the supported magnitude. An adverse opinion is tempting given management's refusal, but adverse is for pervasive failure; refusal to remediate is reported, but it does not make a contained weakness pervasive.

wrong_explanations.A: Acknowledgment does not remove a material weakness. An unmodified opinion would misstate the control environment.
