questions.subtopic: Audit Risk Model. Setting Detection Risk Given High IR x CR
questions.question: An IS auditor assesses inherent and control risk as high for a billing system, and the target audit risk is low. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Set detection risk high and accept a higher audit risk
options.B: Set detection risk low and expand substantive testing
options.C: Recommend control fixes first to lower control risk
options.D: Set detection risk according to the available audit budget

questions.key_concept: The auditor directly controls only detection risk; when inherent and control risk are high, detection risk is set low through more extensive substantive work.
questions.pre_read: Audit risk is roughly inherent times control times detection risk. Ask which of those the auditor can change this period.
questions.correct_explanation: With inherent and control risk both high, the only lever the auditor controls is detection risk, which must be set low through larger samples, stronger substantive procedures and specialist help where needed. Recommending control fixes is valuable, but control risk belongs to management and the current period's controls have already operated, so the auditor must still gather sufficient evidence now.

wrong_explanations.A: Accepting higher audit risk contradicts the low target. High inherent and control risk demand more work, not less.
wrong_explanations.C: Control risk is set by management's controls, and this period's controls have already operated. The auditor still needs evidence now.
wrong_explanations.D: Budget may constrain work, but detection risk follows the risk assessment; underfunded effort must be escalated, not accepted silently.

tips: Eliminate: A abandons the audit risk target, and D lets budget rather than risk set the effort.
Final two: B beats C because the auditor controls only detection risk; recommending fixes does not change this period's evidence needs.
Exam cue: high inherent and control risk always point to low detection risk and more substantive testing.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ITAF Performance Standards on Risk Assessment
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit-risk model applied detection-risk calibration - high IR x high CR + low AR target requires low DR (more effort)'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1202. All scenario specifics (EV-charging network, 12M sessions/month, IPO preparation, weak tariff-change controls) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_062 (model definition foundational). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Audit Plan Adjustment. Resource Constraint Mid-Year
questions.question: Mid-year, an IS audit function loses two of six auditors with no backfill for months. What is the MOST appropriate response by the audit director?

options.A: Cancel the remaining engagements until new staff arrive
options.B: Complete every engagement at reduced depth to hold the schedule
options.C: Reprioritize engagements by risk and brief the audit committee
options.D: Outsource the remaining audit engagements whatever the cost

questions.key_concept: When resources change, the audit plan is re-prioritized by risk, changes are documented, and the audit committee is informed of the revised coverage.
questions.pre_read: Coverage and quality cannot both be kept with less staff. Decide which one a risk-based plan protects.
questions.correct_explanation: A risk-based plan should flex with resources: deliver the highest-risk engagements at full scope, defer lower-risk ones, document the changes and brief the audit committee on the revised coverage. Completing every engagement at reduced depth preserves the appearance of the plan, but thin work on high-risk areas gives assurance the evidence cannot support.

wrong_explanations.A: Stopping all audits leaves high-risk areas without coverage for months and abandons the risk-based plan entirely.
wrong_explanations.B: Cutting depth across the board weakens evidence on the highest-risk areas while appearing to deliver the full plan.
wrong_explanations.D: Co-sourcing can help, but committing regardless of cost bypasses budget governance and a risk-based choice of what to source.

tips: Eliminate: A drops all coverage, and D ignores budget governance and risk-based choices.
Final two: C beats B because quality on the highest risks matters more than nominal completion; thin work creates false assurance.
Exam cue: when capacity shrinks, reprioritize by risk and tell the audit committee; never trade quality for schedule.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Planning
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit plan adjustment under resource constraint - re-prioritize by risk preserving risk-based discipline, distinct from cancel-all / degrade-all / fully-outsource'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1202. All scenario specifics (regional public-broadcaster, 6-to-4 staff reduction, 7 remaining engagements, June timing) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_106 (risk-environment changes mid-cycle). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Sampling. Sample Re-Design when Initial Sample Insufficient
questions.question: An IS auditor's attribute sample finds a deviation rate below the tolerable rate but above the planned expected rate, leaving the result inconclusive. What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Conclude the control is unreliable and report the deviations
options.B: Discard the sample and select a fresh one of equal size
options.C: Exclude deviations that management can reasonably explain
options.D: Extend the sample or redesign it, documenting the rationale

questions.key_concept: When results fall between the expected and tolerable rates, the auditor extends or redesigns the sample, documenting why, before concluding.
questions.pre_read: Compare the result with both the expected and the tolerable rate. Ask whether the evidence yet supports any conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: The sample rate sits below the tolerable rate, but because deviations exceeded the planned expectation, sampling risk leaves the conclusion open. The auditor extends the sample under the same design, or redesigns it, keeping the deviations already found and documenting why. Concluding the control is unreliable fits when the rate clearly exceeds tolerable; here that verdict would be premature.

wrong_explanations.A: The observed rate is below tolerable. Calling the control unreliable now outruns the evidence; that verdict fits when the rate clearly exceeds tolerable.
wrong_explanations.B: Discarding results throws away evidence of deviations. Found deviations must be evaluated, not replaced.
wrong_explanations.C: Deviations are judged against the control's design, not management explanations; excluding them biases the result.

tips: Eliminate: B discards valid evidence, and C lets management explanations remove deviations.
Final two: D beats A because the rate is below tolerable but inconclusive; more evidence is needed before any verdict on the control.
Exam cue: clearly above tolerable means conclude unreliable; below tolerable but above expected means extend or redesign before concluding.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling; AICPA AU-C 530 (Audit Sampling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'sample re-design when initial sample insufficient - extend under original design or re-design entirely, both preserving prior findings, distinct from premature conclusion / discard / leap-to-failure'. Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling. All scenario specifics (medical-device manufacturer, warranty-claim transactions, 60-item attribute sample, 5 deviations, 3% acceptable rate) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_086 multi-objective design and d1_107 MUS projection. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Audit Reporting. Disagreement with Management Position
questions.question: Management rejects an IS auditor's high-severity rating for unencrypted vendor remote access to SCADA systems, citing cost. How should the audit director MOST appropriately report the finding?

options.A: Report the auditor's rating and include management's response
options.B: Adopt management's rating and note the auditor's view separately
options.C: Hold the report until senior management agrees the rating
options.D: Settle on a medium rating that reflects both positions

questions.key_concept: Findings reflect the auditor's evidence-based judgment; management's disagreement is reported alongside the finding, not used to change it.
questions.pre_read: Ask whose judgment the report represents, and who should resolve a disagreement that persists.
questions.correct_explanation: The report states the finding at the severity the evidence supports and includes management's response, so the audit committee can see both and decide. Waiting for agreement seems courteous, but it lets management control the timing of an unresolved high-severity risk and delays governance from acting on exposure in critical infrastructure.

wrong_explanations.B: Adopting management's rating lets the audited party set the conclusion, which compromises the auditor's independence.
wrong_explanations.C: Holding the report lets management delay disclosure of a high-severity risk; disagreement is reported, not used as a gate.
wrong_explanations.D: A compromise rating is not supported by evidence and dilutes the auditor's objective judgment.

tips: Eliminate: B and D both let management's view change the auditor's evidence-based rating.
Final two: A beats C because persistent disagreement is reported to the committee; it does not give management a veto on timing.
Exam cue: when management disagrees, report your finding with their response and let governance decide.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ITAF Performance Standards on Communication of Results; ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (Independence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'auditor-management disagreement in reporting - preserve auditor judgment in report, disclose management position, audit committee evaluates'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1401 + Code of Professional Ethics. All scenario specifics (regional water utility, SCADA unencrypted remote access, three management mitigations) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_050 severity-calibration at exit conference, d1_068 exit-conference purpose, d1_079 tone calibration. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Continuous Auditing. Decision to Suspend Production on Detected Anomaly
questions.question: An IS auditor's continuous-auditing tool flags a trader executing 1,200 trades in three minutes, far above normal; compliance staff are in a meeting. What should the auditor do FIRST?

options.A: Trigger the automated halt on the trader's account
options.B: Email the trader asking for an explanation
options.C: Page on-call compliance leaders and preserve the evidence
options.D: Queue the alert for compliance review after the meeting

questions.key_concept: In continuous auditing, the audit role is detection, escalation and evidence preservation; operational responses such as halting trading belong to management or compliance.
questions.pre_read: The anomaly is urgent, but ask who has the authority to stop trading, and what the auditor's role is.
questions.correct_explanation: The auditor's role is to detect, escalate urgently to those with authority and preserve the evidence, so paging on-call compliance leaders gets the decision to the right people within minutes. Halting the account is decisive, but it is an operational decision with business and regulatory consequences; taking it would place the auditor in a management role and impair independence.

wrong_explanations.A: Halting trading is an operational decision for compliance or management. Taking it puts the auditor in a management role.
wrong_explanations.B: Contacting the trader directly may tip off a possible bad actor and compromise evidence.
wrong_explanations.D: A 1,200-trade spike is urgent; waiting for the meeting to end lets exposure grow when on-call escalation exists.

tips: Eliminate: B may tip off the trader, and D delays an urgent alert despite on-call escalation.
Final two: C beats A because auditors escalate to those with authority; executing the halt themselves is a management action that impairs independence.
Exam cue: auditors detect, escalate and preserve; they do not take operational control actions.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Continuous Auditing; ISACA IT Audit Standard 1207 (Irregularities and Illegal Acts); ITAF General Standards on Independence (audit role distinct from operations)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'continuous-auditing detected-anomaly escalation - audit detects and escalates to authorized decision-maker (compliance), audit does not unilaterally take operational action'. Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques + ISACA Standard 1207. All scenario specifics (high-frequency trading firm, 1,200 trades in 3 minutes, $14M exposure, senior MD trader, compliance meeting) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_046 technique selection, d1_083 continuous-online application, d1_110 architecture trade-offs. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS audit manager is facilitating a control self-assessment workshop with production managers. Which facilitation practice is MOST important?

options.A: Presenting the auditor's list of weaknesses for participants to confirm
options.B: Using open questions and recording participants' views and dissent
options.C: Letting discussion run freely without structure or documentation
options.D: Replacing the group session with individual interviews

questions.key_concept: CSA facilitation draws out participants' own assessment of their controls, records dissent, and avoids steering them toward the auditor's conclusions.
questions.pre_read: CSA's value comes from the process owners' knowledge. Ask which practice draws that out instead of replacing it.
questions.correct_explanation: A CSA workshop exists to capture the process owners' own assessment of their controls, so the facilitator uses open questions, records consensus and dissent, and avoids steering. Presenting a prepared list of weaknesses feels efficient and structured, but it anchors participants on the auditor's view, turning self-assessment into confirmation and losing the insight only they can provide.

wrong_explanations.A: A pre-built list anchors participants on the auditor's conclusions, so the workshop confirms the auditor's view rather than eliciting theirs.
wrong_explanations.C: Without structure or documentation, the workshop produces no reliable record of findings to support later work.
wrong_explanations.D: Individual interviews are a different technique and lose the group discussion that makes CSA useful.

tips: Eliminate: C lacks structure and documentation, and D abandons the workshop format.
Final two: B beats A because CSA must elicit participants' own assessment; a prepared list steers them toward the auditor's answers.
Exam cue: in CSA, the auditor facilitates and records; the process owners assess.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Techniques; IIA Practice Guide on Control Self-Assessment
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'CSA workshop facilitation discipline - elicits participants own assessments through open-ended questions, structured capture, no steering'. Public source: ISACA Standards on CSA + IIA Practice Guide. All scenario specifics (Big-Four advisory firm, manufacturing client production-scheduling) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_020 (limitations), d1_059 (deployment decision), d1_073 (definition). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: CSA. Results Integration into Audit Conclusions
questions.question: A department's control self-assessment rates its segregation of duties as strong, but the IS auditor's walkthrough finds gaps. How should the auditor MOST appropriately use the CSA results?

options.A: Base the conclusion on the CSA since owners know best
options.B: Set aside the CSA results because they conflict with testing
options.C: Have the department repeat the CSA until it matches
options.D: Use CSA as one input but conclude on independent testing

questions.key_concept: CSA results complement audit work and inform scope, but audit conclusions rest on the auditor's independent procedures.
questions.pre_read: The two views conflict. Decide which one supports the conclusion, and whether the other still has value.
questions.correct_explanation: CSA results inform scope and show how process owners perceive their controls, but the audit conclusion rests on the auditor's independent evidence. Setting the CSA aside seems rigorous, yet the gap between the department's belief and the walkthrough is itself a finding about control awareness and is worth reporting, so the results should be kept and analyzed.

wrong_explanations.A: Self-assessment is not independent evidence. Relying on it would let the audited area conclude on its own controls.
wrong_explanations.B: Discarding the CSA loses useful information; the divergence reveals a control-awareness gap worth reporting.
wrong_explanations.C: Pressing the department to change its assessment manipulates the evidence and destroys its value as a perspective.

tips: Eliminate: A relies on non-independent self-assessment, and C pressures the department to change its view.
Final two: D beats B because the divergence itself is useful evidence; CSA informs the audit while independent testing decides it.
Exam cue: CSA complements audit work; it never replaces the auditor's own testing.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Techniques; IIA Practice Guide on Control Self-Assessment
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'CSA results integration - CSA as one input, auditor independent procedures as conclusion basis, divergence as analytical observation'. Public source: ISACA CSA standards + IIA Practice Guide. All scenario specifics (regional credit union, loan-origination CSA workshop) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_020/059/073/131. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor extracts database records and system logs as evidence for a SaaS audit. Which practice MOST supports relying on the integrity of this evidence?

options.A: Hashing extracts at capture and documenting chain of custody
options.B: Storing extracts on a restricted-access audit team file share
options.C: Letting the auditee review the extracts before analysis
options.D: Compressing extracts to minimize evidence storage costs

questions.key_concept: Electronic evidence integrity rests on controlled capture, tamper-evident verification such as hashing, and a documented chain from source to work paper.
questions.pre_read: Restricting access protects files going forward. Ask what proves the file is unchanged from the moment it left the source.
questions.correct_explanation: Hashing extracts when they are captured, and re-verifying the hash at use, proves the evidence has not changed, while a documented chain of custody shows how it moved from source to work paper. Restricting access to the file share is a sound protective control, but it cannot demonstrate that the files were unaltered before storage or since.

wrong_explanations.B: Access restrictions reduce the chance of tampering but do not prove the files are unchanged since extraction.
wrong_explanations.C: Giving the auditee the evidence before analysis creates an opportunity to alter it and weakens independence.
wrong_explanations.D: Compression addresses storage cost, not integrity, and does nothing to show the evidence is unaltered.

tips: Eliminate: C hands evidence back to the auditee, and D addresses cost rather than integrity.
Final two: A beats B because a hash proves the file is unchanged, while access control only reduces the chance of change.
Exam cue: for electronic evidence, prefer controls that demonstrate integrity over controls that merely protect it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Evidence; ITAF Tools and Techniques on CAATs
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'electronic evidence integrity - controlled capture, hash verification, secure storage, documented chain'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1205. All scenario specifics (cloud-SaaS provider, database extracts and system logs) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_004 reliability principle, d1_095 reliability ranking, d1_102 sufficiency vs appropriateness. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Audit Evidence. Third-Party Confirmation (Positive vs Negative)
questions.question: An IS auditor supporting an integrated audit assesses risk as high on receivables concentrated in a few large customers. Which confirmation approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Negative confirmations, since prior response rates were high
options.B: Testing subsequent cash receipts instead of confirming balances
options.C: Mixing positive and negative requests to manage cost
options.D: Positive confirmations requesting a reply from each customer

questions.key_concept: Positive confirmations are used when assessed risk is high or balances are large, because they require an explicit reply from the third party.
questions.pre_read: Large balances and high risk change what silence can mean. Ask which method treats non-response as non-evidence.
questions.correct_explanation: With high assessed risk and a few large balances, the auditor needs explicit, independent evidence from each customer, which positive confirmations provide. Testing subsequent cash receipts is a valid alternative procedure, typically used when confirmations go unanswered, but it relies on client records rather than direct third-party evidence and is weaker as a primary procedure here.

wrong_explanations.A: Negative confirmations treat silence as agreement, which is unacceptable when risk is high or balances are large.
wrong_explanations.B: Subsequent receipts are an alternative procedure for non-responses; client records are weaker than direct third-party replies.
wrong_explanations.C: Using negative requests for any of a few large, high-risk balances still treats silence as evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A and C both rely on negative confirmations, which treat silence as agreement despite high risk.
Final two: D beats B because direct third-party replies outrank client records; receipts testing is the fallback for non-responses.
Exam cue: high risk or large balances point to positive confirmations; negative ones suit low-risk, many small balances.
questions.framework_ref: AICPA AU-C 505 (External Confirmations); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Evidence
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'positive vs negative confirmation - positive required for high risk + large items, negative acceptable only for low risk + small items + high response expected'. Public source: AICPA AU-C 505 + ISACA Standard 1205. All scenario specifics (manufacturer AR audit, concentrated large customers, high IR/CR) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): stem frames the auditor's role in an integrated audit.

questions.subtopic: Prescriptive Frameworks. Cross-Walking NIST CSF and ISO 27001
questions.question: A client uses one control set to meet both NIST CSF and ISO/IEC 27001. What should the IS auditor do FIRST to assess whether both are satisfied?

options.A: Accept ISO certification as evidence of CSF alignment
options.B: Map client controls to each framework's requirements and note gaps
options.C: Test against the more recent framework and infer the other
options.D: Test operating effectiveness of the controls common to both frameworks

questions.key_concept: Cross-walking frameworks starts with a documented mapping of controls to each framework's requirements, exposing gaps that one framework's compliance would not reveal.
questions.pre_read: The two frameworks overlap but are not equivalent. Ask what must exist before you know which controls to test.
questions.correct_explanation: The auditor first builds a documented mapping from the client's controls to each NIST CSF outcome and each ISO/IEC 27001 requirement, exposing gaps where one framework asks for something the other does not. Testing the common controls is useful work, but without the mapping the auditor cannot know which controls are common or which requirements are left uncovered.

wrong_explanations.A: Certification to one framework does not establish alignment with another; their scope and orientation differ.
wrong_explanations.C: Recency does not make one framework a superset of the other, so inferring compliance leaves gaps untested.
wrong_explanations.D: Testing shared controls before mapping skips requirements unique to either framework and assumes the overlap is already known.

tips: Eliminate: A and C both assume one framework's compliance implies the other's.
Final two: B beats D because mapping defines what is common and what is missing; testing comes after scope is known.
Exam cue: when two frameworks apply, map first, then test; never assume equivalence.
questions.framework_ref: NIST Cybersecurity Framework (NIST CSF) v2.0 (February 2024); ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Information Security Management Systems; ISACA Risk IT Framework; ITAF Performance Standards on Application Audits
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'framework cross-walking NIST CSF and ISO 27001 - documented mapping plus gap identification plus orientation-difference recognition'. Public source: NIST CSF v2.0 + ISO/IEC 27001:2022. All scenario specifics (cybersecurity MSP, dual U.S./EU client) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_038 (DFARS+NIS2 prescriptive framework scenario). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Prescriptive Frameworks. Cross-Walking SOX and COBIT
questions.question: Management runs its IT controls on COBIT 2019, and the IS auditor is testing IT general controls for SOX 404. How should the auditor MOST appropriately use COBIT?

options.A: Map relevant COBIT objectives to the in-scope ITGC areas
options.B: Test every COBIT objective as part of the SOX scope
options.C: Disregard COBIT, since SOX testing uses regulatory criteria
options.D: Require management to replace COBIT with a SOX framework

questions.key_concept: COBIT supports SOX work when its relevant objectives are mapped to the IT general controls over financial reporting; scope stays limited to ICFR relevance.
questions.pre_read: SOX scope covers controls relevant to financial reporting. Ask how a broader governance framework fits that narrower scope.
questions.correct_explanation: SOX 404 covers IT general controls relevant to financial reporting, so the auditor maps the relevant COBIT objectives, mainly in delivery, build and alignment areas, to access, change and operations controls over in-scope systems. Testing every COBIT objective sounds thorough, but most fall outside financial-reporting relevance, wasting effort and blurring the risk-based SOX scope.

wrong_explanations.B: COBIT is far broader than SOX needs; testing every objective dilutes effort away from controls relevant to financial reporting.
wrong_explanations.C: COBIT is a recognized control framework that management may use; mapping it to SOX scope is efficient, not prohibited.
wrong_explanations.D: Management chooses its control framework. SOX does not require a specific one, and COBIT is commonly used.

tips: Eliminate: C rejects a recognized framework without reason, and D dictates management's framework choice.
Final two: A beats B because SOX scope is limited to financial-reporting relevance; mapping keeps testing risk-based.
Exam cue: use broad frameworks through mapping to the specific regulatory scope, not by testing them wholesale.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 404 (Management Assessment of Internal Controls); COBIT 2019 (Management Objectives across DSS, BAI, APO domains); PCAOB AS 2201 (Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'SOX/COBIT cross-walking - COBIT for design and operation, SOX for audit scope and reporting, mapping between'. Public source: SOX Section 404 + COBIT 2019 + PCAOB AS 2201. All scenario specifics (publicly-traded retail chain, SOX 404 ICFR audit, COBIT-managed IT environment) invented for this question. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Audit Team Training. Engagement-Specific Competency-Gap Diagnosis
questions.question: An IS audit manager's team has strong general IT skills but no industrial control system experience for an upcoming ICS security audit. What should the manager do FIRST?

options.A: Start fieldwork and let the team learn ICS on the job
options.B: Reassign the audit to another internal team with prior ICS experience
options.C: Identify the specific skill gaps and plan targeted expert support
options.D: Remove the ICS audit from the annual audit plan

questions.key_concept: Before an engagement starts, the manager diagnoses specific competency gaps and closes them through experts, training or co-sourcing.
questions.pre_read: The team is strong but lacks one specialty. Ask what must be understood before choosing any fix.
questions.correct_explanation: The manager first pins down which ICS knowledge is missing, such as industrial protocols or safety systems, then closes the gap with an expert, targeted training or co-sourcing. Reassigning to an experienced team may work, but it skips the diagnosis, assumes such a team is available, and may sacrifice the existing team's strong IT knowledge that the audit still needs.

wrong_explanations.A: Learning on the job means fieldwork starts without the proficiency the engagement requires, risking missed ICS-specific issues.
wrong_explanations.B: Reassignment may not be feasible and skips diagnosis; the existing team's IT skills remain valuable with targeted support.
wrong_explanations.D: A skills gap does not remove the risk. Dropping a planned audit leaves an important area without coverage.

tips: Eliminate: A starts without proficiency, and D removes coverage of a risk area instead of fixing the gap.
Final two: C beats B because diagnosing the gap comes first and allows a targeted fix that keeps useful existing skills.
Exam cue: for competency gaps, diagnose first, then supplement with experts or training before fieldwork.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1006 (Proficiency); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1206 (Using the Work of Other Experts); ITAF General Standards on Proficiency
related_concepts: Using the work of other experts
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'engagement-specific competency gap diagnosis - identify specific gap, target remediation through expert / training / co-sourcing'. Public source: ISACA Standards 1006 + 1206. All scenario specifics (oil-services contractor, ICS cybersecurity audit, three-IT-auditor team without ICS experience) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_044 (function-level training plan). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Effect of Laws and Regulations. Sector-Specific Cases (HIPAA + Finance)
questions.question: A hospital system holds patient health records under HIPAA and patient financing data under GLBA. What is the MOST appropriate approach for the IS auditor?

options.A: Audit against HIPAA, since healthcare rules take precedence
options.B: Audit against both, noting requirements unique to each
options.C: Audit against ISO 27001 as a common substitute baseline
options.D: Defer the audit until regulators issue joint guidance

questions.key_concept: When several laws apply to one system, the auditor evaluates each set of requirements explicitly, including those unique to each regime.
questions.pre_read: Two laws apply to different data in the same system. Ask whether any single standard can stand in for both.
questions.correct_explanation: Each regulation imposes its own legal requirements, so the auditor evaluates the system against both, noting where HIPAA protects health information and GLBA protects financial data, and where they differ or conflict. ISO 27001 is a strong common baseline, but it is a voluntary security standard and does not cover each law's specific legal obligations.

wrong_explanations.A: No general rule makes HIPAA supersede GLBA; both apply to their respective data, so auditing one leaves the other untested.
wrong_explanations.C: A security standard can support compliance, but it does not capture each law's specific legal requirements.
wrong_explanations.D: Both regimes already apply. Waiting for joint guidance leaves current compliance risk unassessed.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores GLBA, and D delays an audit of requirements that already apply.
Final two: B beats C because legal obligations must be tested against the laws themselves; a voluntary standard cannot substitute for them.
Exam cue: when multiple regulations apply, evaluate each explicitly and map overlaps rather than picking one.
questions.framework_ref: HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 CFR Part 164); GLBA Safeguards Rule (16 CFR Part 314); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'sector-overlap regulatory audit - audit both regimes explicitly, document differences, identify conflicts, escalate to legal'. Public source: HIPAA + GLBA + ISACA Standard 1202. All scenario specifics (multi-state hospital chain extending in-house financing) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_022 (parent regulatory effect on planning). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Assessing a US-listed company's compliance with SOX Section 407, an IS auditor finds no audit committee member qualifies as a financial expert. What is the MOST appropriate conclusion?

options.A: The company must disclose this and explain why none serves
options.B: Every committee member must first obtain a CPA or similar certification
options.C: The board must appoint a financial expert before the next filing
options.D: The chief financial officer should join the committee as a voting member

questions.key_concept: SOX Section 407 is disclose-or-explain: the company states whether a financial expert serves on the audit committee and, if not, why.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem cites one specific rule. Ask whether it mandates an appointment or only a disclosure.
questions.correct_explanation: Section 407 is a disclosure rule: the company must state whether at least one audit committee member is a financial expert and, if none is, explain why. The auditor checks that disclosure and reports any gap. Appointing an expert sounds like the stronger fix, but the section does not mandate one; whether and whom to appoint is the board's decision, not a compliance condition.

wrong_explanations.B: No rule requires members to hold a professional certification. Financial-expert criteria rest on experience and understanding, not on a designation.
wrong_explanations.C: Section 407 requires disclosure of whether an expert serves, not an appointment. Choosing members is the board's decision; the auditor reports any disclosure gap.
wrong_explanations.D: A sitting CFO is management. Placing them on the committee would destroy its independence from the people it oversees.

tips: Eliminate: B invents a certification rule, and D puts management on the body meant to oversee it.
Final two: A beats C because Section 407 requires disclosure of whether a financial expert serves, not that one be appointed.
Exam cue: when a stem cites a specific rule, pick what that rule actually requires, not a stronger-sounding version of it.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 407; SEC Regulation S-K Item 407(d)(5); Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 301 (Audit Committee Requirements)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit committee financial-expert composition under SOX 407 + SEC rules - at least one expert OR disclosed absence, criteria functional not credential-based'. questions.subtopic: Agile Auditing. Sprint Design and Retrospectives
questions.question: An IS audit manager is running the function's first agile audit in two-week sprints. Which retrospective practice BEST supports the agile approach?

options.A: No retrospectives, so the team stays focused on fieldwork
options.B: A team retrospective each sprint that feeds the next sprint plan
options.C: A single team retrospective held at the end of the engagement
options.D: A private review by the manager after each sprint

questions.key_concept: Agile audit sprints end with a team retrospective whose lessons feed directly into planning the next sprint.
questions.pre_read: Ask when the lessons would be used. A practice that only helps future engagements misses the point of sprints.
questions.correct_explanation: Agile auditing relies on short feedback loops: each sprint delivers a defined increment and ends with a team retrospective whose lessons shape the next sprint. That is how the engagement adapts while it is still running. A single end-of-engagement retrospective does capture lessons, but they arrive too late to improve this audit, which defeats the purpose of working in sprints.

wrong_explanations.A: Dropping retrospectives removes the feedback loop that makes sprints worthwhile. The team repeats problems instead of correcting them.
wrong_explanations.C: Lessons gathered only at the end cannot change the current engagement; it becomes a waterfall audit with a post-mortem.
wrong_explanations.D: A manager-only review loses the team's insight into what worked, and agile retrospectives are a whole-team activity.

tips: Eliminate: A removes the feedback loop entirely, and D shuts the team out of a whole-team practice.
Final two: B beats C because per-sprint lessons improve this engagement, while end-of-engagement lessons only help the next one.
Exam cue: in agile questions, prefer the option where feedback is frequent, shared by the team and fed into the next iteration.

questions.question: After an IS auditor preserves evidence of suspected fraud, the audit committee engages a forensic firm working under counsel's privilege. What is the auditor's MOST appropriate role going forward?

options.A: Continue independent analysis in parallel with the forensic firm
options.B: Withdraw from the matter entirely once the forensic firm starts
options.C: Support the forensic firm and report through the audit director
options.D: Take over coordination with external counsel from the audit director

questions.key_concept: When forensic specialists are engaged, the IS auditor supports the investigation and reports through established channels, without independent investigation.
questions.pre_read: Notice who now holds authority for the investigation. Ask what the auditor adds without duplicating or weakening that work.
questions.correct_explanation: Once authorized specialists take over, the IS auditor shifts to a supporting role: providing system context and access, preserving evidence and reporting through the established audit line. This keeps one controlled investigation under counsel's privilege. Parallel analysis looks diligent, but duplicate interviews or data handling can taint the chain of custody, waive privilege and alert suspects.

wrong_explanations.A: Running a second, unprivileged investigation risks contaminating evidence and undermining counsel's privilege over the forensic work.
wrong_explanations.B: The auditor still holds system knowledge and evidence the forensic team needs; walking away breaks continuity and the reporting channel.
wrong_explanations.D: Managing counsel is a legal and audit-director responsibility. The auditor bypassing the reporting line confuses authority over the matter.

tips: Eliminate: B abandons knowledge the investigators need, and D bypasses the audit director's authority over the reporting line.
Final two: C beats A because parallel analysis duplicates the specialists and risks tainting evidence and privilege; the auditor supports, not competes.
Exam cue: once fraud work is formally assigned to specialists, the auditor's best role is support and reporting, not independent investigation.

questions.question: An IS audit director is defining the audit universe for a group with 15 subsidiaries under four regulatory regimes and a shared IT services entity. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: One consolidated entity covering the entire group
options.B: One entry for each legal entity, mirroring the corporate structure exactly
options.C: Entries limited to subsidiaries above a revenue threshold
options.D: Entries per subsidiary and regime, plus shared services as cross-cutting

questions.key_concept: A multi-entity audit universe maps entities to their regulatory obligations and adds shared services as cross-cutting auditable entities.
questions.pre_read: Notice the shared IT services entity in the stem. Ask how a failure there would affect every subsidiary.
questions.correct_explanation: The audit universe should reflect where risk actually sits. Mapping each subsidiary to its regulatory regime captures differing compliance obligations, and treating shared IT services as cross-cutting entries recognizes that one failure there affects every subsidiary. Mirroring the legal structure covers every entity, but it hides the shared-service risk inside one subsidiary and ignores regime differences.

wrong_explanations.A: A single entity cannot distinguish regulatory regimes or risk profiles, so planning cannot prioritize anything within the group.
wrong_explanations.B: A legal-entity list treats shared IT services as just another subsidiary and misses that its controls support all fifteen.
wrong_explanations.C: Small subsidiaries still carry regulatory and control risk; they need a place in the universe, even if covered on rotation.

tips: Eliminate: A gives no granularity for prioritizing, and C drops small entities that still carry regulatory risk.
Final two: D beats B because risk follows regimes and shared services, which a legal-entity mirror cannot show.
Exam cue: define auditable entities by where risk concentrates, such as shared services and regulatory obligations, not by the org chart.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Planning

questions.question: An IS auditor must estimate the dollar value of billing errors in a population with known cargo-type strata that show different error patterns. Which sampling approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Stratified sampling, sizing the sample for each cargo type
options.B: Monetary-unit sampling across the whole population as one group
options.C: Judgmental selection of the largest transactions in the period
options.D: Attribute sampling to estimate the rate of billing deviations

questions.key_concept: When a population has known strata with differing error patterns, stratified sampling is more efficient and supports per-stratum conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem tells you the strata behave differently. Ask which design uses that knowledge instead of ignoring it.
questions.correct_explanation: When a population divides into known strata with different error patterns, stratified sampling sizes each stratum to its own variability. This gives a more efficient sample and supports conclusions per stratum as well as overall. Monetary-unit sampling is a strong choice for dollar errors, but it ignores the known structure, so error-prone small strata may be undersampled.

wrong_explanations.B: Monetary-unit sampling is valid for dollar estimates, but it weights only by value and ignores the known differences in error patterns between strata.
wrong_explanations.C: Judgmental selection cannot be projected statistically, so it cannot support an estimate of total dollar error.
wrong_explanations.D: Attribute sampling estimates how often a deviation occurs, not its dollar value, so it misses the stated objective.

tips: Eliminate: C cannot be projected to the population, and D measures a rate rather than a dollar amount.
Final two: A beats B because known strata with different error patterns call for design per stratum, which monetary-unit sampling ignores.
Exam cue: when the stem gives known subgroups that behave differently, stratification is usually the intended answer.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling; AICPA AU-C 530 (Audit Sampling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'sampling-technique selection between equally-defensible techniques - structural-fit deciding factor, stratified for known-strata-with-different-patterns'. questions.question: An IS audit director is scoping an audit of a machine-learning hiring model with known concerns in training data, validation, monitoring and retirement. Which scope is BEST?

options.A: Training-data controls, as data quality drives later stages
options.B: Each lifecycle stage, integrated into one end-to-end conclusion
options.C: Production monitoring and drift, as findings there are actionable
options.D: Model retirement, the one stage with a confirmed failure

questions.key_concept: An AI/ML audit covers each lifecycle stage with stage-specific procedures and integrates findings into one conclusion.
questions.pre_read: Count how many lifecycle stages the stem flags. A scope that skips any of them leaves a known concern untested.
questions.correct_explanation: AI risks arise at every lifecycle stage and interact across them; biased data, unrepresentative validation and missing drift monitoring compound each other. Scoping each stage with its own procedures and integrating the results gives a conclusion on the whole model. Focusing on training data is tempting because it feeds everything downstream, but it misses deployment, monitoring and retirement concerns already identified.

wrong_explanations.A: Training data is foundational, but validation gaps, drift and retirement issues can arise even with good data and would go untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Monitoring findings are actionable, but they cannot reveal biased training data or flawed validation upstream.
wrong_explanations.D: Auditing only the known failure ignores the other documented concerns, which may carry greater risk.

tips: Eliminate: C ignores upstream causes like biased data, and D audits one known failure while other concerns go untested.
Final two: B beats A because risks at each stage interact, and data-only scope leaves documented later-stage concerns unexamined.
Exam cue: when the stem lists concerns across several stages, the scope should cover every stage and integrate the results.

questions.subtopic: Continuous Auditing. Implementation Roadmap (Migration from Periodic)
questions.question: An IS audit director with eight staff and limited automation is moving to continuous auditing; the highest-risk system lacks reliable data feeds. Which rollout sequence is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Begin with the highest-risk system, building its data feeds first
options.B: Defer continuous auditing until full automation tooling exists
options.C: Pilot on well-instrumented systems, then expand by risk priority
options.D: Deploy across every key system at once to avoid delay

questions.key_concept: Continuous-auditing rollouts balance risk priority with feasibility: pilot where data is ready, then expand by risk.
questions.pre_read: Notice the constraints: small team, limited automation. Ask which sequence the function could actually execute successfully.
questions.correct_explanation: A small team with limited automation needs to build capability where data is already available, prove value, and then expand coverage in risk order. Starting with the highest-risk system sounds risk-based, but because its data feeds are unreliable, the team would spend months on plumbing before producing any assurance, and the program may stall.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk should drive expansion, but building feeds for the hardest system first stalls a small, inexperienced team before any routine runs.
wrong_explanations.B: Waiting for full tooling delays benefits indefinitely; capability and tooling usually mature together through use.
wrong_explanations.D: Eight staff cannot build and run continuous routines on every system at once; quality and coverage would both suffer.

tips: Eliminate: B postpones the change indefinitely, and D overwhelms a small team with simultaneous deployment.
Final two: C beats A because a working pilot builds capability first and risk then orders expansion; the riskiest system's unready feeds would stall the start.
Exam cue: for implementation roadmaps with limited resources, choose a staged pilot that then expands by risk.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Continuous Auditing; ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'continuous-auditing implementation roadmap - feasibility-led early wins plus risk-led expansion, distinct from pure-risk-first / simultaneous-everywhere / defer'. questions.subtopic: Whistleblower Allegation. Integration into Audit Conclusions
questions.question: Mid-engagement, the audit committee forwards an unsubstantiated whistleblower claim that a portfolio manager overstates performance, an area already in scope. What is the IS auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Disregard the claim because it is anonymous and unproven
options.B: Ask the portfolio manager to explain the reported performance results
options.C: Suspend the audit and refer the claim to law enforcement
options.D: Add targeted procedures on the claim while keeping it confidential

questions.key_concept: An in-flight audit addresses a whistleblower allegation with targeted, confidential procedures and reports only what evidence supports.
questions.pre_read: Notice the claim is unsubstantiated but in scope. Ask what the auditor can do within existing authority without tipping anyone off.
questions.correct_explanation: An allegation in an area already in scope should shape the work: the auditor designs procedures aimed at the specific claim, keeps the source and subject confidential, and reports findings only where evidence supports them. Referring to law enforcement may come later, but an unsubstantiated claim does not justify suspending the audit, and that decision belongs to management and counsel.

wrong_explanations.A: Anonymous claims can still be credible; ignoring one in an in-scope area risks missing a material misstatement.
wrong_explanations.B: Approaching the named individual tips them off and could lead to evidence being altered or destroyed.
wrong_explanations.C: An unverified claim does not yet warrant referral, and referral decisions belong to management and counsel, not the auditor.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores a credible in-scope risk, and B tips off the person named in the claim.
Final two: D beats C because unverified claims call for evidence first; referral is a later decision for management and counsel.
Exam cue: for an unproven allegation, gather evidence discreetly within audit authority before any escalation beyond the audit committee.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1207 (Irregularities and Illegal Acts); ITAF Performance Standards on Fraud Risk; ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'whistleblower allegation integration into audit conclusions - targeted scope expansion plus confidentiality plus confidential-annex documentation plus findings-only-when-supported, distinct from ignore / suspend / confront'. questions.subtopic: Risk Assessment. Method Choice (Heat Map vs FAIR vs ISO 31000)
questions.question: An IS audit director must choose a risk assessment method; the CISO wants dollar-loss figures, and the audit committee wants a regulator-defensible process. Which approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: A heat map, as it is simplest for executives to read
options.B: An ISO 31000 process, with FAIR quantifying priority risks
options.C: FAIR across the entire register, as quantitative results are more rigorous
options.D: Whichever method can be implemented fastest across the register

questions.key_concept: Risk methods can be layered: a principles-based framework for governance, with quantitative modeling applied to priority risks.
questions.pre_read: List what each stakeholder asked for. The best answer satisfies both needs without wasting effort on low-priority risks.
questions.correct_explanation: Methods can be layered to serve different needs. ISO 31000 supplies a principles-based process that regulators recognize, while FAIR quantifies loss exposure for the highest-priority risks where dollar figures matter. Applying FAIR across the whole register sounds rigorous, but it is costly for low-priority risks and still lacks the governance process the audit committee asked for.

wrong_explanations.A: A heat map communicates well but gives neither dollar-loss figures nor a defensible process framework.
wrong_explanations.C: Quantifying every risk is expensive and data-hungry, and FAIR alone does not supply the governance process regulators expect.
wrong_explanations.D: Speed of implementation ignores both stated stakeholder needs; method choice should follow the purpose of the assessment.

tips: Eliminate: D ignores both stated needs, and the heat map in option A gives neither dollar figures nor process.
Final two: B beats C because the framework supplies defensibility and FAIR is reserved for priority risks; FAIR everywhere lacks the governance process.
Exam cue: when stakeholders need different outputs, look for the option that combines methods, each fitted to its purpose.
questions.framework_ref: ISO/IEC 31000:2018 (Risk Management); FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk) Institute; ISACA Risk IT Framework; ITAF Performance Standards on Risk Assessment

Public source: ISO 31000 + FAIR + ISACA Risk IT. All scenario specifics (enterprise SaaS company, CISO + CRO + audit committee stakeholders) invented for this question. questions.subtopic: SOX Context. Continuous Monitoring vs Continuous Auditing Applied
questions.question: Management claims its IT-operated continuous monitoring system also serves as internal audit's continuous auditing, since audit reviews its summary outputs. What is the IS auditor's BEST evaluation?

options.A: Monitoring belongs to management; audit still needs independent procedures
options.B: The claim is valid because audit reviews the summary outputs every quarter
options.C: The claim is valid because it avoids duplicating control work
options.D: Audit should rely on the system once its alert rules are validated

questions.key_concept: Continuous monitoring belongs to management; continuous auditing is audit's independent activity, and one cannot substitute for the other.
questions.pre_read: Notice who operates the system. Ask whether audit's role would remain independent if it relied on that system's outputs.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuous monitoring is a management activity within its own monitoring component; continuous auditing is the audit function's independent testing. Reviewing outputs from a system run by IT operations does not make it independent. Validating the alert rules is useful, and audit may use the results, but management still operates and can change the system, so it cannot replace audit's own procedures.

wrong_explanations.B: Reading summaries produced by management's system is review, not independent testing; audit sees only what that system chooses to report.
wrong_explanations.C: Avoiding duplication is a fair goal, but collapsing the two roles removes the independence that gives audit its value.
wrong_explanations.D: A one-time validation does not make a management-operated system independent; rules can change after audit checks them.

tips: Eliminate: B and C both accept management's claim, though reviewing management's outputs is not independent testing.
Final two: A beats D because a validated system is still run and changed by management; independence needs audit's own procedures.
Exam cue: when management's tool is offered as audit evidence, ask who operates it; if management does, audit still needs independent work.
questions.framework_ref: Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 404 (Management Assessment of Internal Controls); COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework (2013); PCAOB AS 2201 (Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting); ITAF Tools and Techniques on Continuous Auditing

Public source: SOX 404 + COSO 2013 + PCAOB AS 2201/2605. questions.subtopic: External Auditor Coordination. Integrated Audit Boundaries
questions.question: An internal audit director is preparing for a company's first integrated audit, in which the external auditor may rely on internal audit's IT control testing. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Transfer reporting of internal audit to the external audit firm
options.B: Have the external firm preapprove every internal audit procedure
options.C: Coordinate through agreed protocols while keeping separate reporting lines
options.D: Avoid coordination so that each function's independence is protected

questions.key_concept: Internal and external auditors coordinate through agreed protocols while each keeps its own reporting line and independence.
questions.pre_read: Ask where independence actually comes from. Then judge whether coordination threatens it or simply avoids duplicated work.
questions.correct_explanation: Internal and external auditors are expected to coordinate: agreeing which controls each tests, documentation standards and reliance terms avoids duplicated effort. Each function keeps its own reporting line, which preserves independence. Avoiding coordination sounds protective, but independence comes from reporting lines, not isolation, and refusing coordination wastes effort and blocks reliance the standards allow.

wrong_explanations.A: Internal audit reports to the audit committee; reporting to the external firm would subordinate it and break its organizational independence.
wrong_explanations.B: Preapproval hands control of the internal audit plan to the external firm, undermining internal audit's own risk-based priorities.
wrong_explanations.D: Isolation duplicates work and prevents reliance; independence is protected by reporting lines, not by refusing to coordinate.

tips: Eliminate: A breaks internal audit's reporting line, and B hands its plan to the external firm.
Final two: C beats D because independence comes from separate reporting lines, so coordination is expected and enables reliance.
Exam cue: coordination between audit functions is good practice; the red flag is any option that merges or subordinates reporting lines.
questions.framework_ref: PCAOB AS 2605 (Consideration of the Internal Audit Function); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 7.1 (Organizational Independence); Sarbanes-Oxley Act Section 301; ISACA IT Audit Standard 1001 (Audit Charter)

questions.subtopic: Audit Phases. End-to-End Engagement Design Synthesis
questions.question: An IS audit director with a small team plans an engagement whose results go to the audit committee, a regulator and a mission committee. Which engagement design is BEST?

options.A: Each phase optimized on its own for whichever stakeholder it serves
options.B: The three phases compressed into one short sprint
options.C: Separate reports for each audience, each with its own conclusions
options.D: Risk-based scope, tiered fieldwork and one report with tailored sections

questions.key_concept: An engagement links risk-based planning, tiered fieldwork and one report whose sections are tailored to each audience.
questions.pre_read: Separate what changes by audience from what must stay the same. The conclusions should never change.
questions.correct_explanation: Planning, fieldwork and reporting should form one chain: risk-based scope directs where a small team spends effort, and a single report with sections tailored to each audience keeps one set of conclusions. Separate reports per audience seem responsive, but they allow conclusions to diverge, which undermines the audit's objectivity and confuses governance.

wrong_explanations.A: Optimizing phases in isolation breaks the link between scope, evidence and conclusions, so the report may not rest on the planned work.
wrong_explanations.B: Compressing the phases sacrifices planning and supervision quality; a small team still needs disciplined engagement steps to support conclusions for three audiences.
wrong_explanations.C: Tailoring presentation is fine, but divergent conclusions for different readers compromise objectivity and consistency.

tips: Eliminate: A disconnects the phases from each other, and B sacrifices planning and supervision to save time.
Final two: D beats C because one set of conclusions can be presented differently, while separate conclusions compromise objectivity.
Exam cue: tailor how findings are presented to each audience, never what the findings conclude.

questions.subtopic: COSO Component 5. Separate Evaluations vs Ongoing Evaluations
questions.question: An IS auditor is reviewing management's monitoring activities under COSO. Which activity BEST illustrates an ongoing evaluation rather than a separate evaluation?

options.A: An annual control self-assessment completed by the process owners
options.B: Supervisor review of daily exception reports within operations
options.C: A periodic internal audit of access controls
options.D: A one-time external consultant review of key controls

questions.key_concept: COSO ongoing evaluations are embedded in routine operations; separate evaluations are periodic standalone reviews, whoever performs them.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether the activity happens as part of daily work or as a step back at intervals.
questions.correct_explanation: Under COSO, ongoing evaluations are built into normal business processes and run routinely, such as supervisors reviewing daily exception reports. Separate evaluations are periodic, standalone reviews that step back from operations. An annual self-assessment is done by process owners, which makes it feel embedded, but it is still a periodic standalone exercise, so it is a separate evaluation.

wrong_explanations.A: Although process owners perform it, an annual self-assessment is a periodic standalone review, which COSO treats as a separate evaluation.
wrong_explanations.C: Internal audit reviews are the classic example of a separate evaluation, performed periodically and outside daily operations.
wrong_explanations.D: A one-time external review is standalone by nature, so it is a separate evaluation.

tips: Eliminate: C and D are standalone reviews by parties outside daily operations.
Final two: B beats A because ongoing evaluations run inside routine operations; an annual self-assessment is periodic, however close to the process.
Exam cue: classify monitoring by when and how it runs, not by who performs it; routine and embedded means ongoing.

questions.question: An IS auditor must test a full year of tuition-billing transactions for duplicates and gaps, independently of system reports. Which technique is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Generalized audit software run over an extract of the file
options.B: An embedded audit module that flags transactions as they post
options.C: The application's standard duplicate and exception reports
options.D: Test data processed through the billing application

questions.key_concept: Generalized audit software lets the auditor independently query a full extract of existing transaction data.
questions.pre_read: Notice the data already exists for a full year. Ask which technique examines historical records with the auditor's own logic.
questions.correct_explanation: Generalized audit software reads a copy of the data into an auditor-controlled tool and applies the auditor's own queries, such as duplicate and gap tests, across the whole population. That yields independent evidence on historical transactions. An embedded audit module is a strong continuous technique, but it must be built into the system and only captures transactions after installation, not the past year.

wrong_explanations.B: Embedded modules capture transactions going forward; they cannot examine the year that has already been processed.
wrong_explanations.C: System-generated reports are what the auditor must not rely on here; their logic is untested and controlled by the auditee.
wrong_explanations.D: Test data checks how the program processes sample inputs, not what is in the existing transaction history.

tips: Eliminate: C relies on the auditee's own reports, and D tests program logic rather than existing data.
Final two: A beats B because the population is historical; an embedded module only sees transactions processed after installation.
Exam cue: analyzing existing data independently points to audit software; testing processing logic points to test data or ITF.

questions.question: An IS auditor wants to verify that the loan application's credit-decision logic produces expected results during normal production processing. Which technique is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Generalized audit software analysis of extracted loan records
options.B: Test data run in a separate copy of the application
options.C: Fictitious test entities processed alongside live loan transactions
options.D: Parallel simulation of the logic using the auditor's program

questions.key_concept: An integrated test facility runs fictitious entities through the live production system and compares actual with expected results.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem wants the logic tested during normal production. Ask which technique uses the live program itself.
questions.correct_explanation: An integrated test facility creates fictitious entities inside the live system, so test transactions pass through the actual production programs alongside real ones, and the auditor compares results to expected outcomes. Parallel simulation also checks logic, but it reprocesses data through the auditor's own replica of the rules, so it tests the auditor's model rather than the live program.

wrong_explanations.A: Audit software analyzes the data already produced; it does not exercise the decision logic with known inputs and expected outputs.
wrong_explanations.B: A separate copy may differ from what is running in production, so it does not test production processing.
wrong_explanations.D: Parallel simulation compares results using the auditor's replica of the logic, not the live program processing transactions.

tips: Eliminate: A analyzes stored data instead of exercising logic, and B tests a copy that may differ from production.
Final two: C beats D because test entities run through the live program, while parallel simulation tests the auditor's own replica.
Exam cue: testing logic during live production processing with dummy entities points to an integrated test facility.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Tools and Techniques on CAATs

Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques on CAATs. All scenario specifics (savings & loan association, loan-origination credit-decision controls) invented for this question.
