questions.subtopic: Ongoing QA Monitoring. Automated Work-Paper Review
questions.question: An IS audit director adopts a tool that checks work papers for sign-offs, cross-references and attached evidence. What is the MOST important consideration when relying on it for quality monitoring?

options.A: Whether it is limited to papers the director has flagged
options.B: Whether the tool's rule set matches documentation standards
options.C: Whether running it reduces the director's manual review time
options.D: Whether reviewers still assess conclusions and evidence sufficiency

questions.key_concept: Automated work-paper tools check documentation form; human review is still needed for the substance of evidence and conclusions.
questions.pre_read: List what the tool checks. Then ask what quality monitoring needs that those checks cannot see.
questions.correct_explanation: Automated checks confirm the form of documentation, such as sign-offs and attachments, but cannot judge whether evidence is sufficient or conclusions are supported. Quality monitoring therefore still needs human review of substance. Configuring the rules correctly matters, but even a perfectly configured tool only checks form, so it cannot be the main basis of assurance.

wrong_explanations.A: Limiting the tool to flagged papers shrinks coverage and adds bias; the tool's value is consistent checking across all papers.
wrong_explanations.B: Accurate rules are necessary, but they only make the formal checks reliable; they still cannot assess substance.
wrong_explanations.C: Saving time is a benefit, not an assurance consideration; reducing human review is exactly the risk to manage.

tips: Eliminate: A narrows coverage to flagged papers, and C treats saved time as if it were assurance.
Final two: D beats B because correct rules only perfect the formal checks; substance still needs human judgment.
Exam cue: automation can check form, not judgment; the best answer keeps humans on conclusions and evidence sufficiency.
questions.framework_ref: IIA Quality Assessment and Improvement Program (QAIP); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 12.1 (Internal Quality Assessment); ITAF General Standards on Quality
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'automated work-paper review tool - mechanical compliance scope, human substantive review remains required'. Public source: IIA Standard 1311 + ISACA QAIP. All scenario specifics (art-museum endowment fund) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_048 (monitoring failure), d1_076 (internal program design), d1_099 (design depth). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Control Classifications. Preventive vs Detective vs Corrective
questions.question: Management's monthly access review finds active accounts belonging to terminated staff. Which action would an IS auditor BEST classify as a corrective control?

options.A: Revoking the accounts and reviewing activity since termination
options.B: Linking HR termination events to automatic account disablement
options.C: Increasing the frequency of the access review to weekly
options.D: Requiring manager approval for new account requests

questions.key_concept: Preventive controls stop events, detective controls find them, and corrective controls remedy the detected condition and its effects.
questions.pre_read: Ask whether each action happens before the problem, while finding it, or after it has been found.
questions.correct_explanation: A corrective control remedies a condition after it has been detected and limits its effects: revoking the accounts and checking what they did since termination does exactly that. Automatic disablement is the better long-term fix, but it acts before the next termination occurs, which makes it a preventive control rather than a corrective one.

wrong_explanations.B: Automated disablement stops future terminated accounts from staying active; it prevents recurrence rather than correcting the existing condition.
wrong_explanations.C: A more frequent review finds problems sooner; it is still a detective control.
wrong_explanations.D: Approval of new accounts is a preventive control on provisioning and does not address terminated users.

tips: Eliminate: C is still a detective control, and D governs new accounts, not terminations.
Final two: A beats B because corrective controls fix the detected condition; automated disablement prevents future occurrences, so it is preventive.
Exam cue: classify by timing: before the event is preventive, finding it is detective, fixing it afterwards is corrective.
questions.framework_ref: COBIT 2019; ITAF Performance Standards on Control Evaluation; NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 AC-2 (Account Management)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'control classifications preventive vs detective vs corrective - timing-based distinction'. Public source: ISACA IT Audit Standards + COBIT 2019. All scenario specifics (wholesale auto-parts distributor) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_008/012 (classification basics). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Control Relationship to Risk. Multi-Control Defense in Depth
questions.question: An IS auditor is evaluating five layered controls protecting stored payment data. Which approach BEST assesses whether they provide defense in depth?

options.A: Count the layers, as more controls mean stronger protection
options.B: Assess how the layers combine to cover each failure mode
options.C: Test the strongest layer thoroughly and rely on it alone
options.D: Test each layer separately as an independent control

questions.key_concept: Defense in depth is evaluated by whether the layers together cover each failure mode, not by their number.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens when one layer fails. The right approach checks whether another layer catches it.
questions.correct_explanation: Defense in depth works when layers back each other up, so a failure in one is caught or contained by another. The auditor must judge whether the combined layers cover each way the data could be exposed. Testing each layer separately confirms individual effectiveness, but it cannot reveal gaps where every layer shares the same blind spot.

wrong_explanations.A: The number of layers says nothing about whether they cover different failure modes; five overlapping controls can share one gap.
wrong_explanations.C: Relying on one control is the opposite of defense in depth; any failure in it leaves the data unprotected.
wrong_explanations.D: Isolated testing shows each control works, but not whether the layers together leave a gap.

tips: Eliminate: A judges by count rather than coverage, and C relies on a single control.
Final two: B beats D because defense in depth depends on how layers cover each other's failures, which isolated tests cannot show.
Exam cue: for layered controls, look for the option that evaluates combined coverage, not individual layers or their number.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ITAF Performance Standards on Control Evaluation; NIST SP 800-53 (Defense in Depth Concept)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'multi-control defense in depth - individual effectiveness plus complementary failure-mode coverage'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + NIST SP 800-53. All scenario specifics (cable-TV provider, five-layer payment-information defense) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_047 (single-control to risk mapping). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: After an IS audit report is issued, a research committee asks that findings on research access be removed to protect its reputation. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Issue a separate version of the report for the committee
options.B: Remove the findings, since research access carries lower risk
options.C: Add a note that research access was outside the audit's main focus
options.D: Retain the findings and review the evidence with the committee

questions.key_concept: Reported findings change only on new evidence; stakeholder disagreement is addressed by discussing the factual basis.
questions.pre_read: Ask what would legitimately change a finding. Stakeholder preference is not on that list.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit findings rest on evidence, not on how stakeholders feel about them. The auditor keeps the findings and engages the committee on facts, correcting only if evidence shows an error. Adding a note that downplays research access seems like a harmless compromise, but it misrepresents the audit's scope and still bends the report to stakeholder pressure.

wrong_explanations.A: Different versions for different readers produce inconsistent conclusions and undermine the report's objectivity.
wrong_explanations.B: The committee's preference is not evidence of lower risk; removing supported findings sacrifices objectivity.
wrong_explanations.C: A note downplaying the area misstates the audit scope and dilutes supported findings under stakeholder pressure.

tips: Eliminate: A creates inconsistent versions of the report, and B removes findings without evidence.
Final two: D beats C because a scope note that softens findings still yields to pressure; only evidence should change a report.
Exam cue: when stakeholders object to findings, discuss the facts but change the report only if the evidence changes.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ITAF Performance Standards on Communication of Results; ISACA Code of Professional Ethics (Independence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'multi-stakeholder conflict in audit reporting - single coherent report plus appropriate per-stakeholder engagement, decline pressure for coverage / severity adjustments without factual basis'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1401 + Code of Professional Ethics. All scenario specifics (research-university hospital, three stakeholder responses) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_006/016/050/068/079/120/129 prior reporting questions. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Management faces an $850K expected annual fraud loss; new controls cost $500K once plus $300K yearly and cut losses to $80K; insurance costs $620K yearly. Which treatment is MOST defensible?

options.A: Accept the risk, as it needs no upfront spending
options.B: Transfer the risk through the $620K yearly insurance policy
options.C: Reduce the risk with the new fraud-detection controls
options.D: Avoid the risk by discontinuing the affected rewards program

questions.key_concept: Risk treatment is chosen by cost-benefit and residual risk across years, not by the lowest first-year outlay.
questions.pre_read: Compare recurring costs with the yearly loss avoided. Then ask which option actually reduces the underlying risk.
questions.correct_explanation: Reducing the risk cuts expected loss by $770K a year for $300K of running cost, so the $500K upfront spend pays back in about a year against acceptance and about two years against insurance, and residual risk falls sharply. Insurance avoids capital outlay, but it costs more each year than the controls and leaves the weakness in place.

wrong_explanations.A: Acceptance costs about $850K every year with no improvement; avoiding upfront spending is not a cost-benefit argument.
wrong_explanations.B: Insurance costs $620K a year versus $380K for controls plus residual loss, so it overtakes the $500K upfront cost within about two years and leaves the weakness in place.
wrong_explanations.D: Ending the program removes the risk but also its business benefits; avoidance suits risks that cannot be reduced economically.

tips: Eliminate: A keeps paying the full loss every year, and D gives up the program's benefits when cheaper treatments exist.
Final two: C beats B because controls plus residual loss cost $240K a year less than insurance, recovering the upfront spend in about two years.
Exam cue: compare annual cost against loss reduction, and prefer the treatment that lowers residual risk rather than only financing it.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ISO/IEC 31000:2018 (Risk Management); ITAF Performance Standards on Risk Assessment
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'risk treatment specific scenario applied - cost-benefit math with one-time + ongoing + loss-reduction + break-even + residual'. Public source: ISACA Risk IT + ISO 31000. All scenario specifics (commercial bakery, customer-loyalty program, four-option cost-benefit) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_033 (treatment options definition) and d1_124 (multi-control trade-offs). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: The audit committee chair proposes amending the audit charter so IS audit advises operations on control design before implementation. What is the audit director's BEST response?

options.A: Raise the self-review threat and propose recusal safeguards
options.B: Accept the amendment, as early advice improves control design
options.C: Route advisory requests to a single junior auditor
options.D: Reject it, as an approved charter should not be amended

questions.key_concept: Advisory work on controls the function later audits creates a self-review threat that needs disclosure and recusal safeguards.
questions.pre_read: Ask what happens when audit later tests the controls it helped design.
questions.correct_explanation: Advising on control design and later auditing the same controls creates a self-review threat. The director should explain that threat and offer a workable model, such as disclosed advisory work with recusal of those involved from later audits. Accepting the amendment unchanged captures real value from early input, but leaves the independence threat unmanaged.

wrong_explanations.B: Early advice does add value, but accepting without safeguards leaves the function auditing its own recommendations.
wrong_explanations.C: Seniority does not remove a self-review threat; a junior auditor advising on controls the function later audits faces the same conflict.
wrong_explanations.D: Charters can and should be updated; the issue is the independence safeguards, not whether amendments are allowed.

tips: Eliminate: C assumes seniority affects independence, and D treats the charter as unchangeable.
Final two: A beats B because advisory work is acceptable only with safeguards; accepting unchanged leaves auditors reviewing their own advice.
Exam cue: when audit is offered an advisory role, the best answer names the independence threat and proposes safeguards.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1003 (Auditor's Professional Independence); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1001 (Audit Charter); ISACA Code of Professional Ethics; ITAF General Standards on Independence
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit charter modification scenario - identify independence threat (self-review), decline as proposed, offer boundaried alternatives'. Public source: ISACA Standards 1001 + 1003 + Code of Professional Ethics. All scenario specifics (regional pension fund, audit-committee-chair proposing consultative responsibility) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_001/052/113 prior charter questions. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Sampling. Combined Attribute and Substantive in One Engagement
questions.question: An IS auditor must test whether dual approval operates on large invoices and estimate the dollar value of unauthorized payments. Which sampling plan is MOST appropriate?

options.A: One combined sample sized for the larger objective
options.B: Separate attribute and variables samples, sharing items where valid
options.C: One judgmental sample of 100 high-value invoices
options.D: An attribute sample, inferring dollar impact from the deviations

questions.key_concept: Compliance and substantive objectives require separate attribute and variables sample designs, with shared items reused where valid.
questions.pre_read: Notice the stem has two different questions: a yes/no control test and a dollar estimate.
questions.correct_explanation: The two objectives need different designs: an attribute sample sized to a tolerable deviation rate for the control, and a variables or monetary-unit sample for the dollar estimate. Reusing items where they overlap keeps effort down. A single combined sample sounds efficient, but it cannot be sized correctly for both objectives, so at least one conclusion would lack statistical support.

wrong_explanations.A: One sample sized for either objective will be the wrong size or design for the other, weakening one conclusion.
wrong_explanations.C: Judgmental selection cannot be projected statistically, so neither the deviation rate nor the dollar value can be estimated.
wrong_explanations.D: A deviation rate does not translate into a dollar value; the substantive objective needs its own estimation sample.

tips: Eliminate: C cannot be projected statistically, and D tries to get a dollar estimate from a deviation rate.
Final two: B beats A because each objective needs its own design, and overlap can still be reused to save effort.
Exam cue: control operation calls for attribute sampling; dollar estimation calls for variables sampling; two objectives mean two designs.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling; AICPA AU-C 530 (Audit Sampling)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'combined attribute and substantive sampling in one engagement - two designs with shared selection where valid, distinct from one-sample-for-both / judgmental-shortcut / management-representations'. Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Sampling. All scenario specifics (aerospace parts manufacturer, supplier-invoice-approval system, dual-approval threshold, dollar-value substantive estimation) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_086 (multi-objective scenario including 100% testing for zero-tolerance), d1_143 (selection between equally-defensible techniques). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: A continuous auditing routine shows fees on one trading pair deviating about 6% from schedule, consistently for three weeks, though tiny per trade. What is the IS auditor's MOST appropriate response?

options.A: Log it as noise, given the tiny per-trade impact
options.B: Refer it to law enforcement as possible financial crime
options.C: Investigate likely causes such as misconfiguration with targeted tests
options.D: Keep monitoring for another full month to confirm the pattern first

questions.key_concept: A consistent anomaly from continuous auditing signals a systematic cause that warrants targeted investigation, even if per-item impact is small.
questions.pre_read: Notice two signals: the deviation is consistent over time, and small amounts add up.
questions.correct_explanation: A deviation that persists for three weeks points to a systematic cause rather than noise, and small per-trade amounts can be material in aggregate. The auditor should identify plausible causes, such as fee misconfiguration, rounding or manipulation, and test them. Further monitoring seems prudent, but the pattern is already established, and waiting only extends the exposure.

wrong_explanations.A: A consistent pattern is not noise; small per-trade differences can add up to a material total.
wrong_explanations.B: No cause has been identified yet; referral before investigation is premature and outside the auditor's authority.
wrong_explanations.D: Three weeks of consistent deviation already confirms the pattern; more waiting adds loss without adding insight.

tips: Eliminate: A dismisses a consistent pattern as noise, and B escalates before any cause is known.
Final two: C beats D because the pattern is already established; investigating now finds the cause while waiting prolongs exposure.
Exam cue: a consistent anomaly means a systematic cause; investigate it with targeted procedures before escalating or dismissing.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Continuous Auditing; ISACA IT Audit Standard 1207 (Irregularities and Illegal Acts); ISACA "Auditing Cryptocurrency Operations" guidance
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'CA anomaly investigation depth - pattern consistency plus aggregate impact drives investigation depth, distinct from document-and-move-on / suspend-operations / direct-law-enforcement-referral'. Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques + ISACA Standard 1207. All scenario specifics (cryptocurrency exchange, trading-fees revenue deviation, 6% over 3 weeks) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_046/083/092/110/130/145/148 prior CA questions. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor is auditing a vendor-hosted AI model; the vendor withholds training data and design but provides a SOC 2 Type 2 report without AI coverage. Which approach is BEST?

options.A: Exclude the model from scope as it cannot be inspected
options.B: Rely on the SOC 2 report as sufficient model assurance
options.C: Suspend the audit until the vendor fully discloses its training data
options.D: Use the SOC 2 report and test outputs on company data

questions.key_concept: For third-party AI models, combine the vendor's assurance report with output testing on the company's own data.
questions.pre_read: Check what the SOC 2 report actually covers. Then ask how to test what it leaves out.
questions.correct_explanation: When inner workings are hidden, the auditor combines sources: the SOC 2 report gives assurance on the vendor's general controls, and testing outputs against the company's own data shows whether the model behaves as expected in this use. Relying on the SOC 2 report alone is tempting, but it does not cover the model's behavior, so the key risk is untested.

wrong_explanations.A: Limited transparency does not remove the risk; the model can still be tested through its outputs.
wrong_explanations.B: The report covers the vendor's general controls, not model accuracy or bias, so model risk would remain untested.
wrong_explanations.C: Demanding trade secrets the vendor will not release stalls the audit when alternative procedures can still provide evidence.

tips: Eliminate: A drops a risk that can still be tested, and C stalls the audit on an unrealistic demand.
Final two: D beats B because the report omits model behavior; output testing covers the gap it leaves.
Exam cue: when a third-party report does not cover a key risk, add procedures for that risk rather than relying on the report.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA "Auditing Artificial Intelligence" (IT Audit and Assurance Program); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1206 (Using the Work of Other Experts); ITAF Performance Standards on Third-Party Audit Reports (SOC 2)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'vendor AI/ML model audit - layered approach (SOC 2 + transparency + output + contract + limitations), distinct from exclude / demand-full / sole-SOC-reliance'. Public source: ISACA Auditing AI program + ISACA Standard 1206 + ITAF SOC 2 reliance guidance. All scenario specifics (national retail chain, customer-segmentation vendor AI, vendor cloud-hosted with SOC 2) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_018/057/066/080/085/108/119/144 prior AI/ML questions. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Management's self-assessment rated all controls effective, but the IS auditor's testing found two control failures it did not report. How should the auditor BEST address this in the report?

options.A: Report the failures and note the gap in management's monitoring
options.B: Report the failures without referring to the self-assessment
options.C: Align the findings with management's self-assessment results
options.D: Present both sets of results and let readers reconcile them

questions.key_concept: When management's self-assessment misses failures the auditor found, that gap is a separate observation on monitoring effectiveness.
questions.pre_read: Ask what it means that management's own process missed these failures.
questions.correct_explanation: The auditor's independently tested findings form the conclusion. The fact that management's self-assessment missed both failures is itself evidence that management's monitoring is not working, so it deserves its own observation. Reporting only the failures is accurate, but it hides a second weakness: the process meant to catch these failures did not.

wrong_explanations.B: The failures are reported, but the monitoring weakness that let them go unnoticed is left out.
wrong_explanations.C: Management's view does not override independent evidence; aligning to it would compromise objectivity.
wrong_explanations.D: The auditor must reach a conclusion; leaving readers to reconcile conflicting results abdicates that responsibility.

tips: Eliminate: C lets management's view override evidence, and D leaves readers to draw the conclusion.
Final two: A beats B because the missed failures reveal a monitoring weakness, which is itself a reportable observation.
Exam cue: when management's monitoring misses what the auditor finds, the monitoring gap is a finding too.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ITAF Performance Standards on Communication of Results; COSO Internal Control - Integrated Framework (2013) Component 5
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit-vs-self-assessment divergence as a finding about monitoring effectiveness, distinct from omit / align / fragment'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1401 + COSO 2013 Component 5. All scenario specifics (state professional-licensing agency, audit findings vs management quarterly self-assessment) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_098/118/151 management-monitoring questions. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Legal counsel issues a litigation hold, and prior-year IS audit work papers related to the matter are due for routine destruction. What should the audit function do FIRST?

options.A: Destroy them according to the approved retention schedule
options.B: Suspend destruction and preserve them under access controls
options.C: Transfer all related work papers to legal counsel's custody
options.D: Decline the hold because audit work papers are privileged

questions.key_concept: A litigation hold suspends routine retention; the audit function preserves relevant documentation under control and coordinates scope with counsel.
questions.pre_read: Notice the conflict between the hold and the retention schedule, and the word FIRST. Decide which obligation takes priority.
questions.correct_explanation: A litigation hold overrides the normal retention schedule. The audit function must immediately suspend destruction of potentially relevant documentation and preserve it under access controls, then coordinate with counsel on hold scope. Destroying covered records risks spoliation sanctions. Handing everything to counsel may seem compliant, but the audit function remains custodian of its records and must still manage them.

wrong_explanations.A: Following the schedule after a hold notice risks spoliation of evidence. The hold supersedes routine retention.
wrong_explanations.C: Counsel directs the hold, but wholesale transfer is not required. The audit function stays responsible for preserving its records.
wrong_explanations.D: Audit work papers are generally not privileged, and privilege calls belong to counsel, not the audit function.

tips: Eliminate: A risks spoliation of evidence, and D misreads privilege, which counsel, not audit, determines.
Final two: B beats C because preservation in place is the immediate duty; transferring custody is not required and abdicates responsibility.
Exam cue: a litigation hold always suspends routine destruction; preserve first, then coordinate the scope with counsel.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1208 (Audit Documentation); ITAF Performance Standards on Documentation; Federal Rules of Civil Procedure Rule 37 (Failure to Make Disclosures or to Cooperate in Discovery — Sanctions, including spoliation)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'litigation hold response - suspend retention + coordinate with counsel + apply prospectively and retrospectively + document, distinct from standard retention / refuse / full delegation'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1208 + FRCP Rule 37. All scenario specifics (food-and-beverage distributor, former-customer litigation, 3-year-old work papers, ongoing audit) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_043/101/122 prior documentation questions. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: Mid-fieldwork, an IS auditor finds operations gave inaccurate planning information that undermines the risk assessment; the audit committee meets tomorrow to decide the engagement's future. What should the audit director do FIRST?

options.A: Continue fieldwork as planned and note the issue in the report
options.B: Pause work and brief the audit committee on options
options.C: Quietly investigate the inaccurate information before telling anyone
options.D: Revise the risk assessment and expand scope immediately

questions.key_concept: When material new facts undermine an engagement, pause, document and let the audit committee decide how to proceed.
questions.pre_read: Notice the risk assessment is now unreliable and the committee is already engaged. Ask who should decide the next step.
questions.correct_explanation: When the basis of the engagement is undermined, the director should pause, document why, and give the audit committee options such as resuming, expanding scope or stopping, so the decision is informed and authorized. Revising the plan is a natural audit reaction, but expanding scope alone preempts a committee that meets tomorrow to decide the engagement's future.

wrong_explanations.A: The plan rests on a risk assessment now known to be unreliable; continuing produces conclusions on a flawed basis.
wrong_explanations.C: Withholding a material issue from the audit committee undermines governance and exceeds the auditor's authority.
wrong_explanations.D: The plan may need revising, but the committee is about to decide the engagement's future and needs the options first, not a scope change already made.

tips: Eliminate: A carries on with a flawed plan, and C hides a material issue from the audit committee.
Final two: B beats D because material changes need the committee's decision; expanding scope alone preempts its governance role.
Exam cue: when the engagement's basis collapses, pause, document and let those charged with governance decide the path forward.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Engagement Planning); Standard 1203 (Performance and Supervision); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1207 (Irregularities and Illegal Acts); ITAF Performance Standards on Engagement Conduct
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'mid-engagement stop-work decision when material new information emerges - stop + document + report with options + audit committee decides + preserve evidence'. Public source: ISACA Standards 1201/1203/1207. All scenario specifics (regional logistics carrier, dispatch-management audit, three concurrent disruption facts) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_106 (mid-cycle update for plan), d1_127 (resource constraint plan adjustment), d1_165 stop-work specifics. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem. Learner-impact review (Oct 2026): stem now says the committee meets tomorrow to decide the engagement's future, so revising scope alone is clearly second.

questions.subtopic: Audit Resource Management. Engagement-Level Budget Reduction
questions.question: Halfway through an engagement, before substantive testing starts, the IS audit director's budget is cut by 30%. What is the director's BEST response?

options.A: Issue the report now based on procedures already completed
options.B: Reprioritize remaining procedures by risk and disclose the scope reduction
options.C: Reduce sample sizes evenly across every remaining procedure in the program
options.D: Replace remaining substantive tests with written management representations

questions.key_concept: When budgets shrink mid-engagement, reallocate remaining effort by risk and disclose any resulting scope reduction.
questions.pre_read: Notice the work is half done with no substantive testing yet. Ask how to spend reduced hours where risk is highest.
questions.correct_explanation: A budget cut changes how much work can be done, not the evidence needed for what is concluded. The director should redirect remaining effort to the highest-risk areas and disclose the resulting scope reduction so readers know what was not covered. Cutting samples evenly also saves time, but it spreads the shortfall across high- and low-risk areas alike and leaves the riskiest conclusions thinly supported.

wrong_explanations.A: Reporting on half-finished work, with no substantive testing done, leaves the conclusions without sufficient evidence.
wrong_explanations.C: Uniform cuts are not risk-based; high-risk areas lose the same coverage as trivial ones, weakening the conclusions that matter most.
wrong_explanations.D: Management representations cannot replace substantive evidence; they are the weakest evidence type and test no transactions or balances.

tips: Eliminate: A reports without the substantive evidence still needed, and D substitutes representations for testing.
Final two: B beats C because risk-based reprioritization protects the riskiest conclusions, while even cuts thin every area equally.
Exam cue: when resources shrink, cut low-risk work first and disclose what was not covered.

questions.subtopic: Risk-Based Planning. Cyber-Incident Triggered Scope Expansion
questions.question: After a contained ransomware incident, the audit committee asks whether to add an incident-response audit; the IS audit team lacks incident-response expertise. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Decline, since the committee-approved annual plan cannot change mid-cycle
options.B: Add the audit and staff it with the existing internal team
options.C: Add the audit and co-source specialists with incident-response expertise
options.D: Rely on the incident team's own post-incident review report

questions.key_concept: Material incidents justify revising the audit plan; missing expertise is filled by specialists or co-sourcing, with the auditor retaining responsibility.
questions.pre_read: Two facts matter: a material incident changes risk, and the team lacks the skills. The best answer addresses both.
questions.correct_explanation: A material incident is a change in risk that justifies revising the audit plan, and the audit committee is asking for it. Because the team lacks incident-response skills, the director should bring in qualified specialists through co-sourcing while retaining responsibility for the work. Staffing it with the existing team adds the audit but without the proficiency needed to reach reliable conclusions.

wrong_explanations.A: Risk-based plans are meant to change when risk changes; a material incident is a classic reason to revise the plan.
wrong_explanations.B: Auditors must have the skills for the work they perform; an unskilled team risks missing the real control failures.
wrong_explanations.D: The incident team reviewing its own response lacks independence; its report is useful input, not audit assurance.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the approved plan as frozen, and D relies on the responders assessing themselves.
Final two: C beats B because proficiency is a precondition of audit work; co-sourcing fills the skill gap while the director keeps responsibility.
Exam cue: when the team lacks a skill, obtain it through specialists or co-sourcing rather than skipping the work or proceeding unskilled.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1206 (Using the Work of Other Experts); ITAF Performance Standards
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'cyber-incident triggered scope expansion - careful engagement design + co-sourcing for expertise + audit-committee brief + documented trigger'. Public source: ISACA Standards 1202 + 1206 + ITAF. All scenario specifics (healthcare insurer, ransomware on 15% of file shares, regulator notification) invented for this question. questions.subtopic: Audit Reporting. Special-Purpose Report (Regulatory Filing Support)
questions.question: A regulator requires an IT controls attestation, as of a specific date and in its own wording, that the annual IS audit report does not match. What is the IS auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Submit the annual report unchanged with a cover letter explaining differences
options.B: Reword the annual report to match the regulator's required attestation
options.C: Decline and refer the company to a different audit provider
options.D: Plan an engagement scoped to the regulator's criteria, date and wording

questions.key_concept: Special-purpose reports need engagements planned for the user's criteria, date and wording, with added procedures where existing work falls short.
questions.pre_read: Notice that both the date and the wording differ from the annual report. Ask what evidence the new attestation would need.
questions.correct_explanation: A special-purpose report must be backed by work designed for that purpose. The auditor should scope the engagement to the regulator's criteria and effective date, perform any procedures the annual audit did not cover, and then issue the required wording. Simply rewording the annual report would attest to things the evidence may not support, such as controls at the specific as-of date.

wrong_explanations.A: The annual report does not meet the regulator's criteria or date, so submitting it fails the stated requirement.
wrong_explanations.B: Rewording without extra procedures attests beyond the evidence; the annual work may not cover the required date or scope.
wrong_explanations.C: Declining is unnecessary; a properly planned special-purpose engagement can meet the requirement.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores the regulator's stated criteria, and C abandons a request that proper planning can meet.
Final two: D beats B because the attestation must rest on evidence gathered for that purpose; rewording only changes the label.
Exam cue: a report's wording can never claim more than the procedures performed support.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ITAF Performance Standards on Special-Purpose Reports; AICPA SSAE 18 / AT-C Section 205 (Examination Engagements) and the foundational AT-C Section 105

questions.subtopic: Audit QA. Repeat-Finding Pattern Across Years
questions.question: An IS audit director notes that the same access-review finding has recurred for three annual cycles despite management's remediation commitments each year. What is the BEST response?

options.A: Drop the finding, since management has already acknowledged it
options.B: Find the root cause and escalate to the audit committee
options.C: Downgrade its severity, since no loss has resulted so far
options.D: Reissue the finding with a firmer remediation deadline for management

questions.key_concept: Recurring findings signal remediation failure; analyze the root cause and escalate to the audit committee for accountability.
questions.pre_read: Notice the commitments were made and missed three times. Ask who can hold management accountable when its promises fail.
questions.correct_explanation: A finding that recurs despite repeated commitments is itself a signal: remediation is failing, and the risk management is carrying may not be what the board intended. The director should identify the root cause and escalate the pattern to the audit committee, which holds management accountable. Reissuing with a firmer deadline repeats the approach that has already failed three times.

wrong_explanations.A: Acknowledgement is not remediation. Silencing an unresolved finding hides a persistent weakness from governance.
wrong_explanations.C: Absence of loss so far does not reduce the underlying risk; severity reflects exposure, not luck.
wrong_explanations.D: A firmer deadline repeats the cycle that has already failed and leaves governance unaware of the pattern.

tips: Eliminate: A hides an unresolved weakness, and C lowers severity just because no loss has happened yet.
Final two: B beats D because repeated failure needs root-cause analysis and governance escalation, not another management deadline.
Exam cue: when management repeatedly fails to act, the auditor escalates to the audit committee rather than negotiating again.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1402 (Follow-up Activities); ITAF Performance Standards on Quality Assurance; IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 15.2 (Confirming the Implementation of Recommendations or Action Plans)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'repeat-finding pattern as analytical observation about remediation failure - investigate root cause + escalate + adjust audit handling, distinct from continue-mechanically / stop / re-classify'. Public source: ISACA Standard 1402 + IIA Standard 2500. All scenario specifics (credit-card processor, weak access-review documentation pattern across three years) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_015/078 (follow-up activities). Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Internal Audit Function. Conflict Between IIA Standards and ISACA ITAF
questions.question: An internal audit function committed to both IIA Standards and ITAF finds they set different cadences for documenting supervisory review. What is the audit director's BEST approach?

options.A: Apply the more rigorous requirement and document the difference
options.B: Follow the framework listed first in the audit charter
options.C: Replace both with a single internally written procedure
options.D: Apply the more lenient requirement, since either standard alone suffices

questions.key_concept: When committed standards differ, apply the more rigorous requirement, which satisfies both, and document the difference.
questions.pre_read: Notice the function is committed to both frameworks. Ask which option keeps both commitments at once.
questions.correct_explanation: When a function commits to two frameworks, it must meet both. Applying the more rigorous cadence satisfies the stricter standard and, by definition, the lenient one too; documenting the difference supports quality review. Following whichever framework the charter lists first sounds orderly, but it knowingly breaches the other commitment the function has made.

wrong_explanations.B: Charter order does not rank the standards; following one knowingly breaches the other commitment the function made.
wrong_explanations.C: Abandoning recognized standards for a home-grown procedure undermines conformance and the credibility of the function's work.
wrong_explanations.D: The lenient cadence breaches the stricter standard, so the function no longer conforms to both commitments.

tips: Eliminate: C abandons recognized standards, and D meets only the weaker requirement.
Final two: A beats B because the stricter requirement satisfies both frameworks; charter order does not excuse breaching one.
Exam cue: when two applicable requirements differ, meeting the stricter one usually satisfies both.
questions.framework_ref: IIA International Professional Practices Framework (IPPF); ISACA IT Audit and Assurance Standards / ITAF; ISACA Code of Professional Ethics; ITAF General Standards on Compliance with Multiple Frameworks
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'conflict between IIA Standards and ISACA ITAF - apply the more rigorous (conservative approach satisfies both), document, report, distinct from pick-lenient / abandon-both / favor-one-categorically'. Public source: IIA IPPF + ISACA ITAF. All scenario specifics (non-bank financial-services firm, dual-standard commitment, procedural-cadence conflict) invented for this question. questions.subtopic: Audit Reporting. Distribution and Restricted-Use Considerations
questions.question: An IS audit report on a government office's case system details access-control weaknesses that could be exploited. What is the MOST appropriate distribution approach for the IS auditor?

options.A: Circulate the full report to every staff member for transparency
options.B: Hold the report until the weaknesses are fully remediated
options.C: Restrict distribution to those who must act on it
options.D: Publish the full report online for external stakeholders

questions.key_concept: Report distribution follows need-to-know; sensitive findings carry restricted-use terms but still reach governance and responsible management.
questions.pre_read: Notice the weaknesses are exploitable but still open. Balance confidentiality against the need for someone to act.
questions.correct_explanation: Audit results must reach those accountable for acting on them, but exploitable detail should not spread further than necessary. Restricting the report to governance, responsible management and counsel, with restricted-use terms, achieves both. Holding the report until remediation sounds protective, but it denies management and the audit committee the information they need to fix and oversee the weaknesses.

wrong_explanations.A: Circulating exploitable details to every employee widens exposure without helping anyone remediate.
wrong_explanations.B: Delay keeps accountable managers and the audit committee uninformed, so the weaknesses may never be fixed.
wrong_explanations.D: Public posting hands attackers a roadmap to weaknesses that are still open.

tips: Eliminate: A and D spread exploitable details far beyond those who must act.
Final two: C beats B because results must reach the people accountable for fixing them; delay protects no one.
Exam cue: sensitive findings go to those who need to know, with restricted-use wording, not to everyone and not to no one.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ITAF Performance Standards on Communication of Results
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'audit-report distribution and restricted-use - need-to-know recipients plus restricted-use language plus sensitive-content protection, distinct from broad-distribution / withhold / public-posting'. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.question: An IS auditor plans to rely on an inventory report produced by the audited system. What is the MOST important step before relying on it?

options.A: Test controls over the report or independently reproduce it
options.B: Accept it, since the system produces it consistently each period
options.C: Obtain management's written confirmation that the report is accurate
options.D: Trace a sample of report lines to source records

questions.key_concept: System-generated evidence needs completeness and accuracy established, by testing generating controls or independent reproduction, before reliance.
questions.pre_read: Notice the report comes from the system under audit. Ask what could be wrong with it that a line-by-line check would miss.
questions.correct_explanation: Information produced by the audited system is only as reliable as the system and logic behind it. The auditor should establish completeness and accuracy by testing controls over the report's generation or by reproducing it independently. Tracing a sample of lines to source records checks accuracy, but it cannot reveal items the report omitted, so completeness remains untested.

wrong_explanations.B: Consistency is not accuracy; a flawed query or altered logic produces the same wrong report every time.
wrong_explanations.C: Management's confirmation is a representation from the audited party, not independent evidence of the report's reliability.
wrong_explanations.D: Tracing listed lines checks accuracy; it cannot detect records the report left out.

tips: Eliminate: B mistakes consistency for accuracy, and C relies on the audited party's own representation.
Final two: A beats D because reliance needs completeness and accuracy; tracing listed lines cannot detect omitted records.
Exam cue: before relying on a system-generated report, ask whether it is complete and accurate, and test from the population side too.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1205 (Evidence); ITAF Performance Standards on Evidence; ITAF Tools and Techniques on CAATs
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'computer-output evidence reliability - control-testing on generating system OR independent reproduction, distinct from face-value / management-attestation / categorical-rejection'. Distinct from d1_004/095/102/133/134 prior evidence questions. Exam-style v2 rewrite (Oct 2026): shortened to ISACA item format; scenario folded into a 1–2 sentence stem.

questions.subtopic: Continuous Auditing. Cost-Benefit Threshold for Deployment
questions.question: An IS audit director is deciding whether to deploy continuous auditing, costing $400K plus $80K yearly, in one business area. What should MOST influence the decision?

options.A: Whether continuous auditing is now standard practice in the industry
options.B: The area's risk and transaction volume weighed against total cost
options.C: The audit hours the tool would save versus its cost
options.D: The team's preference to avoid learning new analytical tools

questions.key_concept: Deploy continuous auditing where risk and transaction volume justify the total cost; efficiency gains are secondary to risk coverage.
questions.pre_read: Notice the large upfront and recurring cost. Ask what benefit would justify it in one specific area.
questions.correct_explanation: Continuous auditing pays off where risk is high and transaction volume is large, because ongoing analysis catches issues that periodic testing would miss. The director should weigh that risk coverage against deployment and running costs over a defensible horizon. Audit hours saved are a real benefit, but judging only by efficiency ignores the main value: earlier detection in high-risk areas.

wrong_explanations.A: Industry popularity does not show the deployment fits this area's risk or justifies its cost.
wrong_explanations.C: Hours saved are one benefit, but valuing efficiency alone ignores the assurance and early detection that justify the investment.
wrong_explanations.D: Team comfort is not a risk-based criterion; skills gaps are addressed through training, not by avoiding tools.

tips: Eliminate: A follows industry fashion, and D lets team comfort override risk.
Final two: B beats C because continuous auditing earns its cost through risk coverage at volume; saved hours are only part of the benefit.
Exam cue: audit investment decisions are risk-driven first; efficiency is a secondary benefit.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Continuous Auditing; ITAF Tools and Techniques on CAATs
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'CA cost-benefit threshold for deployment - risk + volume + anomaly value + audit-effort substitution evaluated against deployment + ongoing costs over time horizon, distinct from universal / low-risk-only / skip-CA'. Public source: ITAF Tools and Techniques on Continuous Auditing. All scenario specifics (agricultural cooperative, $400K + $80K/year deployment costs) invented for this question. questions.question: Management plans to delete a retired AI forecasting model and its data once the replacement goes live. What should the IS auditor be MOST concerned about?

options.A: Higher licensing costs for the replacement model's vendor platform
options.B: User resistance to forecasts produced by the new model
options.C: Whether the replacement model was validated before going live
options.D: Loss of records needed to explain past model decisions

questions.key_concept: Retiring an AI model must preserve evidence (version, data lineage, decision logs) so past production decisions can be reconstructed.
questions.pre_read: Notice management plans to delete the old model and its data. Ask what could no longer be explained afterwards.
questions.correct_explanation: Deleting the retired model and its data destroys the evidence needed to explain decisions it made in production, which regulators, litigants or auditors may later question. Retirement should preserve the model version, data lineage and decision logs under the retention policy. Validating the replacement matters, but it is a go-live control; the irreversible risk in the stem is losing the old model's record.

wrong_explanations.A: Licensing cost is a business consideration, not an audit risk created by deleting the old model's evidence.
wrong_explanations.B: User acceptance is a change-management concern and does not address the loss of decision records.
wrong_explanations.C: Validation is a go-live control for the new model; it does not preserve the retired model's decision history.

tips: Eliminate: A is a cost issue and B a change-management issue; neither addresses the planned deletion.
Final two: D beats C because deletion is irreversible and destroys accountability for past decisions; validation concerns the new model.
Exam cue: when anything is retired or decommissioned, ask first what records must survive it.

Public source: ISACA Auditing AI program + NIST AI RMF + ISACA Standard 1208. All scenario specifics (home-improvement retail chain, demand-forecasting model retirement) invented for this question. questions.subtopic: Audit Programs. Tools and Techniques Template Adaptation
questions.question: An IS audit manager wants to use a generic ITAF audit program template for a fintech's deposit account-opening workflow. What is the MOST important consideration?

options.A: Use the template unchanged, since ITAF templates are authoritative
options.B: Append fintech-specific steps but leave the original template steps unchanged
options.C: Tailor its procedures to the workflow's risks and document changes
options.D: Discard it and write a custom program from scratch

questions.key_concept: Audit program templates are adapted to engagement-specific risks and controls, keeping their structure and documenting each change.
questions.pre_read: Notice the template is generic and the workflow is specialised. Ask whether the program's procedures fit the actual controls.
questions.correct_explanation: Templates provide structure, not a finished program. The manager should keep the template's objectives and evidence discipline but tailor each procedure to the workflow's actual risks and controls, such as partner-bank identity checks, and document why. Appending fintech steps looks efficient, but the original steps stay untailored, so some test controls that do not exist while real risks stay under-tested.

wrong_explanations.A: Templates are generic starting points; using one unchanged tests controls the engagement may lack and misses its specific risks.
wrong_explanations.B: Appending steps leaves generic procedures untailored, wasting effort on irrelevant tests and under-testing the real controls.
wrong_explanations.D: Discarding the template loses proven structure and consistency; adapting it is more efficient and defensible.

tips: Eliminate: A treats a generic template as finished, and D throws away useful structure.
Final two: C beats B because every procedure must fit the engagement's risks; bolting on extra steps leaves the generic ones untailored.
Exam cue: standard tools and templates are adapted to the engagement's risks, never applied blindly or discarded.
questions.framework_ref: ITAF Tools and Techniques (Information Technology Assurance Framework); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Engagement Planning); FinCEN regulations 31 CFR Part 1020 (KYC/CIP for financial institutions)

questions.subtopic: Risk Assessment. Quantifying Intangible Risks (Reputation, Brand)
questions.question: A film studio's risk assessment ranks risks by estimated financial loss. How should the IS auditor BEST treat intangible risks such as brand damage from a content leak?

options.A: Exclude them, since they cannot be measured in money
options.B: Rate them qualitatively on a separate list from the financial ranking
options.C: Assign each the same high placeholder value to stay cautious
options.D: Estimate financial impact from indirect indicators, stating the assumptions

questions.key_concept: Intangible risks are quantified through indirect indicators and stated assumptions so they can be prioritized alongside tangible risks.
questions.pre_read: Notice the assessment ranks by financial loss. Ask how a brand risk can compete fairly in that ranking.
questions.correct_explanation: Intangible risks can still be translated into financial terms using indirect indicators, such as peer incident costs, customer churn or replacement costs, with likelihood ranges and assumptions stated. That places them on the same scale as other risks so they rank fairly. A separate qualitative rating is legitimate in general, but here it keeps the most strategic risks out of the ranking decision-makers will use.

wrong_explanations.A: Excluding hard-to-measure risks leaves material exposures out of the assessment; difficulty of measurement is not absence of risk.
wrong_explanations.B: A separate qualitative list cannot be compared with the financial ranking, so intangible risks lose out in prioritization.
wrong_explanations.C: A uniform placeholder ignores real differences in impact and makes the ranking arbitrary.

tips: Eliminate: A drops material risks because they are hard to measure, and C assigns arbitrary identical values.
Final two: D beats B because the assessment ranks by financial loss; indirect estimates let intangibles compete on the same scale.
Exam cue: hard to measure does not mean unmeasurable; estimate with stated assumptions rather than exclude or guess.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA Risk IT Framework; ISO/IEC 31000:2018 (Risk Management); FAIR (Factor Analysis of Information Risk); ITAF Performance Standards on Risk Assessment
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'intangible risk quantification - indirect indicators + documented assumptions + qualitative layering, distinct from decline / $0-default / arbitrary-uniform'. questions.subtopic: Audit Engagement. Three-Way Coordination (Internal, External, Regulator)
questions.question: Internal audit, the external auditor and a certification assessor are all testing overlapping cybersecurity controls this year. What is the BEST coordination approach for the IS audit director?

options.A: Share test plans through agreed protocols while each reports independently
options.B: Avoid any contact so each party's independence stays protected
options.C: Cancel internal audit's overlapping work and rely on the assessor's results
options.D: Have the other two parties rely on internal audit's testing

questions.key_concept: Multiple assurance providers coordinate plans through agreed protocols while each preserves its own reporting line and conclusions.
questions.pre_read: Notice three parties serve different stakeholders. Ask how to reduce overlap without anyone giving up independent judgment.
questions.correct_explanation: Coordination improves coverage and avoids duplicated effort, and it does not impair independence when each party keeps its own reporting line and conclusions. Sharing test plans and timing through agreed, authorized protocols achieves both. Having the others rely on internal audit sounds efficient, but the external auditor and assessor must decide for themselves whether and how far to use others' work.

wrong_explanations.B: Independence comes from reporting lines and objectivity, not isolation; refusing coordination wastes effort and leaves gaps.
wrong_explanations.C: The assessor serves a different stakeholder and objective; cancelling internal audit's work leaves the board without its own assurance.
wrong_explanations.D: Each assurance provider decides its own reliance on others' work; internal audit cannot impose it.

tips: Eliminate: B confuses isolation with independence, and C drops internal audit's assurance to the board.
Final two: A beats D because coordination keeps each party's conclusions independent; reliance on others' work is each provider's own decision.
Exam cue: coordinate with other assurance providers to share coverage, but each keeps its own conclusions and reporting line.

questions.question: Midway through a substantive sample designed at 95% confidence, the audit committee asks the IS auditor to provide 99% confidence. What is the auditor's BEST response?

options.A: Decline, since sample design cannot change once fieldwork begins
options.B: Enlarge the sample and agree the extra cost
options.C: Restate the existing results as 99% confidence without changes
options.D: Add analytical procedures rather than selecting more sample items

questions.key_concept: Raising the confidence level increases the required sample size; the auditor expands the sample and communicates the resource impact.
questions.pre_read: Notice the sample was designed at 95%. Ask what must change in the design to support a 99% conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: Confidence level is a sample-design input: raising it from 95% to 99% increases the required sample size for the same tolerable misstatement. The auditor should enlarge the sample, agree the time and cost impact with the committee, and evaluate results at the new level. Analytical procedures add useful evidence, but they do not raise the statistical confidence of the sample conclusion.

wrong_explanations.A: Design can be revised mid-engagement when needs change, provided the change is documented and the sample re-planned.
wrong_explanations.C: At 99% the same sample gives a wider precision interval; simply relabeling the results overstates what the evidence supports.
wrong_explanations.D: Analytics complement the sample but do not change its statistical confidence, so the stated 99% would be unsupported.

tips: Eliminate: A treats the design as frozen, and C relabels unchanged results with a stronger claim.
Final two: B beats D because higher confidence comes from a larger sample; analytics add evidence but do not raise statistical confidence.
Exam cue: higher confidence or lower tolerable error means a larger sample; know which way each parameter pushes size.

questions.question: A hospital's IS audit director is preparing the annual audit plan, where HIPAA, reimbursement audits and healthcare-targeted ransomware are major risk drivers. What is the BEST planning approach?

options.A: Use a generic risk-based plan that ignores sector-specific drivers
options.B: Build the plan around the sector's regulatory examination calendar
options.C: Apply the risk-based method, weighting sector-specific drivers
options.D: Run separate generic and sector plans as parallel audit programs

questions.key_concept: Sector-specific drivers are inputs to one risk-based audit plan, weighting likelihood, impact and cadence; they do not replace the method.
questions.pre_read: Notice several sector-specific pressures. Ask whether they replace the risk-based method or feed into it.
questions.correct_explanation: Risk-based planning is the method; sector drivers are inputs that change likelihood and impact scores. The director should keep one risk-based plan and weight in healthcare-specific risks, frameworks and cadences. Building the plan around the regulatory examination calendar sounds sector-aware, but it lets compliance timing, not relative risk, decide what is audited and underweights risks such as ransomware.

wrong_explanations.A: Ignoring sector drivers misstates likelihood and impact, so the plan under-covers the risks that matter most to a hospital.
wrong_explanations.B: Calendar-driven planning lets examination timing, not relative risk, set priorities, underweighting risks no regulator is examining.
wrong_explanations.D: Two parallel plans duplicate effort and cannot rank sector and general risks against each other.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores the sector's risks, and D duplicates effort in two plans that cannot be ranked together.
Final two: C beats B because the plan must stay risk-based; a regulatory calendar sets priorities by timing, not by risk.
Exam cue: industry context feeds the risk assessment; it never replaces the risk-based method.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1202 (Risk Assessment in Planning); ITAF Performance Standards on Audit Planning; HITRUST CSF (Common Security Framework); HIPAA Security Rule (45 CFR Part 164)

questions.subtopic: Audit Phases. Engagement-Conclusion Synthesis with Limitation Disclosure
questions.question: At engagement close, a vendor has refused logs for one module and management disputes one finding; other work is complete. How should the IS auditor BEST frame the conclusion?

options.A: Issue an unqualified conclusion, since management has committed to remediation
options.B: Disclaim a conclusion on the whole engagement due to the limitation
options.C: Drop the disputed finding so the report reflects agreed positions
options.D: Conclude overall, disclosing the module's limitation and management's dispute

questions.key_concept: Report conclusions disclose confined scope limitations and record management's disputed responses; disclaimers suit pervasive limitations.
questions.pre_read: Notice the limitation affects one module only. Ask how far it should reach into the overall conclusion.
questions.correct_explanation: The report should give the auditor's overall conclusion while transparently disclosing what limits it: the specific module that could not be audited, and management's disagreement alongside the auditor's position. A disclaimer over the whole engagement overreacts, since the limitation is confined to one module and the rest of the work supports a conclusion. Readers need both the conclusion and its boundaries.

wrong_explanations.A: Remediation commitments do not erase findings or the scope limitation; an unqualified conclusion would mislead readers.
wrong_explanations.B: A disclaimer suits a pervasive limitation; here it affects one module, so it discards supportable conclusions on the rest.
wrong_explanations.C: Disputed findings stay in the report with management's response; dropping them compromises the auditor's independence.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores both the findings and the limitation, and C lets management's disagreement remove a finding.
Final two: D beats B because the limitation is confined to one module; disclose it rather than disclaiming work that was completed.
Exam cue: match the response to the limitation's reach; confined issues are disclosed, pervasive ones may prevent a conclusion.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA IT Audit Standard 1401 (Reporting); ISACA IT Audit Standard 1201 (Engagement Planning); Standard 1203 (Performance and Supervision); ITAF Performance Standards on Communication of Results
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'end-to-end engagement-conclusion synthesis - overall conclusion + severity-tiered findings + scope-limitation disclosure + management response + traceability, distinct from unmodified-when-warranted-modified / disclaimer-overuse / omit-limitations'. Public source: ISACA Standards 1201/1203/1401 + ITAF. All scenario specifics (nonprofit-housing cooperative, tenant-services audit, three engagement-level facts) invented for this question. Distinct from d1_036/109/150/168 prior reporting and synthesis questions. THIS IS THE FINAL D1 QUESTION (d1_180/180). questions.question: An experienced IS audit manager signs off an audit report without reviewing working papers that contained obvious errors. Which ITAF general-standard requirement does this MOST directly breach?

options.A: Exercising the diligence expected of a reasonable practitioner
options.B: Possessing the knowledge and skills the engagement requires
options.C: Keeping the audit function free from organizational interference
options.D: Defining audit authority and accountability in an approved charter

questions.key_concept: ITAF Standard 1005 (Due Professional Care) requires the diligence of a reasonable practitioner, including proper review before sign-off.
questions.pre_read: Notice the manager is experienced. Ask whether the failure was a lack of skill or a lack of diligence.
questions.correct_explanation: ITAF Standard 1005 (Due Professional Care) requires the diligence a reasonable practitioner would apply, including review before conclusions are issued. Signing off without reviewing flawed working papers is a lapse of diligence. Proficiency (Standard 1006) is the close alternative, but the manager is experienced: the skills existed and simply were not applied, which is the essence of a due-care failure.

wrong_explanations.B: Proficiency concerns having adequate knowledge and skills. The manager is experienced, so the failure lies in applying them.
wrong_explanations.C: Organizational independence concerns freedom from interference; nothing in the stem suggests anyone pressured the manager.
wrong_explanations.D: The audit charter defines the function's authority and scope; skipping a review does not breach the charter itself.

tips: Eliminate: C concerns interference, which the stem does not mention, and D concerns the function's mandate, not engagement conduct.
Final two: A beats B because the manager had the skills but failed to apply them; that is a due-care lapse, not a proficiency gap.
Exam cue: 'could not do it' points to proficiency; 'could but did not' points to due professional care.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA ITAF 4th Edition, General Standard 1005 (Due Professional Care)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'ITAF general standard purposes — Due Professional Care (1005)'. questions.subtopic: IIA International Standards. Independence and Objectivity
questions.question: A chief audit executive reporting to the board assigns an IS auditor to review a process the auditor managed until last month. What is the GREATEST concern?

options.A: The auditor lacks the proficiency to assess the process
options.B: The audit function's organizational independence is impaired
options.C: The assigned auditor's individual objectivity is impaired
options.D: The audit charter may not cover the process

questions.key_concept: The audit function must be organizationally independent, and each auditor must be individually objective; self-review impairs the individual, not the function.
questions.pre_read: Notice the reporting line is sound. Ask whether the problem lies with the function or with the person assigned.
questions.correct_explanation: Professional standards separate two ideas: the audit function's organizational independence and each auditor's individual objectivity. Here the chief audit executive reports to the board, so the function's independence holds. The problem sits with the individual: reviewing a process one managed until last month is a self-review threat, which impairs that auditor's objectivity. Reassigning the engagement resolves it without any structural change.

wrong_explanations.A: Having managed the process, the auditor likely knows it well; the stem raises no doubt about competence.
wrong_explanations.B: Reporting to the board keeps the audit function organizationally independent; the impairment lies with the individual auditor.
wrong_explanations.D: Charter coverage concerns the function's mandate; it does not address the self-review created by this assignment.

tips: Eliminate: A raises competence, which the stem does not question, and D concerns the charter's mandate, not this assignment.
Final two: C beats B because the reporting line keeps the function independent; reviewing one's own recent work impairs the individual's objectivity.
Exam cue: independence belongs to the function's position; objectivity belongs to the individual's state of mind.
questions.framework_ref: IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 2.1 (Individual Objectivity); IIA Global Internal Audit Standards (2024), Standard 7.1 (Organizational Independence)
questions._provenance: Authored from concept: 'IIA International Standard 1100 Independence and Objectivity'. questions.question: An IS auditor has collected hundreds of system screenshots, but none relate to the control objective being tested. What is the MOST significant weakness in this evidence?

options.A: There is too little of it to support a conclusion
options.B: It was not retained for the required retention period
options.C: Screenshots can be altered, so it lacks reliability
options.D: It lacks relevance, so it is not appropriate evidence

questions.key_concept: Sufficiency is the quantity of evidence; appropriateness is its quality, comprising relevance and reliability.
questions.pre_read: Notice the volume is large but unrelated to the objective. Ask which evidence attribute fails first.
questions.correct_explanation: Appropriateness is evidence quality, made up of relevance and reliability; sufficiency is quantity. Evidence that does not relate to the control objective is not relevant, so it is not appropriate, and no volume can make up for that. Screenshots can be less reliable, but reliability only matters once evidence is relevant; here relevance fails first and is decisive.

wrong_explanations.A: Hundreds of items is ample quantity; the problem is quality, since more irrelevant evidence never becomes sufficient.
wrong_explanations.B: Retention concerns documentation after the audit; it does not explain why this evidence fails to support the objective.
wrong_explanations.C: Reliability matters only once evidence is relevant; screenshots unrelated to the objective fail before reliability is considered.

tips: Eliminate: A ignores that hundreds of items were collected, and B is a documentation-retention issue.
Final two: D beats C because evidence must first be relevant to the objective; reliability is weighed only after relevance is met.
Exam cue: sufficiency is how much; appropriateness is how good, meaning relevant first, then reliable.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA ITAF Performance Standard 1205 (Evidence); AICPA AU-C 500 (Audit Evidence)

questions.question: An IS auditor must test whether duplicate vendor payments occurred among two million transactions. What is the PRIMARY benefit of using CAATs for this test?

options.A: Monitoring payments continuously in real time for management
options.B: Testing the entire payment population efficiently for duplicates
options.C: Replacing the auditor's judgment on which exceptions matter
options.D: Generating the final audit report automatically from results

questions.key_concept: CAATs let auditors extract, analyze and test electronic data efficiently, often covering entire populations rather than samples.
questions.pre_read: Notice the volume and the single, well-defined pattern to find. Ask what software changes about coverage.
questions.correct_explanation: CAATs let auditors extract and analyze electronic data directly, so a duplicate-payment test can cover all two million transactions quickly instead of a small sample. That gives stronger evidence at lower effort. Continuous real-time monitoring is a related use of similar tools, but it is a management or continuous-auditing activity, not the purpose of this one-off audit test.

wrong_explanations.A: Real-time monitoring is an ongoing management or continuous-auditing activity; the stem describes a single audit test.
wrong_explanations.C: CAATs flag exceptions; the auditor still judges which matter and what they mean.
wrong_explanations.D: Reporting is an auditor judgment task; CAATs produce evidence, not the audit report.

tips: Eliminate: C hands judgment to software, and D confuses evidence gathering with reporting.
Final two: B beats A because the stem is a one-off audit test where CAATs cover the whole population; ongoing monitoring is management's function.
Exam cue: large data volume plus a specific pattern to find points to CAATs analyzing the full population.
questions.framework_ref: ISACA ITAF 4th Edition Tools and Techniques (Use of CAATs); ISACA CISA Review Manual, Domain 1 — Use of CAATs

questions.subtopic: SOC Report Types. SOC 1 vs SOC 2 vs SOC 3
questions.key_concept: SOC 1 covers controls relevant to user entities' financial reporting; SOC 2 covers Trust Services Criteria; SOC 3 summarizes SOC 2 publicly.
questions.framework_ref: AICPA SSAE 18; AICPA Trust Services Criteria (TSC 2017, revised); AICPA SOC for Service Organizations framework
questions.question: An IS auditor is relying on an outsourced payroll processor whose output feeds the client's financial statements. Which service organization report is MOST appropriate?

options.A: The provider's SOC 3 general-use seal report
options.B: A SOC 2 report on the Trust Services Criteria
options.C: A SOC 1 report from the service auditor
options.D: The provider's internal audit report on IT controls

questions.correct_explanation: SOC 1 reports address a service organization's controls relevant to user entities' internal control over financial reporting, which is exactly the assurance requested. SOC 2 reports address the Trust Services Criteria such as security and availability; they cover IT controls but are not designed around financial reporting. Matching the report's subject matter to the audit objective is the deciding factor.

wrong_explanations.A: SOC 3 is a brief general-use summary of SOC 2 work. It lacks control detail and does not target financial reporting.
wrong_explanations.B: SOC 2 covers security and related criteria. It is relevant to IT risk but not designed for financial reporting reliance.
wrong_explanations.D: Internal audit reports are not independent attestations prepared for user entities and may not be shareable or reliable for this purpose.

tips: Eliminate: A is only a high-level summary, and D lacks the independent attestation that user auditors rely on.
Final two: C beats B because the objective is financial reporting; SOC 2 addresses security-type criteria, not reporting controls.
Exam cue: financial statements point to SOC 1; security, availability or privacy point to SOC 2; a public summary is SOC 3.
questions.pre_read: Notice the output feeds financial statements. Match the report's subject matter to that objective, not to IT security generally.

questions.question: An IS auditor wants to estimate the percentage of change requests deployed without approval. Which sampling approach is MOST appropriate?

options.A: Attribute sampling to estimate the deviation rate
options.B: Discovery sampling to find at least one unapproved change
options.C: Variable sampling of the changes' recorded monetary values
options.D: Convenience selection of the most recent changes

questions.key_concept: Attribute sampling estimates the rate of a characteristic, typically control deviations; variable sampling estimates monetary amounts.
questions.pre_read: Notice the objective is a percentage of changes. Ask whether you need a rate, an amount or just one example.
questions.correct_explanation: Attribute sampling estimates how often a characteristic occurs, such as the rate of changes deployed without approval, which is exactly the objective. Variable sampling estimates monetary amounts instead. Discovery sampling is the close alternative: it belongs to the attribute family but is designed to find at least one occurrence when the expected rate is near zero, not to estimate a percentage.

wrong_explanations.B: Discovery sampling answers whether any deviation exists; it is not designed to estimate the deviation rate the auditor needs.
wrong_explanations.C: Variable sampling estimates monetary amounts; the objective here is a rate of occurrence, not a value.
wrong_explanations.D: Convenience selection is not statistical and is biased toward recent changes, so it cannot support a population rate estimate.

tips: Eliminate: C measures monetary values, not a rate, and D is a biased, non-statistical selection.
Final two: A beats B because the objective is estimating a rate; discovery sampling only shows whether at least one deviation exists.
Exam cue: 'how often' means attribute sampling; 'how much' means variable sampling; 'is there any' means discovery sampling.
questions.framework_ref: AICPA AU-C 530 (Audit Sampling); ISACA ITAF 4th Edition Tools and Techniques (Audit Sampling)
